[FARRA:v1p1#2/r1] FARRA, d. 207 · القراء | reports | Reciters and codex scribes omit the alif in the familiar basmala because its meaning is obvious and Arabic usage favors brevity in repeated, familiar expressions.
[FARRA:v1p1#2/r2] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | They retain the alif in “fa-sabbih bi-ismi rabbika” because this name is not used with the preposition as frequently as Allah’s name. | mentions 87:1
[FARRA:v1p1#2/r3] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | Do not omit the alif of ism with a name other than Allah or with a preposition other than bi; lām and kāf do not follow this spelling convention.
[FARRA:v1p1#2/r4] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | Arabic speakers shorten frequent expressions even more, as in “aysh ʿindak” and the altered form of shayʾ.
[FARRA:v1p1#2/r5] FARRA, d. 207 · author | rejects | The claim that alif was dropped because bāʾ cannot be paused on is disproved by other non-pauseable letters that Arabs still write in similar forms.
[MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r1] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Al-Fātiḥa is Umm al-Kitāb because it is written first in codices and recited before every other surah in prayer.
[MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r2] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Unhamzated sūra derives from the tiers of a building, one level after another.
[MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r3] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | reports | Those who hamza sūra take it as a piece of the Qur’an; a surah is cut off from another, and joined surahs make the Qur’an.
[MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r4] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Al-Nābigha’s verse uses sūra to mean rank or status.
[MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r5] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | reports | Some Arabs hamza sūra and associate it with asʾartu, while the source distinguishes that form from this word.
[MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r6] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | The verb before bi-smi Allāh is elliptical: the sense is to begin in God’s name before everything and as the first thing.
[MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r7] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Ibn Rawāḥa’s verse witnesses بدينا as a form of بدأنا; بدأنا and بديت are both used, with بدينا noted as a dialect form.
[AKHFASH:v1p3#2/r1] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | In the basmala, ism is an added connective that shifts the phrase from the force of an oath to seeking blessing; the underlying wording is billāh.
[AKHFASH:v1p3#2/r2] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The alif is omitted in writing bism because the phrase is frequent and the prefixed bāʾ already supplies the linkage; it remains in bismi al-Raḥmān and similar phrases.
[AKHFASH:v1p3#2/r3] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The initial alif in ism is hamzat waṣl: the form sumayy shows that it is not pronounced and is dropped.
[AKHFASH:v1p3#2/r4] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | Hamzat waṣl is supplied to let speech begin despite an initial sukūn, then becomes unnecessary when the word is joined to what precedes it. | mentions 5:12, 2:60, 36:14, 19:28, 111:4
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p38/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | The basmala is an ellipsis meaning “I begin in the name of God” or “I began in the name of God.”
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p157/r18] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abu Ubayda says the word اسم is added in بسم الله, whose intended meaning is بالله.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p24/r8] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · ابن مسعود | reports | The critics say Ibn Masʿūd's codex differed from others, omitted the Opening, and erased the two protective sūras, which he denied belonged in the Book.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p34/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · أبي | reports | The author's father thought the regular qunut supplication was Quran because he saw the Prophet repeat it in prayer, and held to this despite the Companions' disagreement.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p34/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | rejects | Ibn Qutayba doubts the report that Abdullah omitted Fatiha from his codex and says no Muslim should infer that this learned, Quran-devoted Companion did not know it was Quran.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p34/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · النبي | reports | The Prophet praised Abdullah's recitation, telling people who wanted the Quran fresh as revealed to follow Ibn Umm ʿAbd's reading.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p34/r4] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · عمر | reports | Umar described Abdullah as a container filled with knowledge, supporting Ibn Qutayba's case for his learning.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p34/r5] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · النبي | reports | The Prophet's statement لا صلاة إلا بسورة الحمد supports Fatiha's indispensable place in prayer.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p34/r6] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | Fatiha is the seven oft-repeated and Mother of the Book, meaning its greatest and earliest part; Mecca is similarly called Mother of Villages because it is oldest. | mentions 3:96
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p34/r7] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · أهل النظر | reports | The theorists explain that Abdullah did not write Fatiha because compilation guarded against doubt, forgetting, additions, and omissions, while it was short and repeated every prayer and rakʿa.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p34/r8] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | Ibn Qutayba concludes that Abdullah knew Fatiha was Quran but saw no need to write it, since no Muslim could neglect learning it or praying with it.
[TUSTARI:1:1/r1] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Sahl assigns the letters of basmala to the majesty, radiance, and glory of God.
[TUSTARI:1:1/r2] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Allah is the greatest name encompassing all names; its veiled inner reality is accessible only to the purified who live on lawful sustenance through faith.
[TUSTARI:1:1/r3] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Al-Rahman has a distinctive connection to the veiled letter between alif and lam.
[TUSTARI:1:1/r4] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Al-Rahim shows mercy through provision in descendants and origin, in accordance with God's prior eternal knowledge.
[TUSTARI:1:1/r5] TUSTARI, d. 283 · أبو بكر | reports | Abu Bakr says God creates from the breath of His spirit whatever He wills in His kingdom as mercy because He is merciful.
[TUSTARI:1:1/r6] TUSTARI, d. 283 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | Ali says the two tender names differ in tenderness and remove despair from God's believing servants.
[TAB:1:1/r1] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī identifies al-Fātiḥa as a Meccan sūra consisting of seven verses.
[TAB:1:1/r10] TAB, d. 310 · عُظْم أهل الكوفة | reports | Most Kufan authorities count the basmala as one of al-Fātiḥa’s seven verses; this view is also transmitted from a group of Companions and Successors.
[TAB:1:1/r11] TAB, d. 310 · عظم قرأة أهل المدينة ومتقنيهم | reports | Most leading Medinan reciters exclude the basmala from the seven and count “those You favored” as the seventh verse.
[TAB:1:1/r12] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī says he has treated the correct count elsewhere and will give the full disagreement in another legal work, without resolving it in this passage.
[TAB:1:1/r13] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The seven are “oft-repeated” because al-Fātiḥa is recited in every prayer, obligatory or voluntary. | mentions 15:87
[TAB:1:1/r14] TAB, d. 310 · الحسن البصري | reports | Al-Ḥasan identifies the seven oft-repeated verses as al-Fātiḥa and explains that it is repeated in every recitation—or, as the narrator hesitates, every prayer. | mentions 15:87
[TAB:1:1/r15] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Abū al-Najm’s verse pairs al-Fātiḥa’s praise with the Qurʾān and the “oft-repeated,” supporting the name’s association with al-Fātiḥa.
[TAB:1:1/r16] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | An anonymous rajaz verse likewise calls the Mother of the Book seven oft-repeated verses, describing them as doubled from the Qurʾān’s verses.
[TAB:1:1/r17] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Calling al-Fātiḥa the seven oft-repeated does not prevent the whole Qurʾān, or the sūras following the hundred-verse group, from also being called “mathānī” for another understood reason.
[TAB:1:1/r18] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | “Seeking refuge” means seeking protection or asylum.
[TAB:1:1/r19] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The refuge formula means asking God alone to protect one from Satan harming one’s religion or diverting one from a duty owed to the Lord.
[TAB:1:1/r2] TAB, d. 310 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Al-Ṭabarī calls the report sound: the Prophet names al-Fātiḥa the Mother of the Qurʾān, the Opening of the Book, and the seven oft-repeated verses.
[TAB:1:1/r20] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | In Arabic, “Satan” can mean any rebellious being among jinn, humans, animals, or anything else; the Qurʾān accordingly speaks of human and jinn satans. | mentions 6:112
[TAB:1:1/r21] TAB, d. 310 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | When a bucking barẕawn kept prancing despite ʿUmar’s blows, he dismounted and called it a satan that had made him lose himself.
[TAB:1:1/r22] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | A rebel is called a satan for departing from its kind’s usual character and deeds and for being far from good; another proposed derivation connects the word with “being distant.”
[TAB:1:1/r23] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Nābigha’s “shatūn” means distant, supporting a derivation of “Satan” as fayʿāl from shatana.
[TAB:1:1/r24] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt’s “shāṭin” supports shatana yashṭunu; if the word came from shāṭa yashīṭ, the form would be “shāʾiṭ.”
[TAB:1:1/r25] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | “Rajīm” is a passive faʿīl form meaning accursed or reviled; “stoning” can be verbal abuse or physical throwing.
[TAB:1:1/r26] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Abraham’s father uses “stone you” as a verbal threat, illustrating that rajm can be done with speech. | mentions 19:46
[TAB:1:1/r27] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Satan may also be called “the stoned” because God expelled him from heaven and pelted him with piercing meteors.
[TAB:1:1/r28] TAB, d. 310 · عبد الله بن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās reports that Gabriel first taught Muhammad to seek

refuge, then say the basmala, then recite 96:1; Ibn ʿAbbās calls this the first sūra revealed through Gabriel. | mentions 96:1
[TAB:1:1/r29] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | God taught the Prophet to put His beautiful names before all actions and made this instruction a practice for everyone beginning speech, letters, books, or needs.
[TAB:1:1/r3] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | It is called the Opening of the Book because it begins written Qurʾāns and is recited in prayers, opening the following sūras in writing and recitation.
[TAB:1:1/r30] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The preposition bāʾ requires a governing verb, omitted here; the listener supplies it from the act underway, just as an answer like “food” can omit an already evident verb.
[TAB:1:1/r31] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Before reciting, standing, sitting, or another action, the phrase means beginning that act by naming and remembering God.
[TAB:1:1/r32] TAB, d. 310 · عبد الله بن عباس | reports | In Ibn ʿAbbās’s report, Gabriel glosses the basmala as reading, standing, and sitting in remembrance of God.
[TAB:1:1/r33] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī rejects construing the phrase as “by God” in every act: it means beginning with God’s naming and remembrance, not claiming that an action is performed by God.
[TAB:1:1/r34] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The scholarly consensus that saying “by God” at slaughter does not fulfill the prescribed “in the name of God” supports his distinction between the formula and “by God.”
[TAB:1:1/r35] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Here “name” stands for “naming”: Arabic often uses a verbal noun in a form different from its regular pattern, as in karāmah for ikrām and kalām for taklīm.
[TAB:1:1/r36] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Poetic examples use ʿaṭāʾ for iʿṭāʾ, ṭawl for iṭāla, and muṣāba for iṣāba, supporting the unusual verbal-noun form in the basmala.
[TAB:1:1/r37] TAB, d. 310 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | rejects | A report has Jesus explain the letters of “bism” as God’s glory, splendor, and kingdom; al-Ṭabarī suspects a transmitter’s error and thinks separate alphabet letters may have been run together, since the gloss makes no sense in the full basmala.
[TAB:1:1/r38] TAB, d. 310 · مقدم في العلم بلغة العرب | rejects | An unnamed authority in Arabic usage reads Lubayd’s “then the name of peace be upon you” as simply “then peace be upon you”; al-Ṭabarī rejects that reading as linguistically unsound.
[TAB:1:1/r39] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | If “name” could simply mean its referent, Arabic would also permit “I ate the name of honey”; the unanimous rejection of such usage undermines that reading of Lubayd.
[TAB:1:1/r4] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | It is the Mother of the Qurʾān because it precedes the other sūras in reading and writing, while they follow it.
[TAB:1:1/r40] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī’s likelier reading of Lubayd is an exhortation to keep God’s name and remembrance after a delayed exhortative word, while leaving off remembering and grieving for the dead.
[TAB:1:1/r41] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | A second possible reading of Lubayd invokes God’s name for protection over the two people.
[TAB:1:1/r42] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | To support the delayed exhortation reading, al-Ṭabarī cites Arabic word order that places the thing urged before the delayed “take it” command.
[TAB:1:1/r43] TAB, d. 310 · عبد الله بن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās explains Allah as the one worshipped by every thing and served by all creation.
[TAB:1:1/r44] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī derives Allah from al-ilāh by inference rather than direct attestation; ilāh means the worshipped one, supported by Arab use of taʾallaha for worship and seeking God.
[TAB:1:1/r45] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Ruʾba’s “min taʾalluhī” means devotion and seeking God through worship, showing the root’s sense.
[TAB:1:1/r46] TAB, d. 310 · ابن عباس ومجاهد | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAbd Allāh, and Mujāhid read “wa-ilāhataka” at 7:127 as “your worship”; Pharaoh was worshipped rather than worshipping. | mentions 7:127
[TAB:1:1/r47] TAB, d. 310 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report attributed to the Prophet has Jesus gloss Allah as “the god of gods,” which al-Ṭabarī uses in explaining how God is worshipped by the servant and worships the servant in the stated idiom.
[TAB:1:1/r48] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Allah’s form comes from al-ilāh: the initial hamza is dropped, then the two lām sounds meet and assimilate into one doubled lām.
[TAB:1:1/r49] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The contraction is comparable to “lākinn huwa Allāh rabbī” from “lākinn anā huwa Allāh rabbī,” and to the poem’s “lākinn iyyāki” from “lākinn anā iyyāki.”
[TAB:1:1/r5] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Arab usage calls a comprehensive or leading thing with dependent followers an “umm”; examples include the membrane around the brain and an army’s gathering banner.
[TAB:1:1/r50] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | “Al-Raḥmān” follows faʿlān from raḥima, like ghaḍbān, sakrān, and ʿaṭshān from their verbs.
[TAB:1:1/r51] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | “Raḥīm” follows faʿīl as a form of praise; Arabic uses faʿīl for praise or blame even when the verb’s vowel differs, as in ʿālim/ʿalīm and qādir/qadīr.
[TAB:1:1/r52] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | In Arabic, al-Raḥmān is farther from the ordinary faʿila yafʿalu pattern than al-Raḥīm, and that greater departure intensifies praise.
[TAB:1:1/r53] TAB, d. 310 · العرزمي | reports | Al-ʿArzami says al-Raḥmān extends mercy to all creation, while al-Raḥīm is mercy toward believers.
[TAB:1:1/r54] TAB, d. 310 · عيسى ابن مريم | reports | A report says Jesus distinguished al-Raḥmān as mercy in this world and the next, and al-Raḥīm as mercy in the next world.
[TAB:1:1/r55] TAB, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Ṭabarī accepts both transmitted distinctions: al-Raḥmān denotes God’s mercy to all creation, while al-Raḥīm denotes mercy specified for some, whether in this life, the next, or both.
[TAB:1:1/r56] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | God’s universal worldly mercy includes provision, rain-bearing clouds, plants, bodily and mental health, and countless other blessings shared by believers and unbelievers. | mentions 14:34
[TAB:1:1/r57] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | In the hereafter, universal mercy means God’s just judgment: He wrongs no one even by an atom’s weight and repays each soul for what it earned. | mentions 4:40
[TAB:1:1/r58] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | God’s special mercy to believers in this life is the gracious aid that enables obedience, faith, following revelation, and avoiding sin, which He withholds from those He leaves astray. | mentions 33:43
[TAB:1:1/r59] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | In the next life, special mercy to believers is the lasting bliss, triumph, and honor prepared for them rather than unbelievers.
[TAB:1:1/r6] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Dhu al-Rumma’s banner poem uses “umm” for the standard around which companions gather for travel and battle.
[TAB:1:1/r60] TAB, d. 310 · عبد الله بن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās glosses al-Raḥmān as tender toward those God wills to show mercy, and al-Raḥīm as gentle toward those He wills to treat gently, but severe toward those He wills to chastise.
[TAB:1:1/r61] TAB, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Ṭabarī prefers the Prophet-attributed and al-ʿArzami distinctions to Ibn ʿAbbās’s account, while acknowledging that Ibn ʿAbbās also gives the words distinguishable meanings.
[TAB:1:1/r62] TAB, d. 310 · عطاء الخراساني | reports | ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī says God’s name was al-Raḥmān, then paired it with al-Raḥīm after the impostor Musaylima appropriated al-Raḥmān.
[TAB:1:1/r63] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī considers ʿAṭāʾ’s explanation plausible: God uniquely combines the two names to distinguish His name, even if their individual meanings differ or overlap.
[TAB:1:1/r64] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī rejects the claim that Arabs did not know “al-Raḥmān”: denial by polytheists does not prove ignorance, just as people who know Muhammad can still reject him. | mentions 25:60, 2:146
[TAB:1:1/r65] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Pre-Islamic verses by an unnamed poet and Salāma ibn Jandal use “al-Raḥmān,” demonstrating that the name was known among Arabs.
[TAB:1:1/r66] TAB, d. 310 · بعض من ضعفت معرفته بتأويل أهل التأويل | reports | An unnamed, weakly informed interpreter equates al-Raḥmān with “possessor of mercy” and al-Raḥīm with “merciful,” then inconsistently treats the pair as equivalent forms like nadmān and nadīm.
[TAB:1:1/r67] TAB, d. 310 · author | rejects | Al-Ṭabarī objects that “possessor of mercy” asserts an established attribute, whereas “merciful” can describe past, present, or future action; the terms therefore do not simply mean the same thing.
[TAB:1:1/r68] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Arabic normally names the subject first and follows it with attributes, so the sequence places the referent before its descriptions.
[TAB:1:1/r69] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The order puts Allah first because worship belongs to Him alone, al-Raḥmān next because it is also reserved for Him, and al-Raḥīm last because creatures may share some quality of mercy. | mentions 27:60, 27:61, 27:62, 27:63, 27:64, 17:110
[TAB:1:1/r7] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Two explanations are reported for Mecca as “Mother of the Towns”: it precedes and gathers the towns, or the earth was spread out from it.
[TAB:1:1/r70] TAB, d. 310 · الحسن البصري | reports | Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī says al-Raḥmān is a name barred from use by others; al-Ṭabarī adds that the community’s consensus on the prohibition suffices as proof.
[TAB:1:1/r8] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Ḥumayd ibn Thawr’s verse calls fifty one’s “mother” because it encompasses all numbers below it.
[TAB:1:1/r9] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | All Qurʾān readers and scholars agree that al-Fātiḥa has seven verses; they disagree over which words make the count seven.
[TAB:1:7/r54] TAB, d. 310 ·

 أهل الإلحاد الطاعنون في القرآن | reports | Critics ask why al-Fātiḥa has seven verses when, they argue, the meaning of its remaining verses is already contained in “Master of Judgment Day” and “You alone we worship and ask for help.”
[TAB:1:7/r55] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Earlier scriptures each contain some meanings found together in the Qur'an: the Torah gives admonitions and detail, the Psalms praise and glorify, and the Gospel admonishes and reminds; the Qur'an gathers these and adds more.
[TAB:1:7/r56] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī says the prior books lack a miracle certifying their recipients, whereas the Qur'an's unmatched composition defeats all attempts to produce even a short surah and proves Muhammad's prophethood.
[TAB:1:7/r57] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The Qur'an's varied contents—encouragement, warning, commands, prohibitions, stories, argument, and parables—also make its extended expression purposeful.
[TAB:1:7/r58] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Fātiḥa's inimitable arrangement proves prophethood, while its praise and glorification direct people to recognize God's greatness, sovereignty, power, and dominion and to thank Him for His favors.
[TAB:1:7/r59] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | The account of those favored through knowledge of God and His enabling teaches that every religious and worldly blessing comes from Him, directing requests to God rather than idols or rivals.
[TAB:1:7/r60] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | Recounting punishments for disobedience warns people away from sin and from incurring God's anger, whose consequences lead to destruction.
[TAB:1:7/r61] TAB, d. 310 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet said God answers the worshipper's recitation: He calls al-ḥamdu praise, al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm commendation, Mālik Yawm al-Dīn glorification, and the rest of the surah the servant's share.
[TAB:1:7/r62] TAB, d. 310 · أبو هريرة | reports | A second Abū Hurayra version gives the same recitation exchange but is not attributed to the Prophet.
[TAB:1:7/r63] TAB, d. 310 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh reports the divine saying that the prayer is divided between God and His servant, with the servant receiving what he asks; the first three praises are God's, and what follows is for the servant.
[TAB-FULL:v1p111#3/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | God taught Muhammad to put His beautiful names before every action, establishing a practice for people opening speech, letters, books, and requests.
[TAB-FULL:v1p111#3/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The prefixed bāʾ requires a governing verb omitted from the wording; the listener recovers it from the immediately accompanying action or speech.
[TAB-FULL:v1p111#3/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | At Qurʾān recitation the implicit verb is read, while in other acts it is rise, sit, or the relevant action, all begun with God’s name.
[TAB-FULL:v1p113/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبد الله بن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās reports Gabriel first taught seeking refuge and then instructed Muhammad to read, rise, and sit in remembrance of his Lord.
[TAB-FULL:v1p113/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The phrase means beginning by naming and remembering God, rather than claiming that the act itself is performed through God’s power.
[TAB-FULL:v1p113/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Arabic can use a verbal noun in a form normally associated with a noun; thus bismillah can express beginning with the act of naming.
[TAB-FULL:v1p115/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Poetic usage confirms verbal nouns can take other noun forms: ʿaṭāʾika means iʿṭāʾika, ṭūl means iṭāla, and muṣāb means iṣāba.
[TAB-FULL:v1p115/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Accordingly, the name stands for naming: the phrase means that one begins an action or recitation by naming God.
[TAB-FULL:v1p116/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبد الله بن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās reports Gabriel’s instruction that Muhammad read and undertake actions in remembrance of God his Lord.
[TAB-FULL:v1p116/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Ṭabarī adopts the interpretation that recitation starts with God’s naming and remembrance, using His beautiful names and exalted attributes.
[TAB-FULL:v1p116/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | The wording does not mean simply “by God”; the consensus on slaughter treats saying bi-llāh without bismillah as omitting the prescribed invocation.
[TAB-FULL:v1p116/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The present question concerns whether the attached “name” is a noun or a verbal noun meaning naming; the broader identity of name and named is outside this discussion.
[TAB-FULL:v1p118/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | Ṭabarī rejects taking Labīd’s “name of peace” simply as “peace”; that reading would license impossible Arabic such as eating the name of honey.
[TAB-FULL:v1p118/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | One possible reading makes al-Salām a divine name: “adhere to God’s name” after a year, with the command for adherence delayed in the wording; Ṭabarī finds this likelier.
[TAB-FULL:v1p118/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | A second possible reading is a protective invocation: may God’s name be upon the two addressed people against harm.
[TAB-FULL:v1p118/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Of the two defensible readings of Labīd, the first—taking al-Salām as God’s name and an exhortation to keep His remembrance—is more apt.
[TAB-FULL:v1p120/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report says Jesus explained the letters bāʾ, sīn, and mīm as God’s beauty, splendor, and dominion when a teacher asked about bism.
[TAB-FULL:v1p120/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | Ṭabarī suspects a transmitter mistakenly joined the beginner’s alphabet letters b-s-m into bism; the explanation is impossible in ordinary Arabic when the whole basmala is recited.
[TAB-FULL:v1p121/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبد الله بن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās defines God as the one whom everything worships and every creature serves.
[TAB-FULL:v1p121/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The proposed derivation of Allāh from ilāh is an inference rather than an attested form heard directly from Arab speech.
[TAB-FULL:v1p121/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Arab usage of taʾallaha for worship and seeking God supports the root’s devotional sense; a line by Ruʾba uses taʾalluhī in that sense.
[TAB-FULL:v1p121/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبد الله بن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās reads the Pharaoh passage’s ilāhataka as worship, explaining that Pharaoh worshipped rather than being worshipped. | mentions 7:127
[TAB-FULL:v1p121/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid likewise glosses ilāhataka in the Pharaoh passage as worship, a reading also attributed there to Ibn ʿAbbās. | mentions 7:127
[TAB-FULL:v1p121/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | These explanations establish that alaha means worship and ilāha is its verbal noun, supporting the interpretation of God as the worshipped one. | mentions 7:127
[TAB-FULL:v1p124#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Raḥmān follows the faʿlān pattern from raḥima, while al-Raḥīm follows faʿīl, a praise form that can occur despite the root’s vowel pattern.
[TAB-FULL:v1p124#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | In Arabic, the more distant a praise name is from its ordinary verbal pattern, the stronger its commendation; thus al-Raḥmān adds intensity beyond al-Raḥīm.
[TAB-FULL:v1p124#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · العرزمي | reports | Al-ʿAzramī distinguishes al-Raḥmān as mercy extending to all creation and al-Raḥīm as mercy toward believers.
[TAB-FULL:v1p124/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عيسى ابن مريم | reports | A prophetic report quotes Jesus telling his teacher that Allāh is the god of gods.
[TAB-FULL:v1p124/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Ṭabarī proposes that Allāh derives from al-ilāh: the initial hamza is dropped and the adjacent lām sounds assimilate into one doubled lām.
[TAB-FULL:v1p124/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The contraction is comparable to the Qurʾānic form lakinnā from wa-lākin anā, illustrated by a poet’s similar elision and assimilation. | mentions 18:38
[TAB-FULL:v1p127/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عيسى ابن مريم | reports | A report from the Prophet quotes Jesus distinguishing al-Raḥmān as merciful in this world and the next, and al-Raḥīm as merciful in the next.
[TAB-FULL:v1p127/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Ṭabarī reconciles both transmitted distinctions: al-Raḥmān denotes universal mercy and al-Raḥīm particular mercy, whether in this life, the next, or both.
[TAB-FULL:v1p127/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Universal worldly mercy includes provision, rain, crops, bodily and intellectual health, and other blessings shared by believers and unbelievers. | mentions 16:18
[TAB-FULL:v1p127/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | In the afterlife God’s universal mercy includes just treatment of everyone without the slightest wrong, while special mercy reserves guidance and the promised Garden for believers. | mentions 33:43
[TAB-FULL:v1p129/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عبد الله بن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās glosses al-Raḥmān as tender toward those God wills to show mercy and severe toward those He wills to chastise; al-Raḥīm is the gentle toward those shown mercy.
[TAB-FULL:v1p129/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Ṭabarī finds the prophetic report and al-ʿAzramī’s distinction more apt than Ibn ʿAbbās’s wording, while agreeing the names carry distinguishable meanings.
[TAB-FULL:v1p129/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عطاء الخراساني | reports | ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī says al-Raḥmān was an exclusive divine name, then was separated from God’s name when Musaylima appropriated it.
[TAB-FULL:v1p129/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Ṭabarī explains that adding al-Raḥīm distinguishes God from Musaylima: no one else has ever combined al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm as name

[TAB-FULL:v1p129/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | Ṭabarī rejects the claim that Arabs did not know al-Raḥmān: their question in the Qurʾān can be denial despite knowledge, as with people who recognized but rejected Muhammad. | mentions 25:60, 2:146
[TAB-FULL:v1p131/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · سلامة بن جندل الطهوي | reports | A pre-Islamic poem invokes al-Raḥmān as Lord, further demonstrating the name was familiar in Arabic.
[TAB-FULL:v1p131/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | Ṭabarī rejects the gloss of al-Raḥmān as merely possessing mercy and al-Raḥīm as merciful: the latter need not assert that mercy is a settled attribute.
[TAB-FULL:v1p131/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Arabic convention places a referent’s name before its attributes; Ṭabarī applies that order to the divine names.
[TAB-FULL:v1p131/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Ṭabarī rejects the gloss of al-Raḥmān as merely possessing mercy and al-Raḥīm as merciful: the latter need not assert that mercy is a settled attribute.
[TAB-FULL:v1p131/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Arabic convention places a referent’s name before its attributes; Ṭabarī applies that order to the divine names.
[TAB-FULL:v1p133/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | Ṭabarī explains that God’s unique name remains exclusive even if people bear names such as Saʿīd while being its opposite.
[TAB-FULL:v1p133/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Ṭabarī places Allāh first because no other being shares divine worship, then al-Raḥmān, which is also reserved for God, before the shared descriptor al-Raḥīm.
[TAB-FULL:v1p133/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Allāh and al-Raḥmān are reserved for God, while al-Raḥīm may describe creatures; no one shares God’s divinity or deserves His exclusive names. | mentions 27:60
[TAB-FULL:v1p133/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الحسن البصري | reports | Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī calls al-Raḥmān a forbidden name for others; Ṭabarī says the community’s consensus already establishes the prohibition.
[TAB-FULL:v1p147#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Ṭabarī argues the basmala is not a verse of the Opening: otherwise al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm would repeat immediately, word for word and sense for sense, without an intervening divider.
[TAB-FULL:v1p147#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · جماعة من أهل التأويل | reports | Some interpreters treat al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm as advanced in meaning before rabb al-ʿālamīn, making the apparent repetition part of reordered description rather than adjacent verses. | mentions 1:4
[TAB-FULL:v1p149/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Poetry by Jarīr and Qurʾān 18:2 illustrate fronting and delaying in Arabic; the apparent order can place the “upright” description before its intended antecedent. | mentions 18:2
[TAB-FULL:v1p149/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | These reorderings support the interpreters who deny that the basmala belongs to the Opening as a verse.
[TAB-FULL:v1p203#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · جابر بن عبد الله الأنصاري عن رسول الله | reports | The Prophet says the prayer is divided between God and the servant: the opening praise, mercy, and judgment belong to God, and the remainder is the servant’s request. | mentions 1:2, 1:1, 1:4
[TAB-FULL:v1p203/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو هريرة عن رسول الله | reports | The Prophet reports God praises the servant’s recitation of praise, mercy, and sovereignty, then says the invocation from You alone we worship through the end belongs to the servant. | mentions 1:2, 1:1, 1:4, 1:5
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p25/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says the first revelation began with the command to say the basmala and to read by remembering God, rising and sitting in His remembrance.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p25/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Dahhak assigns the letters of bism to God's splendor, sublime glory, and dominion, and glosses Allah as God of creation.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p25/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · أبو الشعثاء جابر بن زيد | reports | Jabir ibn Zayd says Allah is the Greatest Name because every Qur'anic sura begins with it before any other name.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p25/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas explains al-Rahman as the Arabic intensive form of mercy and says it is an Arabic expression.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p25/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet calls the basmala one of God's names and compares its nearness to Allah's name with the closeness of the eye's black and white.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p25/r6] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas glosses al-Rahim as gentle and caring toward those God wills to show mercy, and severe toward those He wills to chastise.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p26/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan says al-Rahman is a name people cannot appropriate for themselves; it belongs to God.
[SULAMI:v1p21/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · قيل | reports | One unnamed view says al-Fātiḥa is named for opening the delight of intimate address, making it an opening to every good.
[SULAMI:v1p21/r6] SULAMI, d. 412 · قيل | reports | Another view treats the title as God's first opening of discourse: proper conduct grants access to later subtleties, while failure bars them.
[SULAMI:v1p24#2/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · أبو القاسم الحكيم | reports | The opening formula signals love as the beginning.
[SULAMI:v1p24#2/r10] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The bāʾ is the means by which they reach God's name.
[SULAMI:v1p24#2/r11] SULAMI, d. 412 · جعفر بن محمد | reports | The letters mean God's abiding, names, and sovereignty; faith recalls His abiding, service recalls His names, and gnosis leaves the kingdom for its owner.
[SULAMI:v1p24#2/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · العباس بن عطاء | reports | The letters signify God's inspiration of prophecy to prophets, nearness and intimacy to knowers, and enduring compassionate attention to seekers.
[SULAMI:v1p24#2/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · الجنيد | reports | He reads bism as divine awe, al-Rahman as aid, and al-Rahim as affection and love.
[SULAMI:v1p24#2/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The prophets appear and pass away through God; His manifestation beautifies beauty, and His illumination opens and makes things generous.
[SULAMI:v1p24#2/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · الجنيد | reports | Knowers empty and purify their hearts for God; their first gift is annihilation of all besides Him and exclusive affiliation to Him rather than Adam.
[SULAMI:v1p24#2/r6] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The formula preserves created forms: opening by God's essence would dissolve creation, except prophets and saints; the name illuminates knowers' hearts.
[SULAMI:v1p24#2/r7] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Bismillah marks the people of reality, who adorn themselves only with the Real and swear only by Him.
[SULAMI:v1p24#2/r8] SULAMI, d. 412 · أبو بكر بن طاهر | reports | He assigns the letters the meanings of God's secret among knowers, peace upon them, and His love for them.
[SULAMI:v1p24#2/r9] SULAMI, d. 412 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report attributed to the Prophet, explicitly qualified as possibly unauthentic, maps the letters to God's splendor, radiance, and majesty.
[SULAMI:v1p26/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The letters are the gate of prophecy, the prophetic secret entrusted to the Prophet's close followers, and the kingdom of the religion given to all peoples.
[SULAMI:v1p26/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · محمد بن موسى الواسطي | reports | Invoking any divine name gives the invoker some personal share, but the name Allah calls only to oneness and contains no deficiency.
[SULAMI:v1p26/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Unlike other names, which imply compensation when invoked, Allah is a name reserved uniquely for the Real.
[SULAMI:v1p26/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Ordinary utterance of Allah is habitual; when God takes charge of a speaker who is veiled from self-awareness, faults and slips disappear.
[SULAMI:v1p26/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · الحسين | reports | Saying Bismillah resembles God's creative command Be: with acknowledgment of God's favor, things become actual through the formula.
[SULAMI:v1p26/r6] SULAMI, d. 412 · الشبلي | reports | No one truly says Allah except God, since every other speaker says it from a personal share and shares cannot reach realities.
[SULAMI:v1p26/r7] SULAMI, d. 412 · أبو سعيد الخراز | reports | He describes a seeker who has forgotten personal interests and needs, loses ordinary self-description, becomes filled with hidden divine light, and ultimately cannot utter the name in the limit of nearness.
[SULAMI:v1p28/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · الحسين بن منصور | reports | No one can remember God in His reality: He has no limit or cause, while letters and breaths are created and intellect cannot grasp Him.
[SULAMI:v1p28/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The letters of Allah signify beginning, recognition, blessings, the meanings of commands and prohibitions, and the ultimate hidden reality beyond worship's grasp.
[SULAMI:v1p28/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Another letter reading makes alif God's favors, the lām His gentleness and encounter, and hāʾ the awe that leaves lovers unable to know Him.
[SULAMI:v1p28/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · الجنيد | reports | Junayd checks that Nuri still observes prayer, then challenges whether God or Nuri himself says Allah; Nuri answers that it is love, and his ecstasy subsides.
[SULAMI:v1p28/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · الشبلي | reports | Al-Shibli says Allah alone, rather than There is no god but God, because he will not use the latter to negate a rival.
[SULAMI:v1p28/r6] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Because the name itself is inaccessible in reality, pleasures are even more inaccessible, teaching creatures their inability to name God's essence.
[SULAMI:v1p30/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The letters signify oneness, then the erasure of indication and of that erasure in the disclosure of hāʾ.
[SULAMI:v1p30/r10] SULAMI, d. 412 · أبو سعيد الخراز | reports | Only God can name, see,

[SULAMI:v1p30/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Alif signifies God's self-subsistence and separation from creation; letters depend upon it, while it depends on none.
[SULAMI:v1p30/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Dropping letters from Allah leaves successive divine indications—lillah, lahu, then hāʾ—which is the utmost signification.
[SULAMI:v1p30/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Created beings are enraptured variously: their secret by divine majesty, heart by forms of gnosis, or tongue by constant remembrance.
[SULAMI:v1p30/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · الجنيد | reports | Junayd tells Ibn Shibli that mentioning an absent God is backbiting; if one is absent it is such mention, while witnessing Him makes speech a breach of reverence.
[SULAMI:v1p30/r6] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Uttering Allah through letters cannot truly name Him, since He exceeds letters, concepts, and imaginings; the formula is accepted because no other mode of affirming oneness is possible.
[SULAMI:v1p30/r7] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | All names' meanings are contained in Allah, but Allah's name derives from none; God alone bears it, though creatures share derivations of other names.
[SULAMI:v1p30/r8] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعض البغداديين | reports | The visible letters are not God Himself; when the letters disappear, the indication is that He is God.
[SULAMI:v1p30/r9] SULAMI, d. 412 · أبو العباس بن عطاء | reports | The name Allah manifests divine awe and majesty.
[SULAMI:v1p31/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · حكيم من الحكماء | reports | The ultimate goal is God; the supplication asks for guidance to Him, steadfastness in His presence, freedom from substitutes, and settlement at the encounter.
[SULAMI:v1p31/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · أبو سعيد الخراز | reports | God first called servants to the single name Allah; people of realities need that name, while further descriptions in the chapter serve successively lower ranks.
[SULAMI:v1p31/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Every divine name may be emulated except Allah, which is for attachment to God rather than taking on His name.
[SULAMI:v1p31/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | In Allah, the two lām letters and hāʾ are connected while alif is separate, indicating that the reference to God is not made through the servant's own self.
[SULAMI:v1p31/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · جعفر | reports | The four letters form a complete, unique name: alif is the pillar of oneness, the two lām letters signify the Tablet of the Pen and of Prophecy, and hāʾ is the utmost indication; God exceeds apprehension.
[SULAMI:v1p32/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | All enduring graces for believers issue through al-Rahman, and no creature can bear that name because creatures cannot give what lasts.
[SULAMI:v1p32/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | Al-Rahman's mercy lets seekers detach from everything below Him; its worldly bounty reaches friend and enemy alike.
[SULAMI:v1p32/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Al-Rahman signifies the sweetness of benefaction, witnessed nearness, and careful service.
[SULAMI:v1p32/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | Lovers, the fearful, repentant, and sinners each receive a distinct spiritual fruit from the meanings of al-Rahman: intimacy, security, purification, or remorse and seeking forgiveness.
[SULAMI:v1p32/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · ابن عطاء | reports | Al-Rahman means God's aid and victory.
[SULAMI:v1p32/r6] SULAMI, d. 412 · الواسطي | reports | One approaches al-Rahman only through His all-encompassing mercy, while al-Rahim is approached through obedience; the Prophet also bears the latter name (9:128). | mentions 9:128
[SULAMI:v1p33/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Al-Rahim denotes mercy for creatures' livelihood and bodily welfare, so creatures may be called rahim, unlike the uniquely divine Rahman.
[SULAMI:v1p33/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The Prophet, called compassionate and merciful toward believers, is a means by which people reach God and the two divine names; the Merciful accepts the returning person despite faults and preserves even one who turns away. | mentions 9:128
[SULAMI:v1p33/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · ابن عطاء | reports | Al-Rahim signifies God's affection and mercy.
[SULAMI:v1p33/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · جعفر | reports | Al-Rahman suits those sought by God, immersed in lights and realities; al-Rahim suits seekers remaining with themselves and tending outward practice.
[SULAMI:v1p33/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · جعفر | reports | Al-Rahman's mercy reaches back into pre-eternity and has no endpoint, whereas al-Rahim connects mercy with worldly life, guidance, and provisions.
[THALABI:v10p244/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | In this account, the voice tells the Prophet to recite the basmala and the opening of al-Fātiḥa through its final words, then affirm God’s oneness. | mentions 1:1, 1:7
[THALABI:v1p100/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A second report says God will join the one mercy to the other ninety-nine, completing one hundred for His servants on Judgment Day.
[THALABI:v1p100/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · يحيى بن معاذ الرازي | reports | Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh says al-Raḥmān provides for worldly livelihoods and al-Raḥīm for the afterlife.
[THALABI:v1p100/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسين بن الفضل | reports | Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl says al-Raḥmān removes harm and evil, while al-Raḥīm is compassionate but may be unable to remove them.
[THALABI:v1p100/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو بكر الوراق | reports | Al-Warrāq says al-Raḥmān is merciful to deniers and unbelievers, while al-Raḥīm is merciful to monotheists and the grateful.
[THALABI:v1p100/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن المبارك | reports | Ibn al-Mubārak says al-Raḥmān gives when asked, while al-Raḥīm is displeased when not asked.
[THALABI:v1p100/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet says whoever does not ask God makes Him angry; a poem contrasts God’s anger at unanswered supplication with people’s anger at being asked.
[THALABI:v1p100/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو بكر الوراق | reports | Al-Warrāq distinguishes al-Raḥmān as bestowed blessings and al-Raḥīm as benefits God has spared or withdrawn.
[THALABI:v1p100/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · محمد بن علي المزيدي | reports | Al-Muzaydī says al-Raḥmān rescues people from the Fire and al-Raḥīm admits them to gardens. | mentions 3:103, 15:46
[THALABI:v1p100/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · المحاسبي | reports | Al-Muḥāsibī assigns al-Raḥmān mercy to souls and al-Raḥīm mercy to hearts.
[THALABI:v1p100/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · السري بن مغلس | reports | Al-Sarī ibn Mughlis says al-Raḥmān removes distress and al-Raḥīm forgives sins.
[THALABI:v1p100/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · عبد الله بن الجراح | reports | Ibn al-Jarrāḥ’s first gloss is damaged in the text; he says al-Raḥīm provides protection and divine success.
[THALABI:v1p100/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · مطهر بن الوراق | reports | Muṭahhar al-Warrāq says al-Raḥmān forgives even grave sins, while al-Raḥīm accepts even few acts of obedience.
[THALABI:v1p101/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · قراء المدينة والبصرة والكوفة، مالك، الأوزاعي، أبو حنيفة | reports | The Medinan, Basran, and Kufan reciters, with Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, and Abū Ḥanīfa, treat the basmala as an opening blessing, not a verse of this or other suras, and say it need not be recited; on this count “those You favored” is verse six.
[THALABI:v1p101/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Another group, reporting from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and followed by Meccan and many Hijazi reciters, counts the basmala as a verse of the Fātiḥa and does not count “those You favored” separately.
[THALABI:v1p101/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · الشافعي والشعبي وعبد الله | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī, al-Shaʿbī, and a view attributed to ʿAbd Allāh say it was revealed as the first verse of al-Fātiḥa and is a verse in every sura except al-Tawba; written repetitions and the Naml occurrence are their evidence. | mentions 27:30, 55:13, 77:15
[THALABI:v1p101/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | A report traces the written opening from “In Your name, O God,” to bismillah, then bismillah al-Raḥmān, and finally the full basmala after the verse in Solomon’s letter was revealed. | mentions 11:41, 17:110, 27:30
[THALABI:v1p102/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet calls the basmala the unique verse revealed after Solomon; the author takes his recitation of the full formula to show it is a complete verse of al-Fātiḥa and the sura openings, whereas Naml contains it within a longer verse. | mentions 27:30
[THALABI:v1p102/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says that when a basmala verse was revealed, the Prophet knew the previous sura had ended and another had begun.
[THALABI:v1p102/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In a report from Jābir, the Prophet tells him to say the basmala when beginning prayer after Jābir says al-ḥamdu lillāh.
[THALABI:v1p102/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · مسلمة | reports | The report says the Prophet recited the Fātiḥa verse by verse, counting seven, including the basmala.
[THALABI:v1p103/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | ʿAlī recited the basmala when opening a sura in prayer, said omitting it diminishes the prayer, and called it the completion of the seven oft-repeated verses and the Great Qurʾān.
[THALABI:v1p103/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the seven oft-repeated verses as al-Fātiḥa and counts the basmala as its seventh verse. | mentions 15:87
[THALABI:v1p103/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو هريرة | reports | Abū Hurayra says readers of the Mother of the Qurʾān should not leave the basmala because it is one of its verses and part of the seven oft-repeated.
[THALABI:v1p103/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In the divine report dividing prayer between God and the servant, the basmala glorifies God, al-ḥamdu praises Him, al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm extols H

[THALABI:v1p104/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet tells a man who began reciting al-ḥamdu without the basmala that he cut off his prayer: leaving out this verse cuts off the Fātiḥa and invalidates the prayer.
[THALABI:v1p104/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh says that whoever omits the basmala has omitted a verse from God’s Book.
[THALABI:v1p104/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | The author notes that ʿAlī included the basmala among the verses he counted as the Mother of the Book.
[THALABI:v1p104/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · المهاجرون والأنصار | reports | When Muʿāwiya omitted the basmala while leading prayer in Medina, the Emigrants and Helpers called out that he had forgotten it, so he repeated the prayer with it.
[THALABI:v1p105#2/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | prefers | The author says reciting the basmala aloud in prayer is sunnah, citing commands to read in the Lord’s name and to remember the Lord’s name when praying. | mentions 96:1, 87:15
[THALABI:v1p105#2/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report relayed by al-Mahdī from his father and grandfather, Ibn ʿAbbās, says the Prophet recited the basmala aloud.
[THALABI:v1p105#2/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · عطاء وطاوس ومجاهد | reports | Al-Layth reports that ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, and Mujāhid recited the basmala aloud.
[THALABI:v1p105#2/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · عبد الله بن عباس، عبد الله بن عمر، عبد الله بن الزبير، عبد الله بن صفوان | reports | A report says the four ʿAbādila opened recitation with the basmala and voiced it.
[THALABI:v1p105#2/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · جعفر بن محمد | reports | Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq says the Prophet’s family agreed on voicing the basmala, making up missed night prayer in daytime, and speaking well of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar and their companion.
[THALABI:v1p105#2/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · جعفر بن محمد الصادق | reports | Al-Ṣādiq calls audible recitation the truth and links it to the verse about people turning away when God alone is mentioned in the Qurʾān. | mentions 17:46
[THALABI:v1p105/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · المهاجرون | reports | A separate report says Muʿāwiya recited the basmala for al-Fātiḥa but not the next sura; the Emigrants challenged him, and he repeated the prayer while reading that sura.
[THALABI:v1p105/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The author argues from the arrangement of verse endings and the basmala’s placement that it was written where revealed, rather than inserted merely to divide suras.
[THALABI:v1p105/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The author adds that scribes used black ink for the basmala, unlike non-Qurʾānic marginal material, which supports its status as Qurʾān.
[THALABI:v1p106/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abū Hurayra reports that Gabriel taught the Prophet prayer, after which the Prophet stood, said takbīr, and voiced the basmala.
[THALABI:v1p106/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · الزهري | reports | Al-Zuhrī calls reciting the basmala in the Fātiḥa part of prayer’s sunnah and says one who omits it has not recited the sura; he names ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd as the first to abandon it in Medina.
[THALABI:v1p106/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · أنس بن مالك | reports | Anas reports that he did not hear the Prophet, Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, or ʿUthmān recite the basmala aloud.
[THALABI:v1p106/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | rejects | The author says Anas’s report only denies raising the voice; it does not deny that the basmala is part of the sura, and “not aloud” need not mean whispering or omitting it.
[THALABI:v1p107/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet voiced the basmala in Mecca, prompting pagans to mock the mention of the “god of al-Yamāma,” meaning Musaylima; the author connects this to the command for moderate volume. | mentions 17:110
[THALABI:v1p107/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · أنس بن مالك | reports | Anas says the Prophet, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar opened recitation with al-ḥamdu lillāh; the author interprets this as opening prayer with the sura called al-Ḥamd, not beginning at verse two.
[THALABI:v1p92/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The prefixed bā is an extra particle of attachment or inclusion, as in writing with a pen, where the writing adheres to the pen.
[THALABI:v1p92/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The basmala means that beings came into existence through God and creatures subsist through Him; ism distinguishes the one invoking blessing from its object.
[THALABI:v1p92/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The author identifies name with the named, the existent thing, its essence, and itself, citing the announcement that a boy’s name is Yaḥyā and then addressing him as Yaḥyā. | mentions 19:7
[THALABI:v1p92/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The bā is always kasra because it is an incomplete, inclined letter; imāla signals kasra.
[THALABI:v1p92/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh explains the kasra by saying that kasra is the bā’s only function.
[THALABI:v1p92/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · المبرد | reports | Al-Mubarrad says its kasra restores it to its original form, comparing yāʾ with kasra as wāw with ḍamma and alif with fatḥa.
[THALABI:v1p92/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · القيسي | reports | Al-Qaysi says the opening bā was lengthened and likened to alif-lām so God’s Book would begin with an exalted, emphatic letter.
[THALABI:v1p92/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · عمر بن عبد العزيز | reports | ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz instructed scribes to lengthen the bā, show the sīn, separate them, and round the mīm in reverence for God’s speech.
[THALABI:v1p92/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو خالد بن يزيد المرادي | reports | Abu Khalid ibn Yazid al-Muradi says the alif of ism was dropped for frequent use and its length was transferred to the bā; where ism retains alif, the bā keeps its ordinary form.
[THALABI:v1p92/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The phrase has an omitted command, understood as “say” or “begin” in God’s name.
[THALABI:v1p92/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · آدم | reports | Adam treats ism as an added word, glossing the phrase as “By God, the Merciful, the Compassionate, He is”; Labid’s verse uses ism for “peace.”
[THALABI:v1p93/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The Qurʾānic phrase about people worshiping only names they assigned means the objects themselves, since they worshiped the named beings. | mentions 53:23
[THALABI:v1p93/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The commands to glorify or bless God’s name use “name” to mean God Himself; the report about Mudar likewise says no one would worship Him. | mentions 87:1, 55:78
[THALABI:v1p93/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Although ism is more commonly used for naming than for the named, its plural is asmāʾ; its derivation from samā means to rise, since existence rises above nonexistence, while naming is an expression or description.
[THALABI:v1p93/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In a report from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, Jesus asks his teacher about bismillah; Jesus explains bā as God’s splendor, sīn as His radiance, and mīm as His kingdom.
[THALABI:v1p93/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو بكر محمد بن عمر الوراق | reports | Abu Bakr al-Warraq describes bismillah as a garden of Paradise whose every letter has its own interpretation, expanded in the following segment.
[THALABI:v1p94/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو بكر الوراق | reports | Al-Warraq’s letter gloss gives six b-attributes: creator, seer, provider, everlasting, raiser of the dead, and benefactor; the commentary supplies Qurʾānic proofs for them. | mentions 52:28, 13:26, 55:26, 55:27, 22:7
[THALABI:v1p94/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو بكر الوراق | reports | The sīn gloss gives five attributes: hearing, lordship, swift reckoning, safeguarding creatures from injustice, and forgiving sins, with Qurʾānic proofs. | mentions 43:80, 112:2, 2:202, 59:23, 40:3
[THALABI:v1p94/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو بكر الوراق | reports | The mīm gloss gives twelve attributes, including ruler, owner, benefactor, glorious, giver of security, overseer, powerful, sustainer, ennobler, bestower, and creator; each receives a Qurʾānic proof. | mentions 59:23, 3:26, 49:17, 85:15, 106:4, 54:55, 4:85, 17:70, 31:20
[THALABI:v1p95/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو بكر الوراق | reports | The final mīm glosses are that God grants favor to all creation and forms His creation, supported by verses on divine favor and creation. | mentions 3:108, 59:24
[THALABI:v1p95/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · أهل الحقائق | reports | The people of spiritual realities say the basmala is for blessing and encourages beginning words and deeds with it, following the Qurʾān’s own opening.
[THALABI:v1p95/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · أهل الكوفة | reports | The Kufans derive Allah from ilāh: the definite article magnified the name, then the hamza dropped through frequent use and the two lām letters assimilated.
[THALABI:v1p95/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · أهل البصرة | reports | The Basrans derive Allah from lāh with the definite article, citing a verse that preserves the alleged original form.
[THALABI:v1p95/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · بعضهم | reports | Another account says the definite article replaced the deleted hamza and therefore remains inseparable; this explains why one cannot say “yā ayyuhā Allāh.”
[THALABI:v1p95/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · الخليل بن أحمد وجماعة | reports | Al-Khalil and others say Allah is a proper name, not derived; the verse “Do you know any namesake for Him?” supports its unique reference. | mentions 19:65
[THALABI:v1p95/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · الخليل بن أحمد وجماعة | reports | They say Allah is exclusive to God because it contains lordship and encompasses all meanings; its successive deletions yield li-llāh, lah, and huwa.
[THALABI:v1p95/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | When applied to another being, the source says the form must be qualified or indefinite; Allah and al-ilāh are reserved for God, as in the Israelites’

 request for a god. | mentions 7:138
[THALABI:v1p96/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · قوم | reports | Some say the name came from Syriac lāhā, whose final long vowel was removed when the word entered Arabic.
[THALABI:v1p96/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · النضر بن إسماعيل | reports | Al-Naḍr derives Allah from taʾalluh, worship and devotion; Ibn ʿAbbas’s reading of “your worship” is offered as evidence. | mentions 7:127
[THALABI:v1p96/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس والضحاك | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Daḥḥāk derive ilāh from seeking refuge and relying on someone: creatures turn to God in crises, and He protects them.
[THALABI:v1p96/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو عمرو بن العلاء | reports | Abu ʿAmr derives the name from bewilderment: minds are perplexed by God’s essence, greatness, and unknowable nature.
[THALABI:v1p96/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · المبرد | reports | Al-Mubarrad derives it from finding repose with someone; creatures become calm through remembrance of God. | mentions 13:28
[THALABI:v1p96/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · علي بن عبد الرحيم القناد | reports | Al-Qannād derives it from walāh, loss of reason at losing a beloved; the author says hearts long for God in love and tremble at His remembrance.
[THALABI:v1p98/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · علي بن عبد الرحيم القناد | reports | The Kummayt verse illustrates hearts becoming lovesick for God and yearning at His remembrance.
[THALABI:v1p98/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The source notes a heavy pronunciation of the lām in Allah, with the tongue pressed to the palate in reverence for the name.
[THALABI:v1p98/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · قوم | reports | Some say al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm are synonymous names for the merciful; mercy is either God’s will of good, an essential attribute, or withholding deserved punishment and doing good, an act-attribute.
[THALABI:v1p98/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · قوم | reports | Those who distinguish the names say al-Raḥmān’s intensive pattern denotes one filled with mercy.
[THALABI:v1p98/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · قوم | reports | Some derive ilāh from concealment: God is manifest through signs of lordship yet hidden from minds in His modality.
[THALABI:v1p98/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · قوم | reports | Another derivation is from elevation, since lāh means to rise.
[THALABI:v1p98/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · قوم | reports | One proposed derivation links the name to alāhat, illustrated by a line about delaying the goddess’s return.
[THALABI:v1p98/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · قوم | reports | A derivation from dwelling in a place gives the sense of the eternally abiding and enduring.
[THALABI:v1p98/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · قوم | reports | Another gloss describes God’s essence as His power to subdue.
[THALABI:v1p98/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · الحارث بن أسد المجلسي | reports | Al-Ḥārith says Allah comes from “made them needy”: servants need their Creator for benefits and harms like distressed, overpowered people.
[THALABI:v1p98/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · شهر بن حوشب | reports | Shahr ibn Ḥawshab glosses Allah as the Creator of everything.
[THALABI:v1p98/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو بكر الوراق | reports | Abu Bakr al-Warrāq gives the terse gloss “He is.”
[THALABI:v1p99/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · قوم | reports | One view makes al-Raḥmān merciful to all creation through creation and provision, while al-Raḥīm specially guides believers in this life and grants them Paradise and vision in the next. | mentions 7:156, 33:43
[THALABI:v1p99/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · جعفر بن محمد الصادق | reports | Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq summarizes the distinction as al-Raḥmān being a specific name with general scope and al-Raḥīm a general name with specific scope.
[THALABI:v1p99/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās calls the two names subtle, with one more delicate than the other.
[THALABI:v1p99/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid says al-Raḥmān is for the people of this world and al-Raḥīm for the people of the afterlife.
[THALABI:v1p99/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk assigns al-Raḥmān’s mercy to heaven’s inhabitants through their dwelling, obedience, and protection, and al-Raḥīm’s to earthly people through messengers, scriptures, counsel, and relief from calamities.
[THALABI:v1p99/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · عكرمة | reports | ʿIkrima says al-Raḥmān is associated with one mercy and al-Raḥīm with one hundred; he derives this from the Prophetic report that one mercy was sent to earth and ninety-nine are reserved for Judgment Day.
[THALABI:v1p99/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet reports that God has one hundred mercies: one is shared among creation, while ninety-nine are reserved to show mercy to servants on the Resurrection Day.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r1] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | The Qur’an and Sunna establish that a reciter seeks refuge before reciting, saying I seek refuge in God from Satan the accursed.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r10] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | Alternatively, al-rajim means one who is pelted, specifically with stars.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r11] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | Another explanation of one who is pelted is that he is ill-omened.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r12] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | A third explanation is that al-rajim means accursed, that is, expelled.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r13] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | In the Prophetic formula, Satan’s puff means pride, his spittle means magic, and his provocation means madness.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r14] MAWARDI, d. 450 · قتادة | reports | Qatada holds that the Fatiha is Meccan.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r15] MAWARDI, d. 450 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid holds that the Fatiha is Medinan, contrary to Qatada’s view.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r16] MAWARDI, d. 450 · أبو هريرة | reports | Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet naming the sura Umm al-Qur’an, Fatiha al-Kitab, and the seven oft-repeated verses; no grading is given.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r17] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | It is called Fatiha al-Kitab because the written Qur’an begins with it and it is first in recitation.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r18] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | It is called Umm al-Qur’an because it precedes the rest, which follow it; an army’s banner is also called umm because the army follows it, as Labid’s verse illustrates.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r19] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | The years already lived are also called umm because they precede a person’s present, supported by the cited verse about fifty years.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r2] MAWARDI, d. 450 · أبو سعيد الخدري | reports | Abu Sa‘id reports that the Prophet also sought refuge in God the All-Hearing, All-Knowing from Satan’s puff, spittle, and provocation; no grading is stated.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r20] MAWARDI, d. 450 · الأكثرون | reports | Most scholars allow calling the Fatiha Umm al-Kitab because al-Kitab means the Qur’an.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r21] MAWARDI, d. 450 · الحسن وابن سيرين | reports | Hasan and Ibn Sirin reject calling it Umm al-Kitab, reserving that title for the Preserved Tablet in 43:4. | mentions 43:4
[MAWARDI:1:1/r22] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | Makka is called Umm al-Qura because it precedes the other towns.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r23] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | Alternatively, Makkah is Umm al-Qura because the earth was spread out from it and originated there, like children originating from a mother.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r24] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | The Fatiha is called the seven oft-repeated because everyone agrees it has seven verses.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r25] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | It is oft-repeated because it is recited in every obligatory and voluntary prayer.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r26] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | Calling it al-mathani does not preclude applying that name to other passages; al-A‘sha of Hamdan’s verse calls other passages al-mathani and the long suras.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r27] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | All agree the basmala is Qur’an in sura 27, but disagree whether it belongs in the Fatiha and at the opening of every sura.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r28] MAWARDI, d. 450 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafi‘i and a group affirm the basmala as part of the Fatiha and sura openings.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r29] MAWARDI, d. 450 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa and others deny that the basmala is part of the Fatiha and sura openings.
[MAWARDI:1:1/r3] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | One explanation takes seeking refuge as seeking protection from one possessing power.

[KASHSHAF:1:1/r23] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Naming raises the named one's standing; nabz derives from a word meaning raised voice and also means upper palm bark.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r24] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | The written alif is dropped by analogy with connected pronunciation; the bā is lengthened to compensate for the omission.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r25] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · عمر بن عبد العزيز | reports | Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz told his scribe to lengthen bā, show tooth-like strokes, and round mīm.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r26] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Allah derives from al-ilah, with hamza removed; al-nas likewise derives from al-unas, with the hamza replaced by the article.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r27] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | In the vocative, Allah keeps its hamza pronounced separately, as in ya ilah.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r28] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Ilah is a common noun for anything worshipped truly or falsely, later restricted to the true deity, like words for star and house narrowed to the Pleiades and Kaaba.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r29] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Allah without hamza is uniquely the name of the true God and is never applied to another.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r3] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · أبو حنيفة ومن تابعه | reports | Abu Hanifa and his followers share that position and therefore do not recite it aloud in prayer.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r30] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Ta'allaha, aliha, and ista'lah derive from this name, like verbs formed from camel and stone nouns.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r31] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Allah is a proper name, not an attribute; it is predicated of things but does not describe them, and divine attributes require a named subject.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r32] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | A possible derivation links the name to aliha, be bewildered: minds are confounded by knowing God, helping explain error and scarce sound reflection.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r33] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj says emphatic pronunciation of Allah's lām is Sunna; Arabs all use it, showing inherited usage.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r34] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Rahman follows faʿlan from rahima, like ghadban and sakran; rahim follows faʿil, like marid and saqim.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r35] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Rahman is more intensive than rahim; tradition calls God Rahman of this world and the next, but Rahim of this world.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r36] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Added form means added meaning, illustrated by the heavier name shaqandaf for a light mount compared with shaqdaf.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r37] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | The anecdote contrasts the light mount's name shaqdaf with shaqandaf, whose added letters express greater form.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r38] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj explains ghadban as one filled with anger, illustrating the intensive pattern.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r39] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Rahman is among dominant adjectival names that became proper names, like al-Dubaran and al-Ayyuq; Allah too is a dominant name.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r4] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · قراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما | reports | Meccan and Kufan readers and jurists, with al-Shafii and followers, count it as a verse of al-Fatiha and every surah.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r40] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · بنو حنيفة وشاعرهم | rejects | Banu Hanifa called Musaylima Rahman of Yamama and their poet called him Rahman; al-Zamakhshari condemns this as unbelief.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r41] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Al-Zamakhshari declines Rahman without tanwin, by analogy with ghadban, gharthan, and sakran.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r42] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Though the usual diptote condition requires feminine faʿla, exclusivity does not remove the base pattern; faʿlana is also barred.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r43] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Mercy suggests tenderness, as with a womb bending over its contents; of God it metaphorically means beneficence to servants, like a generous king.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r44] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Rahman precedes rahim though the usual order rises from lesser to greater: it covers great foundational blessings, then rahim adds subtle ones.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r5] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · قراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما | reports | Because they count it as a verse, this group recites it aloud in prayer.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r6] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · قراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما | reports | Their proof is that early Muslims included it in the codex while requiring the Quran be stripped of additions, but omitted Amin.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r7] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says whoever omits the basmala has omitted 114 verses of God's Book.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r8] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | The prefixed bā attaches to an omitted verb, understood as I read or recite in God's name.
[KASHSHAF:1:1/r9] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | holds | Travel formulas, slaughter, and acts begun in God's name similarly omit the verb that states the introduced act.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · قراء المدينة والبصرة والشام وفقهاؤها | reports | They hold that the basmala is not a Qur'anic verse, but was written to separate surahs and for blessing; they therefore do not recite it aloud in prayer.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · أبو حنيفة رحمه الله ومن تابعه | reports | Abu Hanifa shares the view that the basmala is not a verse, and his followers accordingly do not recite it aloud in prayer.

KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · قراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما | reports | They hold that the basmala is a verse of al-Fatiha and every surah; al-Shafi'i and his companions agree and recite it aloud.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | The opposing jurists argue that the early community included the basmala in the codex while excluding Amin, so it must be Qur'an.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says that whoever omits the basmala has omitted 114 verses from God's Book.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r6] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The preposition bi is attached to an omitted verb such as I read or recite in God's name; the reciter supplies the action begun by the basmala.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | In the first-revealed surah, placing the command to read before the basmala is more fitting because the reading command is paramount. | mentions 96:1
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | One analysis makes the name relate to reciting as a pen relates to writing: the believer makes the act God's by beginning with His name, as a prophetic report says.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from the Prophet says that an important matter begun without God's name is cut off.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | prefers | The other analysis treats reciting as occurring in the blessing of God's name; al-Zamakhshari calls this account more idiomatic and better. | mentions 23:20
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The omitted governing verb is placed after the basmala because God's name, the more important element, should come first and signal exclusive invocation of God.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The preposed divine name conveys exclusivity, as in the explicit object-first wording of You alone we worship. | mentions 1:5
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The basmala's omitted verb is illustrated by Arabic prayers for a newly married couple and by a poet's account of being called to a meal.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The construction is supported by Noah's words about embarking and landing in God's name. | mentions 11:41
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The divine basmala and praise on worshippers' tongues teach them how to invoke, praise, glorify, and magnify God.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | One-letter particles usually take fatḥa; lām takes kasra to distinguish it from the introductory lām, while bi takes kasra because it is inherently a preposition.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The noun ism begins with a consonant cluster, so speakers add a connecting hamza at utterance onset; some instead pronounce sim or sum by moving the initial consonant.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Ism is a noun with a deleted ending, originally sumw, derived from elevation because naming raises and publicizes the named one.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The word nabz for a nickname is related to nabr, raising the voice; nabz also names the outer peel of a palm tree.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r6] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The alif in bism is omitted in writing because connected use is frequent; the lengthened bā compensates for it, and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz told his scribe to lengthen the bā. | mentions 96:1
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r7] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Allah derives from al-ilah; the generic word for a deity became specific to the true God, just as al-najm came to denote the Pleiades.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Allah, with its hamza deleted, is uniquely the name of the true God and is not used for another being; verbs meaning to deify derive from it.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Allah is a noun, not an adjective: it can be qualified but does not itself qualify an unspecified thing, and divine attributes require a named subject.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | He also links Allah to aliha, to be bewildered: minds are dazed by trying to comprehend God, and lack of sound reflection lets error spread.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj says pronouncing Allah's lām emphatically is a sunnah; universal Arab practice shows it was inherited generation after generation.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Rahman is the emphatic fa'lan form of mercy, while Rahim is fa'il; the former is more intensive, and added form signals added meaning.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r6] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Rahman functions as an exclusive, established epithet for God, like Allah, and is not ordinarily used of anyone else.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | rejects | Calling Musaylima Rahman of Yamama, including in his poet's praise, is presented as a facet of the Banu Hanifa's unbelieving perversity.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Rahman should be indeclinable by analogy with fa'lan adjectives such as عطشان and سكران, even though its divine specialization prevents a feminine form.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | God's mercy is figurative language for His beneficence: a kindly ruler does good to subjects, whereas harshness withholds favor.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | He raises the question why the more emphatic attribute precedes the lesser when normal usage would progress from the lesser to the greater.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The ordering is complementary: Rahman covers great and foundational blessings, and Rahim completes it by covering blessings that are delicate and subtle.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r1] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · ابن عباس، وموسى بن جعفر عن أبيه، وعلي بن الحسين، وقتادة، وأبو العالية، ومحمد بن يحيى بن حبان | reports | Ibn Abbas, Musa b.
