Habban hold that al-Fatiha is Meccan; 15:87 supports this because al-Hijr is unanimously Meccan. | mentions 15:87
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r10] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · جمهور العلماء | reports | The majority of scholars permit the title Umm al-Quran, contrary to Ibn Sirin's dislike.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r11] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · يحيى بن يعمر | reports | Yahya b. Ya'mar analogizes Umm al-Quran to Umm al-Qura for Mecca and Umm Khurasan for Merv.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r12] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · الحسن بن أبي الحسن | reports | Hasan b. Abi al-Hasan also gives al-Fatiha the name Umm al-Quran.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r13] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | reports | One explanation of al-Mathani is that the surah is repeated in every prayer cycle.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r14] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | reports | Another explanation is that al-Fatiha was reserved as a treasure for this community and had not been revealed to anyone before it.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r15] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن أبي بن كعب | reports | The Prophet told Ubayy that no comparable surah had been revealed in the Torah, Gospel or Qur'an.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r16] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · غير مسمى | reports | An unnamed report says al-Fatiha is equivalent to two-thirds of the Qur'an.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r17] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | The reported equivalence may reflect the surah's meanings or be a divine preference not rationally explained; similar equivalences are reported for al-Ikhlas and al-Zalzala. | mentions 112:1, 99:1
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r18] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · أنس بن مالك عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Anas reports that the Prophet assigned al-Fatiha thirty more merits than other speech.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r19] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A further Prophetic report assigns twenty merits to saying la ilaha illa Allah and thirty to saying al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r2] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · أبي بن كعب | reports | Ubayy's report identifies al-Fatiha as the seven oft-repeated; the seven long surahs were revealed some time after al-Hijr, supporting a Meccan dating. | mentions 15:87
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r20] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | The merit comparison concerns believers seeking reward: al-hamdu combines praise with the monotheism contained in la ilaha illa Allah, while the latter contains monotheism alone.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r21] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | In their role of warding off unbelief and association, la ilaha illa Allah is superior; the Prophet called it the best statement he and earlier prophets had uttered.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r22] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · جعفر بن محمد الصادق | reports | Ja'far al-Sadiq calls the basmala the crowns of the surahs.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r23] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | When a man cursed Satan in the Prophet's presence, the Prophet said this magnified Satan and instructed him to say the basmala, which makes Satan shrink smaller than a fly.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r24] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · علي بن الحسين | reports | Ali b. al-Husayn interprets the turning away in 17:46 when the Lord is mentioned alone as occurring when one says the basmala. | mentions 17:46
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r25] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · جابر بن عبد الله عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Jabir says that when he told the Prophet he opened prayer with al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin, the Prophet told him to say the basmala.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r26] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abu Hurayra reports that Gabriel taught the Prophet prayer and recited the basmala aloud.

27] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | reports | Ibn Atiyya says that, on their face, the Jabir and Abu Hurayra reports imply the basmala is an ayah of al-Fatiha.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r28] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · أبي بن كعب عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | An authentic report has the Prophet ask Ubayy to recite the surah; Ubayy begins with al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin and continues to its end, without the basmala.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r29] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · الله تعالى في الحديث القدسي | reports | The sound hadith qudsi describing prayer as divided between God and the servant quotes the servant beginning with al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin, not the basmala.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r3] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | Prayer became obligatory in Mecca, and no report preserves a Muslim prayer without reciting al-Fatiha; this supports its Meccan origin.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r30] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | No record says the Prophet or Abu Bakr, Umar or Uthman recited the basmala in prayer.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r31] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | The surah is counted as seven verses by consensus, apart from the anomalous report that al-Husayn al-Ju'fi counted six.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r32] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · حسين الجعفي | rejects | Al-Husayn al-Ju'fi reportedly counts six verses in al-Fatiha; Ibn Atiyya calls this anomalous and unreliable.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r33] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · عمرو بن عبيد | rejects | Amr b. Ubayd makes iyyaka na'budu a separate verse, yielding eight; Ibn Atiyya also calls this anomalous.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r34] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | prefers | The statement that God gave the Prophet seven oft-repeated verses in 15:87 settles the verse-count question. | mentions 15:87
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r35] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafi'i counts the basmala as a verse of al-Fatiha.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r36] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · قراء مكة والكوفة | reports | Many Meccan and Kufan reciters do not count an'amta alayhim as a verse.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r37] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · مالك، وأبو حنيفة، وجمهور الفقهاء والقراء | prefers | Malik, Abu Hanifa and the majority of jurists and reciters do not count the basmala as a verse.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r38] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | prefers | If sound, the Jabir and Abu Hurayra reports can be understood as lessons: the Prophet saw them rehearsing prayer outside prayer and taught the basmala for that reason, not because it was a verse.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r39] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | The Prophet did not include the basmala in his exchange with Ubayy because he was identifying the special surah and its virtue, whereas that purpose was absent in the instructional exchanges with Jabir and Abu Hurayra.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r4] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · عطاء بن يسار، وسوادة بن زياد، والزهري محمد بن مسلم، وعبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير | reports | Ata b. Yasar, Sawada b. Ziyad, al-Zuhri and Abd Allah b. Ubayd b. Umayr instead regard al-Fatiha as Medinan.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r40] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · ابن المبارك | rejects | Ibn al-Mubarak holds that the basmala is a verse in every surah; Ibn Atiyya calls this an anomalous view rejected by others.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r41] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · الشعبي والأعمش | reports | Al-Sha'bi and al-A'mash report a progression in the Prophet's written basmala: first Bismika Allahumma, then Bismillah, then Bismillah al-Rahman, and after 27:30 the full formula. | mentions 17:110, 27:30
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r42] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · عمرو بن شرحبيل | reports | Amr b. Shurahbil reports that Gabriel first came to the Prophet saying, “Say: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Compassionate.”
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r43] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas reports that the first thing Gabriel brought down was the basmala.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r44] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · خديجة عن ورقة | reports | In some versions of Khadija's taking the Prophet to Waraqa, Gabriel first tells the Prophet to say the basmala; the Prophet says it, then Gabriel commands him to read, and he replies that he cannot read.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r45] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · بعض الناس | reports | Some say the nineteen letters of the basmala correspond one by one to the nineteen keepers of Hell in 74:30, whose repeated basmala gives them strength. | mentions 74:30
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r46] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | rejects | Ibn Atiyya calls the letter-count explanation a playful exegetical conceit, not sound scholarship.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r47] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | rejects | He compares that numerology with claims that the Night of Decree is the twenty-seventh night because of a word in its surah, and that thirty-some angels rushed to record a thirty-some-letter praise formula. | mentions 97:3
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r48] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | rejects | A similar letter-count claim says thirty-some angels competed to record “Our Lord, to You belongs praise, abundant, good and blessed praise”; Ibn Atiyya presents it as the same sort of numerology.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r49] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · نحاة البصرة | reports | Basran grammarians attach the preposition bi- to an implied noun such as ibtida'i, mustaqirr or thabit, making the whole basmala nominative in their analysis.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r5] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | There is no disagreement that the surah is called Fatihat al-Kitab because its position makes it the opening of the Book.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r50] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · نحاة الكوفة | reports | Kufan grammarians attach bi- to an implied verb, “I begin,” and parse the basmala as accusative.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r51] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · سيبويه | reports | Ibn Atiyya says Sibawayh apparently attaches bi- to a noun, yet treats the phrase as accusative through attachment to thabit or mustaqirr, like Zayd is in the house.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r52] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | reports | The kasra on bi- is explained as matching its grammatical action, because it governs nouns, or to distinguish it from particles that can also be nouns.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r53] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | reports | Al-A'sha's use of kaf is cited as an example of a particle that can function as a noun, motivating a distinctive genitive mark for bi-.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r54] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | The alif is omitted from the written basmala for brevity and ease because the phrase is so frequently used.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r55] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · الكسائي وسعيد الأخفش، ويحيى بن زياد | reports | Al-Kisa'i and Sa'id al-Akhfash omit the alif in bism al-Rahman and bism al-Qahir; Yahya b. Ziyad says omission applies only with Allah because that phrase is especially frequent. Ibn Atiyya says the alif remains with other names.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r56] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · نحاة البصرة | reports | Basran grammarians derive ism from sumuww, elevation, from sama yasmu; the form is associated with either damma or kasra in the initial consonant.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r57] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | The diminutive sumayy, plural asma', and plural-of-plural asami support the Basran etymology; a poetic form simahu is also cited.
[IBNATIYYA:1:1/r58] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · نحاة الكوفة | reports | Kufans derive ism from wasm, a mark, since a name marks its bearer; Ibn Atiyya says this sense is apt but morphology counters it, since the forms should be wasim and awsām.

[TABRISI:1:1#2/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | One reported derivation connects Allah with worship and servitude; on it God alone deserves worship, and a cited Ibn Abbas reading glosses the verb as worship.

[TABRISI:1:1#2/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Another derivation links the name with fleeing for refuge, because creatures turn to God for their needs.
[TABRISI:1:1#2/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · المبرد | reports | Al-Mubarrad derives the name from finding repose with God, since creatures become at rest through remembering Him.
[TABRISI:1:1#2/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | A final derivation takes it from lah, meaning hidden: God is hidden in modality from minds but manifest through signs and proofs.
[TABRISI:1:1#2/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Rahman and Rahim are intensive forms derived from mercy, and Rahman is more intensive; Abu Ubayda distinguishes the possessor of mercy from the merciful one.
[TABRISI:1:1#3/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | rejects | The author rejects Thaʿlab's claim that Rahman is foreign because Arabic poetry attests the word.
[TABRISI:1:1#3/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The preposition bā originally marks attachment and brings an action onto its object; an i

[TABRISI:1:1#3/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو علي الفارسي | rejects | Abu Ali rejects attaching bā to the hidden verbal noun ibtidaʾ because this would leave the implied subject without a predicate.
[TABRISI:1:1#3/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو عمرو الجرمي | reports | The bā is kasra because it must be pronounceable at the start of speech; kasra was chosen as the appropriate connecting vowel.
[TABRISI:1:1#3/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو علي الحسن بن عبد الغفار الفارسي | reports | Abu Ali al-Farsi says any vowel would have served for starting the word; some Arabs use fatḥa, though the author calls that dialect weak.
[TABRISI:1:1#3/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The hamzat al-waṣl of ism drops in connected pronunciation and is omitted in writing here because the basmala is frequent and unambiguous, unlike the less frequent Qur'anic form in 96:1. | mentions 96:1
[TABRISI:1:1#4/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | God's lām is pronounced emphatically after fatḥa or ḍamma to glorify Him and distinguish the name from al-Lāt.
[TABRISI:1:1#4/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Allah is genitive by annexation, and Rahman and Rahim are genitive as adjectives of Allah.
[TABRISI:1:1#4/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | One interpretation makes the basmala an appeal for aid through God's beautiful names and exalted attributes; another simply means seek help from God.
[TABRISI:1:1#4/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abu Ubayda treats the word ism as an extra connective and takes the basmala to mean Allah Himself, as in Labid's verse.
[TABRISI:1:1#4/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | A name can stand for its referent because speech or address attached to the name is in reality attached to the named thing.
[TABRISI:1:1#4/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | prefers | The preferred reading is begin by naming God: the command teaches opening actions with God's name, as in eating, drinking, and slaughter, rather than merely reporting His majesty.
[TABRISI:1:1#4/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | God alone merits worship because He can create bodies, give life, and bestow blessings; defining deity only by earned benefaction wrongly excludes God before creation.
[TABRISI:1:1#4/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Rahman precedes Rahim because Rahman functions like a proper name exclusive to God, while Rahim can describe others too.
[TABRISI:1:1#5/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · عيسى ابن مريم | reports | A prophetic report quotes Jesus as saying Rahman is merciful in this world and Rahim is merciful in the afterlife.
[TABRISI:1:1#5/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · بعض التابعين | reports | Some Successors say Rahman embraces all creation while Rahim is especially for believers; the author explains this by creation and provision for all and guidance, Paradise, honor, and forgiveness for believers.
[TABRISI:1:1#5/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · الصادق | reports | Al-Sadiq formulates the distinction as a special name with a general attribute for Rahman, and a general name with a special attribute for Rahim.
[TABRISI:1:1#5/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · عكرمة | reports | Ikrima says Rahman signifies one mercy and Rahim a hundred mercies.
[TABRISI:1:1#5/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · النبي | reports | The Prophet says God has one hundred mercies, sent one to earth for mutual compassion and reserved ninety-nine to show mercy on Judgment Day.
[TABRISI:1:1#5/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Another report says God will take the earthly mercy back and complete it to one hundred to show mercy to His servants on Judgment Day.
[TABRISI:1:1/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · أصحابنا | holds | The author's companions hold that the basmala is a verse of al-Fatiha and every sura; omitting it invalidates obligatory and supererogatory prayer, and they favor audible recitation.
[TABRISI:1:1/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · سيبويه | reports | On this analysis the alif in lah comes from yā; Sibawayh explains a transposition of the letters and cites lahi as evidence.
[TABRISI:1:1/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · حمزة وخلف ويعقوب واليزيدي | reports | These readers do not use the basmala to separate suras; the other readers do, except between al-Anfal and al-Tawba.
[TABRISI:1:1/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · علي بن موسى الرضا | reports | Al-Rida says the basmala is nearer to God's Greatest Name than the black of the eye is to its white.
[TABRISI:1:1/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · النبي | reports | The Prophet promises absolution for a child, the child's parents, and the teacher when the child learns and recites the basmala.
[TABRISI:1:1/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masud says reciting the basmala protects a person from the nineteen keepers of Hell, one letter serving as protection from each.
[TABRISI:1:1/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · الصادق | reports | Al-Sadiq condemns those who call the basmala an innovation when they recite it aloud, calling it the greatest verse in God's Book.
[TABRISI:1:1/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | prefers | The author prefers deriving ism from sumu, elevation: its original waw is supported by its plural asma and diminutive sumayy.
[TABRISI:1:1/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Allah is an exclusive divine name and is not applied to anyone besides God.
[TABRISI:1:1/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · سيبويه | reports | One analysis derives Allah from lah; the article marks glorification and exaltation, not definiteness, since God's names are already definite.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn ʿUmar says the basmala was revealed in every sūra.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r10] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ records forms with smah among some Qays speakers and some Quḍāʿa speakers, citing a line that uses the form.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r11] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Qarḍāb means a cutter, and a sword can be called qarḍāb.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r12] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · العلماء | reports | Scholars disagree whether the divine name Allāh is derived or an underived proper name.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r13] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الخليل | reports | One view attributed to al-Khalīl says Allāh is not derived and its alif-lām cannot be dropped as it can from al-Raḥmān.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r14] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الخليل عن سيبويه | reports | A second report from al-Khalīl, transmitted by Sībawayh, holds that Allāh is derived.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r15] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو سليمان الخطابي | reports | Al-Khaṭṭābī transmits an etymology from a-l-h, meaning to seek refuge; God is so named as the one who protects and grants safety.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r16] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · غيره | reports | Another etymology derives Allāh from wālah, with initial wāw changed into hamza, as in wisāda and wishāḥ becoming ishāḥ.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · العلماء | reports | Scholars disagree whether the basmala is a complete verse; Aḥmad has two transmitted positions.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · العلماء | reports | Scholars also disagree whether it is part of al-Fātiḥa; two positions are transmitted from Aḥmad.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · القائلون إنها من الفاتحة | reports | Those who count it as part of al-Fātiḥa require its recitation in prayer because al-Fātiḥa itself is obligatory.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · القائلون إنها ليست من الفاتحة | reports | Those who do not count it as part of al-Fātiḥa regard reciting it in prayer as sunnah, while Mālik does not recommend its recitation.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أحمد ومن وافقه | reports | Aḥmad and the listed Companions and early authorities do not regard reciting the basmala aloud in audible prayers as recommended.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī recommends reciting the basmala aloud; this view is also reported from Muʿāwiya, ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, and Mujāhid.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Bismillāh is elliptical for I begin or I began in God's name.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r9] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The word ism has five reported forms, including ism, asm, sim, sum, and samā; the cited poetry witnesses these forms.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · بعضهم | reports | Some derive the divine name from bewilderment: hearts are bewildered when contemplating God's greatness.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r11] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet said no comparable sūra was revealed in the Torah, Gospel, Psalms, or Qur'an; al-Fātiḥa is the seven oft-repeated verses and the great Qur'an given to him.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r12] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Al-Fātiḥa is so named because the book begins with it in recitation and writing; Umm al-Qur'an and Umm al-Kitāb because it leads the book; al-sabʿ al-mathānī is explained later in 15:87. | mentions 15:87
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r13] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · علي بن أبي طالب والحسن وأبو العالية وقتادة وأبو ميسرة | reports | One view holds that al-Fātiḥa was revealed in Mecca.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r14] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو هريرة ومجاهد وعبيد بن عمير وعطاء الخراساني | reports | A second view holds that al-Fātiḥa was revealed in Medina; Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have held both views.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The derivation from hearts' longing is linked to 16:53, where people call upon God in distress. | mentions 16:53
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | On the derivation from longing, the expected form would be maʾlūh like maʿbūd, but it diverges from that pattern to become a proper name, as kitāb and ḥisāb do.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · بعض اللغويين | reports | Some linguists derive the word from alaha yaʾlah, mea

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās glosses Pharaoh's reference to his gods at 7:127 as your worship; taʾalluh means worship, and the deity is the worshiped one. | mentions 7:127
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · رؤبة | reports | A line by Ruʾba uses taʾalluh as evidence for the worship-related derivation.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الجمهور | reports | Most scholars derive al-Raḥmān from mercy as an intensive form, meaning the possessor of unmatched mercy; faʿlān marks intensity.

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r9] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الخطابي | reports | Al-Khaṭṭābī says al-Raḥmān's encompassing mercy covers creatures' provisions and interests and includes believers and unbelievers.
[RAZI:1:1/r1] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi sketches the sūra’s sequence: seek refuge from sins, begin good works in God’s name, praise and recognize his lordship and mercy, heed judgment, worship and seek help, ask guidance, and avoid ignorance and error.
[RAZI:1:1/r10] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Knowing a divine name presupposes knowing its referent, arguments for the referent’s existence, and answers to objections against it; these inquiries alone exceed a thousand questions.
[RAZI:1:1/r11] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | The bāʾ is for attachment and governs an implied verb: “In God’s name I begin performing acts of obedience.”
[RAZI:1:1/r12] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Understanding the implied beginning requires surveying all obedience: true creeds and sincere deeds, their proofs, and answers to objections, a body of inquiry that may exceed ten thousand questions.
[RAZI:1:1/r13] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | The refuge formula negates improper beliefs and acts, while the basmala affirms what ought to be believed and done; sound reason and clear truth support this order.
[RAZI:1:1/r2] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi says the Fātiḥa can yield ten thousand useful questions; he wrote the introduction to show that this claim is attainable, despite the scoffing of envious and ignorant opponents.
[RAZI:1:1/r3] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Seeking refuge in God means seeking protection from every prohibited act, including sins and wrong beliefs.
[RAZI:1:1/r4] RAZI, d. 606 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Razi cites as a famous prophetic report that the community will divide into seventy-three sects, all in the Fire except one; he says this shows the other seventy-two hold false creeds.
[RAZI:1:1/r5] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Each deviant Muslim sect errs across many questions concerning God’s essence, attributes, rulings, acts and names, as well as compulsion, decree, justice, reward, resurrection, promises, threats, legal status and imamate.
[RAZI:1:1/r6] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi says the roughly seven hundred deviant sects outside the Muslim community add further errors in rational theology and questions of essences and attributes, all covered by seeking refuge.
[RAZI:1:1/r7] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Prohibited actions include whatever the Qur’an, mass-transmitted or solitary reports, communal consensus, or sound analogy forbids; their number exceeds a thousand and the refuge formula encompasses them all.
[RAZI:1:1/r8] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | One can seek refuge from something only after knowing it and recognizing its falsehood and ugliness; thus this formula contains thousands of substantial, certain questions.
[RAZI:1:1/r9] RAZI, d. 606 · العلماء | reports | Razi reports the scholarly convention that God has 1,001 sacred names found in scripture and Sunna, and says inquiry into each name is a noble subject.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p100/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Al-Razi rejects 'Possessor of Majesty and Honor' as the greatest name because majesty and honor denote negative and relational attributes, not the unique essence. | mentions 55:27
[RAZI-FULL:v1p100/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Al-Razi cites a prophetic report urging frequent invocation of the Possessor of Majesty and Honor as support for that candidate name.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p100/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | The Prophet asks Ubayy ibn Kaʿb which verse is greatest; Ubayy answers the Throne Verse and receives praise for his knowledge. | mentions 2:255
[RAZI-FULL:v1p100/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Al-Razi rejects al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm as greatest because 'Living' is a cognitive and active attribute and 'Self-subsisting Sustainer' combines negation with relation. | mentions 2:255
[RAZI-FULL:v1p100/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · من يقول إن أسماء الله كلها عظيمة | rejects | Al-Razi rejects the view that every divine name is equally greatest, since a name denoting the unique essence is nobler.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p100/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | The closest view is that 'Allah' is the greatest name because it functions as a proper name for God and denotes His unique essence.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p100/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A name referring to a part of a referent's essence is impossible for God: every composite depends on other parts and is therefore contingent.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p101#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · عمران بن الحصين | reports | A prophetic report says, 'God was and there was no other thing'; al-Razi cites it to show that 'thing' can apply to God.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p101#2/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · جهم بن صفوان | reports | Jahm says the Prophet and Companions never addressed God as 'thing,' a low term; instead they invoked Him as creator of things, earth, and heaven.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p101#2/r11] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-Razi says the disagreement concerns wording only, not whether God exists or has a real essence, and it entails neither disbelief nor condemnation.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p101#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · عائشة | reports | A report collected by ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī says the Prophet described nothing as more jealous than God.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p101#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A thing is anything that can be known and reported about; God's essence can be known and reported about, so it qualifies.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p101#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · جهم بن صفوان | reports | Jahm objects that the Qur'an calls God creator of every thing and powerful over every thing, which would imply He is created and subject to power. | mentions 13:16, 5:120
[RAZI-FULL:v1p101#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Al-Razi counters that excluding God from 'everything' is linguistically disfavored; custom permits exceptions only for a trivial minority, and God cannot be considered trivial. | mentions 13:16, 5:120
[RAZI-FULL:v1p101#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · جهم بن صفوان | reports | Jahm reads 'nothing is like His likeness' to mean God is not a thing, since every thing resembles itself. | mentions 42:11
[RAZI-FULL:v1p101#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Al-Razi says treating the kāf as extra makes part of God's speech vain and false; the verse must retain its force. | mentions 42:11
[RAZI-FULL:v1p101#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · جهم بن صفوان | reports | Jahm argues that 'thing' is a common term including lowly entities and conveys no praise, whereas God's names must express praise and majesty. | mentions 7:180
[RAZI-FULL:v1p101#2/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Al-Razi explains that God's beautiful names denote lofty qualities; the command to invoke Him by them warns against calling Him by an unpraiseworthy term. | mentions 7:180
[RAZI-FULL:v1p101/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | With part-based names excluded, seven attribute-based kinds remain; al-Razi begins with names denoting a real attribute belonging to God's unique essence.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p101/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الجمهور | holds | Most scholars permit calling God 'a thing'; their first proof is the Qur'an's question about which thing is greatest in testimony, answered by saying God witnesses. | mentions 6:19
[RAZI-FULL:v1p101/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | They also cite 'Everything perishes except His face,' understanding His face as His essence; the exception implies that God is included under 'thing.' | mentions 28:88
[RAZI-FULL:v1p103/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | 'Existence' has two meanings: awareness or discovery, and actual subsistence. Knowing that something exists requires it to exist, but it can exist without being known.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p103/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Al-Razi thinks the word first meant awareness or discovery, since people perceive a thing before recognizing its actual existence; he treats the issue as lexical.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p103/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The Qur'anic phrase 'they would have found God' uses existence to mean finding or recognizing Him; the Qur'an does not use the other sense, actual subsistence, here. | mentions 4:64
[RAZI-FULL:v1p103/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | An objector's inference from recognized existence to actual existence fails: nonexistent things can be known, and a word used in one sense does not establish its use in another.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p103/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Muslim consensus permits calling God 'existent'; unlike 'thing,' this term cannot apply to what is nonexistent and therefore conveys praise, including that God's proofs are evident to every mind.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p104#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The Qur'an uses 'self' of God when God says He knows what is in His self and warns people about His self. | mentions 5:116, 3:28
[RAZI-FULL:v1p104#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · عائشة | reports | ʿĀʾisha reports finding the Prophet prostrating beside her and supplicating for refuge in God's pleasure, pardon, and self, saying he cannot praise God adequately.

ة | reports | Abū Hurayra reports a divine saying: God is with the servant who remembers Him, remembers the servant in return, and responds more generously to the servant's approach.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p104#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · عبد الله بن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masʿūd reports that no one loves praise more than God, who praises Himself, and no one is more jealous, so God forbids indecency and sends scripture and messengers to excuse people.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p104#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · عائشة | reports | ʿĀʾisha reports that the Prophet taught a glorification using the number of His creatures, the ink of His words, His self's pleasure, and the weight of His Throne.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p104#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو ذر | reports | Abū Dharr reports a divine saying: God forbade injustice upon Himself and made it forbidden among people, commanding them not to wrong one another.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p104#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn ʿUmar reports that after reciting 'They did not measure God with His true measure,' the Prophet magnified God with names such as the Compeller and Proud; the pulpit shook. | mentions 6:91
[RAZI-FULL:v1p104/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · عائشة | reports | Al-Anṣārī al-Harawī reports from ʿĀʾisha that the Prophet said the greatest reward belongs to a righteous minister who obeys a ruler in God's cause.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p104/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو هريرة | reports | Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet saying that Abraham lied only three times, twice in God's cause.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p104/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · كعب بن عجرة | reports | Kaʿb ibn ʿUjra reports from his father the Prophet's instruction not to insult ʿAlī, who was devoted in God's cause.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p104/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو ذر | reports | Abū Dharr reports that the Prophet called struggle against one's self and desires in God's cause the best jihad.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p104/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النعمان بن بشير | reports | Al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr reports the Prophet naming Satan's traps: pride in God's blessings, boasting of His gifts, arrogance toward God's servants, and following desire outside God's cause.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p104/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Dhāt denotes the relation of a subject to an attribute; attributes cannot regress infinitely through further attributes, so they must belong to a self-subsisting essence, making the term true of God.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p104/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | In these reports, 'in God's dhāt' means seeking God's pleasure, not referring to His essence or nature.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | God is unsurpassed in jealousy, love of excuse, and love of praise; His jealousy is why He forbids public and hidden indecencies and sends messengers.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105#2/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Calling God Light is sound because He illuminates, originates, and creates all lights.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105#2/r11] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God may be called the world's light because His wisdom orders worldly and afterlife benefits, as a town's organizer of welfare is called its light.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105#2/r12] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God may be called Light because He grants faith, guidance, and knowledge, which belong to the kind of spiritual lights. | mentions 24:35
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The divine term person does not mean a body with volume and individuation; it means a particular essence and determinate self.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | The Prophet reports that God created creatures in darkness, then cast some of His light upon them; those touched by it were guided and others went astray.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | God cannot literally be this light or a member of its kind: light is either a created body or an accident in a created body.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Literal light is opposed by darkness, but God is transcendent beyond having any opposite.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Light disappears and undergoes setting, whereas God is beyond disappearance and passing away.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | He treats God as Light of the heavens and earth as an ambiguous verse whose interpretation is governed by rational proofs that God is not literally light. | mentions 24:35
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The phrase His light marks possession, like a thing attributed to its owner, and therefore means God creates light rather than being light in essence. | mentions 24:35
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105#2/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A reading that says God owns the light of the heavens and earth removes the apparent difficulty of calling Him light. | mentions 24:35
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | Adam answers Moses that God chose him, revealed the Torah, and had decreed Adam's act before creating him; Adam thus prevails over Moses three times.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | God says the religion He approves is repaired only through generosity and good character, and people should honor it through both.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | In a divine report, one who insults God's friend is at war with God; God may destroy him, while He dislikes taking the believer's life though death is inevitable.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | A supplication invoking every name God gave or kept hidden asks that the Quran enliven the heart and remove grief; God replaces the supplicant's sorrow with joy.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | The Prophet says he was sent as mercy to the worlds and to break instruments and idols; an unrepentant drinker receives the pus of Hell, called clay of corruption.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p105/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Divine self (nafs) means the thing's essence and identity, not a composite body: every body is composed, possible, and originated, which is impossible of God.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p106/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | The Prophet warns that a believer's discernment looks by God's light.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p106/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | The most prudent person remembers death and prepares for it; turning from the deluding world toward the eternal home lets light expand the heart for preparation.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p106/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | Explaining 39:22, the Prophet says light entering the heart expands it; its signs are turning to the lasting home, leaving delusion, and preparing for death. | mentions 39:22
[RAZI-FULL:v1p106/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | Haritha describes detachment, worship, and seeming to see the Throne, Paradise, and Hell; the Prophet tells him he has recognized faith, urges him to persist, and Haritha later dies a martyr.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p106/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | An angel tells the Prophet that two lights never granted to anyone before him are the Opening of the Book and the closing verses of al-Baqara.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p107#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · إسحاق بن راهويه | reports | Ishaq ibn Rahawayh judges sound the report that God created Adam in the image of the Merciful.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p107#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | In a report from Muadh, the Prophet describes seeing his Lord in the most beautiful form, being asked about the highest assembly, and receiving knowledge of the heavens and earth.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p107#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · العلماء | reports | One interpretation makes the pronoun in Adam's image refer to the person struck, requiring care not to disfigure that person's face.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p107#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · العلماء | reports | A second interpretation says Adam was created in his final adult form at once, without passing through semen, embryo, or infancy.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p107#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · العلماء | reports | A third interpretation takes image as attribute: Adam was made God's earthly vicegerent, exercising control over earthly bodies as God exercises power over the world.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p107#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفلاسفة | reports | Philosophers call God a substance because they define substance as a self-subsisting essence independent of a substrate; they read its root as manifestness and say God is most manifest through proofs.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p107#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النصارى | reports | The text groups Christians with philosophers in applying the term substance to God, while noting the theologians reject the term.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p107#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المتكلمون | reports | Theologians say Muslims unanimously avoid calling God a substance, so the term must be avoided.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p107/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | Ibn Umar's prayer asks God to make him share in each day's guidance-light, mercy, provision, relief from harm, protection from trials, and removal of evil.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p107/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | Asked about Paradise's people, the Prophet says that though unkempt and poorly clothed, one person's light would suffice for all the earth.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p107/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | A second report describes humble, ragged people overlooked by rulers and suitors; their inward need is hidden, and one person's light would suffice for the earth.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p107/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | In a divine report, God says His light is His guidance and that whoever professes His word of divine unity enters His fortress and is safe.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p107/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | The Prophet seeks protection in God's complete words and H

[RAZI-FULL:v1p107/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | The Prophet's well-known prayer asks for light in his heart, hearing, and sight.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p107/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | The Prophet says God created Adam in His image.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p107/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | The Prophet forbids disfiguring faces, saying God created Adam in the image of the Merciful.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p108/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الكرامية | reports | Most Karramiyya call God a body but define this as a self-subsisting existent independent of a substrate, not as a composite of limbs; other groups reject the name.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p108/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Razi denies that Karramiyya mean something other than length, breadth, and depth: their claim that God is above and greater than the Throne entails a spatially extended body.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p108/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | The word body suggests a false meaning and is absent from Quran and hadith, so it should be avoided; theologians say it entails multiplicity of parts.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p109#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God's eternal existence does not require an eternal time: if it needs time, that time is either eternal and requires another time without end, or originated after God already existed.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p109#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Everything eternal is everlasting, but not everything everlasting is eternal; scripture calls the Lord's face enduring and says all perish except His face. | mentions 55:27, 28:88
[RAZI-FULL:v1p109#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Calling God first and last of all things means He has neither beginning nor end, since otherwise He could not be first and last with respect to all else. | mentions 57:3
[RAZI-FULL:v1p109#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The world's creator cannot be originated, since an originated creator would require another creator and an impossible regress; whatever is eternal cannot cease.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p109#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Qadim originally denotes long duration rather than absence of a beginning, as in an old date-palm and an old error; it does not by itself prove eternity. | mentions 36:39, 12:95
[RAZI-FULL:v1p109/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Applied to a thing itself, true means really existent, since its opposite false means nonexistent; Labid's verse says everything apart from God is false.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p109/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Applied to belief, true means a correct belief matching the thing as it is, and therefore deserving of affirmation and preservation.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p109/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Applied to speech or reports, true means truthful correspondence, making the statement worthy of affirmation and preservation.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p109/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God deserves the name True in every sense: His existence cannot cease, belief in Him is correct and unchanging, and speaking of Him is the truest report.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p110/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Azali means related to pre-eternity, but must not imply that God exists inside some pre-eternal thing; it means existence without any beginning.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p110/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Every eternal thing is enduring, but an enduring body or accident need not be eternal; ordinary usage also calls a person enduring, so baqi does not require eternity. | mentions 55:27
[RAZI-FULL:v1p110/r11] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Some say baqi means everlasting and therefore cannot describe bodies, but Razi rejects that restriction because ordinary speakers say may God preserve you.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p110/r12] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God is the one most deserving of the name lasting; the Quran also uses the word for Paradise's fruit. | mentions 13:35
[RAZI-FULL:v1p110/r13] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Necessary existent in itself means that God's essence and reality entail His existence, making Him incapable of nonexistence or perishing.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p110/r14] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Every necessary existent is eternal, but an eternally caused thing could be eternal without being necessary in itself.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p110/r15] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The Persian word khuda means self-arrived: it combines self and came, indicating that God came to existence through Himself rather than another.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p110/r16] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Kain is used in the Quran for God's attributes, though not for His essence; supplications attributed to the Prophet do use it of God's essence.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p110/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Some say no beginning is a positive attribute because negating prior nonexistence amounts to affirming existence.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p110/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Others say no beginning is privative: it negates being preceded by nonexistence, a positive condition distinct from nonexistence itself.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p110/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Razi answers that if being preceded by nonexistence were an additional positive property, that property would itself be originated and require another such property without end.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p110/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Abadi denotes duration into the future.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p110/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Sarmadi derives from succession: since time persists through successive parts, the literal term implies succession, impossible for God; use it metaphorically only if scripture or hadith uses it.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p110/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | The cited Prophetic saying calls the sacred months one single month followed by three consecutive months, illustrating the root sense of succession.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p110/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Mustamirr derives from passing and suits time, which persists as parts pass successively, but not God, whose persistence is intrinsic rather than successive.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p110/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Extended likewise describes time and temporal things because their parts unfold in sequence; of God it is metaphorical.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p111/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | A Prophetic supplication addresses God as existing before every existence, present with every existence, and remaining after every existence.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p111/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Grammarians call kana complete when it means happened or existed, and deficient when it has a subject and predicate, as in God was knowing and wise. | mentions 3:110, 4:11
[RAZI-FULL:v1p111/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Razi challenges grammarians: if kana as a verb denotes an event in time, attaching one noun should express that event fully, making it complete rather than deficient.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p111/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Kana denotes occurrence or existence; for an entity's own occurrence one noun suffices, while occurrence of a quality requires both the subject and predicate.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p111/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | On this analysis, kain and existent have the same meaning, so kain may properly be applied to God.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p112/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة والفلاسفة | reports | Mu'tazilites and philosophers deny that real attributes distinct from existence and its modes subsist in God.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p112/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة والفلاسفة | reports | They argue a self-complete essence needs no attributes, while an incomplete essence perfected by another cannot be divine.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p112/r11] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة والفلاسفة | reports | They say a God composed of essence and attributes would be divided and composite, hence possible rather than necessary.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p112/r12] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة والفلاسفة | reports | They infer from God's condemnation of Christian trinitarianism that affirming attributes is unbelief, since Christians combine one essence with attributes rather than affirming three gods.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p112/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة والفلاسفة | reports | They argue an attribute cannot be necessary in itself, since only one necessary existent exists and an attribute depends on its subject.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p112/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة والفلاسفة | reports | They argue an attribute cannot be possible in itself: if caused by another, God's necessary essence would depend on it; if caused by God's essence, God would be both agent and recipient.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p112/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة والفلاسفة | reports | They add that a produced effect cannot depend on its cause after it exists, which would be circular; dependence during or before production makes the attribute originated.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p112/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة والفلاسفة | reports | They argue eternal essence and eternal attributes would share eternity but differ in their specific natures, making each a composite of parts and generating an impossible infinite regress.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p112/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة والفلاسفة | reports | They say originated attributes cannot subsist in God: either His essence suffices for them and they should be eternally present or absent, or their dependence makes the necessary God contingent.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p112/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة والفلاسفة | reports | They argue an eternally receptive essence would have to be capable of receiving originated events in eternity, which they deem impossible.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p112/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة والفلاسفة | reports | If attributes originated, God existed as God before they appeared, showing that they are unnecessary for divinity.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p112/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة والفلاسفة | reports | They argue attributes are either dispe

[RAZI-FULL:v1p113/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God must be knowing, powerful, and living; the necessary conceptual distinction between God's essence and His being knowing or powerful shows these are not identical.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p113/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | We can conceive God as existent while not attending to His power or knowledge, and conceive power without knowledge, showing distinct concepts.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p113/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Knowledge concerns necessary, impossible, and possible things, while power concerns only possible things, proving their difference.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p113/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Power brings the possible into existence but knowledge does not, so the two attributes differ.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p113/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Not existent contradicts existent, whereas not knowing does not; what is negated by existence and knowledge claims is therefore distinct, likewise for power.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p113/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | These arguments establish that God has attributes, but they might be relational: power is capacity to produce, and knowledge is awareness, each grounded in the divine essence.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p114#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The Quran calls God the Living and Sustainer; these names combine to provide the full praise. | mentions 2:255, 20:111, 40:65
[RAZI-FULL:v1p114#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Hayy alone, meaning perceiving and acting or able to know and act, seems insufficiently praiseworthy; the praise lies in its combination with qayyum.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p114#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Qayyum means sustaining and setting right everything else, which requires complete knowledge and power; thus Hayy qayyum means knowing every possible and acting on every originated thing.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p114/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Knowledge and power are real attributes whose relations to known things and possible effects are concomitant; life alone is a real divine attribute without relation.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p114/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفلاسفة | reports | Philosophers define living as perceiving and acting, but both are relational, so life on their account is not distinct from knowledge and power.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p114/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المتكلمون | reports | Theologians define life as an attribute that makes knowing and having power possible; they argue differing capacities among essences require an additional life attribute.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p114/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Razi rejects that proof: God's essence is distinct from other essences in itself, and differences in receptivity would require another attribute without end.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p114/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A third group defines living as not being unable to know and have power; Razi accepts that this negates a negation, but asks why the resulting positive cannot be the essence itself.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p114/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | The argument that one can conceive God's essence while doubting that He is living fails because the divine essence is known only indirectly, not in itself.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | One class of relational names describes God as known, remembered, praised, and glorified; infinitely many such relations yield infinitely many possible names.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115#2/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Giving little or much yields Withholder or Expander; punishing sins yields Avenger, while foregoing punishment yields Pardoner, Forgiver, Merciful, or Compassionate.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115#2/r11] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Withholding or granting wealth yields Withholder and Expander, while lowering or raising status yields Abaser and Exalter.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115#2/r12] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Because God's possible creations across kinds and species are limitless, the names derived from creating specific things are limitless too.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115#2/r13] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Some oppositions are contraries, such as exalting and humiliating or giving life and death; others are presence and absence, such as withholding versus extending or lowering versus raising.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115#2/r14] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Not honoring someone differs from actively humiliating them; the contrast between honor and abasement is a pair of opposites.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115#2/r15] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Ra'uf and Rahim are close, but Ra'uf leans toward conferring benefit whereas Rahim leans toward removing harm.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115#2/r16] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Fatih suggests creating the means of good; Wahib suggests conveying that good; Nafi suggests conveying benefit with the recipient's benefit in view.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | If bringing things into being is not an additional attribute, acting is a purely relational attribute; names can describe creating in general or creating a specific kind for a wisdom.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Mujid means an agent affecting existence; muhdith more narrowly brings something into existence after nonexistence; mukawwin nearly means mujid.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Munshi derives from growth and denotes gradual production, while mubdi denotes bringing something forth all at once; they are two kinds of general creation.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Mukhtari is close to mubdi, while sani suggests effortful making.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Khaliq means measuring or determining, which in God returns to knowledge; fatir derives from splitting and appears to mean originating at once.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Bari means bringing into being in a way suited to benefit, like shaping a pen to suit its purpose.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Creating benefit or pain yields the names Benefiter or Harmful; creating life or death yields Giver of life or Giver of death.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115#2/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Granting honor yields Kind and Gentle, while imposing subjugation yields Overpowering and Compeller.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة والأشعرية | reports | Mu'tazilites and Ash'arites say God's act of bringing something into being is identical with the thing brought into being.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Those who deny a separate attribute of bringing into being argue that if it acts contingently it is simply power, while necessary effect would make God act by nature rather than choice.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | They argue an eternal creating attribute entails eternal effects, while a created one needs another act of creation and an infinite regress.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | They say power alone either suffices to produce effects once knowledge and will are present, making another attribute needless, or lacks efficacy and is not power.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Proponents of an eternal creating attribute point out that an able agent may act or refrain; God's ability to make a thousand suns does not mean He did so.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p115/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Being an agent who produces cannot mean merely that the effect exists, or explaining an effect by saying God produced it would explain it by itself; therefore producing differs from both power and effect.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p126#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Conceiving a compound requires attending to its parts, but a simple noncomposite essence cannot be brought before the mind through an operation; hence simple conception is pure unity.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p126#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Saying “O He” is pure conception of the divine reality, free of composition and multiplicity, and therefore the highest form of unity.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p126#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God cannot be defined through Himself, constituent parts, or external things: the first is circular, the second assumes composition, and creation is unlike the Creator.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p126#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Because no definition reaches God's essence, “O He” directs mind and spirit toward its light in hope of a glimpse.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p126#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Awe of a mighty king can erase awareness of hunger, pain, and even family; a glimpse of divine majesty similarly leaves only Hu and makes its recitation an imitation of that state.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p126/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi's fifth benefit is that sustained recitation of Hu produces longing for God.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p126/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Longing is the greatest station because it alternates pain at delay with pleasure in arrival, and relief from pain deepens joy.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p126/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi concludes that persevering in Hu yields the highest stations, happiness, and bliss.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p166/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Repetition for emphasis is common in the Qur’an, and reaffirming that God is merciful is especially important.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p166/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الحسن البصري | reports | A rare report has al-Hasan al-Basri count al-Fatiha as eight verses, while the well-known view accepted by most counts seven and identifies them with the seven oft-repeated verses. | mentions 15:87
[RAZI-FULL:v1p166/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Those counting the basmala treat the final phrase from sirat alladhina through the end as one verse; Abu Hanifa, omitting the basmala, splits that ending into two verses.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p166/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Al-Shafi‘i’s count is preferable: the pause after an‘amta ‘alayhim does not match the sura’s verse endings, and verse endings elsewhere are either near-rhyming or matching.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p166/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Starting a verse with ghayr separates a modifier or exception from what it qualifies, though each belongs syntactically with the preceding phrase.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p166/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | The request to guide us to the path of the blessed is incomplete without excluding those under anger or astray; the whole qualified phrase should therefore be one verse. | mentions 14:28
[RAZI-FULL:v1p167/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The verse-count objection disappears if the basmala and the words after it form one verse; a complete verse in al-Fatiha can be part of a longer verse elsewhere, and al-Kawthar’s count covers its distinctive content. | mentions 10:10
[RAZI-FULL:v1p167/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أحمد بن حنبل | reports | Ahmad ibn Hanbal is reported to count the basmala as a verse of al-Fatiha while reciting it quietly in every rak‘a; al-Shafi‘i counts it and recites aloud, while Abu Hanifa does not count it but reads it quietly.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p167/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Razi holds loud recitation to be Sunna: if the sura is recited aloud, its opening basmala should be too, rather than making only part of a sura audible.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p167/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Because the basmala praises and glorifies God, making its remembrance public is fitting; the Qur’an commands abundant remembrance, as one would publicly honor a beloved father. | mentions 2:200
[RAZI-FULL:v1p167/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Open remembrance publicly shows pride in honoring God and indifference to objection; reason commends that, supported by the reported maxim about what Muslims deem good.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p168#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The implied verb with the basmala means beginning acts with God’s help; hearing it teaches dependence on divine protection from sin and aid for good, making its recitation a call to the best good rather than an innovation.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p168#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أنس | reports | Anas reports that the Prophet, Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman began prayer with al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin; Muslim versions say they did not mention, or were not heard saying, the basmala aloud.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p168#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · عبد الله بن المغفل | reports | Ibn al-Mughaffal says his father warned him against introducing the basmala, recalling that the Prophet and first three caliphs began with al-hamdu lillah.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p168#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المخالف | reports | Opponents cite Qur’anic commands to invoke God humbly and remember Him inwardly as proof that the basmala should be quiet; jurists infer this from the verses and earlier reports. | mentions 7:55, 7:205
[RAZI-FULL:v1p168/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Concealment suits a defect, not the greatest honor of remembering God; reports praise dying with a tongue moist in remembrance and Ali’s saying that God’s mention ennobles those who remember Him.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p168/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | Ali is reported to recite the basmala aloud in all prayers, a practice Razi says strongly confirms public recitation.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p168/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafi‘i reports that when Muawiya omitted the basmala and bowing and prostration takbirs in Medina, the Emigrants and Helpers protested and he repeated prayer with them.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p168/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Since Muawiya was powerful, the Companions’ public protest shows that aloud basmala recitation was established among them.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p168/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · البيهقي | reports | Al-Bayhaqi transmits Abu Hurayra’s report that the Prophet recited the basmala aloud, and reports the same practice from Umar, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, and Ibn al-Zubayr.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p168/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | Razi says Ali’s loud recitation is established by mass transmission; he cites the report asking God to keep truth with Ali wherever he turns.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p169#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Conflicting and unstable Anas reports leave the evidence balanced; possible Umayyad pressure against Ali’s practice may explain Anas’s hesitation, and Ali’s lifelong practice should prevail.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p169#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | If reports conflict, Razi prefers Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, and Abu Hurayra over Anas and Ibn al-Mughaffal because they were more knowledgeable and closer to the Prophet.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p169#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi invokes Abu Hanifa’s refusal of solitary reports that oppose analogy: the evident rational case favors openly reciting a phrase that honors God.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p169#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Ali, Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Umar were more learned and eminent than Anas and Ibn al-Mughaffal; their likely proximity, the Prophet’s moderate voice, and gradual increase in volume explain who heard the basmala. | mentions 17:110
[RAZI-FULL:v1p169#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafi‘i interprets Anas’s phrase that the Prophet began with al-hamdu lillah as saying al-Fatiha, named by its opening, came before other suras.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p169#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Ibn al-Mughaffal’s denial of loud recitation can mean only that the Prophet did not raise his voice excessively, as instructed by the Qur’an; an affirmative report outweighs a negative one. | mentions 17:110
[RAZI-FULL:v1p169#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The verses about inward remembrance concern simple recollection; reciting God’s revealed words as worship is a different act for which audible reading is preferable. | mentions 7:205
[RAZI-FULL:v1p169#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشيعة | reports | The Shi‘a hold that the basmala should be recited aloud in both loud and quiet prayers; most jurists disagree.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p169#2/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المخالف | reports | Those denying that the basmala is part of each sura offer two explanations for its codex placement: it separates suras, or it is Qur’an as an independent verse revealed at each opening or once for insertion throughout.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p169/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو حامد الإسفراييني | reports | Abu Hamid al-Isfarayini groups six Anas reports: three support the Hanafi position by omitting the basmala, while three contrary reports recount the protest against Muawiya, loud recitation, or Anas’s uncertainty.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-Rāzī identifies Sūrat al-Fātiḥa as Meccan and says it has seven verses.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | He notes the widely held report that God has 1,001 sacred names found in the Qur’an and Sunna, and says studying each name is a noble discipline requiring knowledge of the named entity, proofs for its existence, and responses to objections, collectively thousands of questions.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The bāʾ in the basmala expresses adhesion and attaches to an elided verb understood as I begin performing acts of obedience in God’s name; unpacking this involves true beliefs, pure deeds, proofs, and answers to objections, perhaps over ten thousand questions.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Seeking refuge in God signifies rejecting improper beliefs and deeds, while saying in God’s name signifies adopting proper beliefs and deeds; sound reason confirms this order.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p170/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafi‘i prefers repeating the basmala before every sura, citing the report that an important matter begun without it is cut off.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p170/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi’s school holds that a menstruating woman or a person in major ritual impurity may not recite the basmala.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p171/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Whether meat from an animal slaughtered without the basmala is lawful is a famous dispute, with Qur’anic commands both to invoke God over offerings and not eat what was not named over. | mentions 22:36, 6:121
[RAZI-FULL:v1p171/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Scholars recommend beginning every activity with the basmala, from sleep and waking to worship, entering and leaving home, eating, drinking, giving, and receiving; they also recommend it at birth, death, burial, resurrection, and the gathering.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p171/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi rejects translated Qur’an as sufficient for prayer for both able and unable reciters; Abu Hanifa allows it for either, while Abu Yusuf and Muhammad allow it only for the unable.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p171/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The rightly guided caliphs prayed with Arabic Qur’an, so their practice binds believers under commands to follow Abu Bakr and Umar and the caliphs’ Sunna.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p172#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو هريرة | reports | Ibn al-Mundhir transmits Abu Hurayra’s report that prayer is invalid without reciting the Opening; a Persian rendering is either called Qur’an, which Razi deems ignorant and contrary to consensus, or not Qur’an.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p172#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · عبد الله بن أبي أوفى | reports | When a man could not recite Qur’an, the Prophet taught him glorification, praise, and takbir instead of a translation, showing the alternative for inability.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p172#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | If Qur’an could be translated as Qur’an, Christians could claim its opening was copied from the Gospel’s matching formula; no one makes that claim.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p172#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A Persian rendering of the cave passage or insults and requests becomes ordinary human speech, barred in prayer; the Arabic original remains distinct through its miraculous arrangement. | mentions 18:19, 68:11, 68:13, 2:61
[RAZI-FULL:v1p172/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The Prophet and Companions recited only Arabic in prayer; the saved group follows their practice. Muslims throughout Islamic lands agree on Arabic recitation, and departing from believers’ way is condemned. | mentions 4:115
[RAZI-FULL:v1p172/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Prayer requires Qur’an recitation, and Persian words are not Qur’an: revelation is in clear Arabic, messengers speak their people’s language, and the challenge to produce its like would be contradicted if a Persian rendering counted. | mentions 26:192, 26:195, 14:4, 41:44, 17:88
[RAZI-FULL:v1p173/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | If every language’s translation were Qur’an, revelation would have more than the seven canonical forms, contradicting the report that it came in seven forms.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p173/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The Hanafi principle would also validate prayer with matching verses from Torah, Gospel, or ordinary writings, an outcome Razi says is alien to Islam.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p173/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A translation of al-Fatiha reduces it to generic praise found in any sermon; allowing this would make prayer valid with all sermons, an unacceptable result.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p173/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | If translation were permitted, the Prophet would have authorized Persians, Romans, and Ethiopians to pray in their languages; such a popular, easier permission would have spread and erased the Arabic Qur’an.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p173/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Although a non-Arab may understand meaning more readily in translation, prayer seeks remembrance and reflection; treating translation as valid would perversely make Arabic recitation prohibited. | mentions 20:14, 47:24
[RAZI-FULL:v1p173/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Prayer preserves both meaning and Arabic wording: the wording carries the inimitable eloquence, and its required recitation safeguards memorization and fulfills God’s promise to preserve the Reminder. | mentions 15:9
[RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · عبد الله بن مسعود | reports | Opponents cite Ibn Mas‘ud teaching an Ajami to replace al-athim with al-yatim, then saying Quranic error is replacing a mercy verse with a punishment verse rather than using a synonym. | mentions 44:43
[RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المخالف | reports | Opponents argue that the Qur’an was in earlier scriptures, whose wording was Hebrew or Syriac rather than the Arabic wording, so meaning can be Qur’an in another language. | mentions 26:196, 87:19
[RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المخالف | reports | Opponents cite God’s statement that this Qur’an was revealed to warn people who do not understand Arabic, arguing that communicated meaning in their language is still Qur’an. | mentions 6:19
[RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Razi objects that Hanafis selectively invoke Ibn Mas‘ud: they reject his reported uncertainty about faith, though they rely on him here; reports that he omitted al-Fatiha and the protective suras likely reflect views he later abandoned.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafi‘i’s newer view requires the follower to recite; his earlier view requires it only when the imam recites quietly, as also held by Malik and Ibn al-Mubarak, while Abu Hanifa discourages recitation behind the imam.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p98#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Human thought knows God only as existent, everlasting, possessed of negative attributes, or possessed of relational attributes; the unique essence differs from all four and so is unknown.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p98#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Human concepts arise from the five senses, bodily states, intellectual concepts such as existence and possibility, or combinations; since God's essence differs from these, it is inconceivable to creatures.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p98#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God's essence causes all its real, relational, and negative properties; if the essence were known, all those properties would necessarily be known, which they are not.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p98#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعضهم | reports | Some argue that finite creaturely intellects cannot reach the infinite God, so only God knows God.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p98#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | He distinguishes indirect from essential knowledge: inferring a builder from a building reveals no nature, just as inferring the Creator from contingent things gives only indirect knowledge of God.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p98#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | In ordinary experience, essential apprehension comes through knowledge or sight; whether God could be essentially known through one or both, or through further modes, exceeds reason's ability to decide.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p98/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God differs from creation by His own essence, not through an added property: if the difference required another property, regress or circularity would result.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p98/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God is neither body nor substance: these are negative concepts, whereas His unique essence is positive and real.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p98/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | God's essence is not identical with power or knowledge, since these are relational notions while His essence is independently subsistent.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p99/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · قدماء الفلاسفة | reports | Ancient philosophers deny that God has a name for His unique essence because naming directs a hearer to a referent, but no creature knows that essence; they allow names for knowable consequences such as eternal and necessary.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p99/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Others say God could grant a close servant knowledge of His unique essence, in which case naming that essence would be possible; the issue rests on the preceding premises.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p99/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | If an essence-name can be assigned, it must be the greatest name and remembrance because their honor follows the honor of what is known and remembered.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p99/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A prophet or angel who encountered that name while its meaning was manifest might be obeyed by all physical and spiritual realms.

[QURTUBI:1:1/r194] QURTUBI, d. 671 · أهل الحق | reports | The people of truth, including al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr and Ibn Fūrak, say name and named are identical.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r195] QURTUBI, d. 671 · ابن الحصار | reports | Ibn al-Ḥaṣṣār contrasts those who say names designate only essence with those who say they denote attributes of the essence.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r196] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Allah is the greatest, most comprehensive divine name, unique to God and not pluralized; 19:65 may mean no one bears that name. | mentions 19:65
[QURTUBI:1:1/r197] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Allah means the true existent who gathers divine and lordly attributes, the one alone worthy of worship.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r198] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الخليل وسيبويه | reports | Al-Khalīl and Sibawayh derive Allah from ilāh, with the article replacing hamza, as nās derives from unās.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r199] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الكسائي والفراء | reports | Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ explain bismillah as bi-ism al-ilāh, with hamza deletion and lām assimilation.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r20] QURTUBI, d. 671 · جبير بن مطعم | reports | Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim reports the Prophet’s opening prayer asking protection from Satan’s hamz, nafkh, and nafth; ʿAmr glosses them as madness, pride, and poetry.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r200] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الخليل | reports | Another proposal derives ilāh from walah, bewilderment, because minds are overwhelmed by God’s attributes.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r201] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says God is called ilāh because creatures turn to Him with needs and plead in hardship.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r202] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الخليل بن أحمد | reports | Al-Khalīl says creatures worship God; the verb has two dialectal vowels.

[QURTUBI:1:1/r204] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | reports | Other proposals derive Allah from elevation, worship, or the pronoun hāʾ extended by a possessive lām and article.
