[QURTUBI:1:1/r206] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الخطابي | reports | Al-Khaṭṭābī argues the article belongs to Allah’s name because it accepts the vocative yā Allah, unlike al-Raḥmān or al-Raḥīm.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r207] QURTUBI, d. 671 · بعضهم | reports | Some say al-Raḥmān is not derived: if from mercy it would take an object, and Arabs would not ask “What is al-Raḥmān?” | mentions 25:60
[QURTUBI:1:1/r208] QURTUBI, d. 671 · ابن العربي | reports | Ibn al-ʿArabī says pagans knew the referent but not the attribute, asking what al-Raḥmān was rather than who.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r209] QURTUBI, d. 671 · ابن الحصار | reports | Ibn al-Ḥaṣṣār counters that 13:30 explicitly says the disbelievers rejected al-Raḥmān. | mentions 13:30
[QURTUBI:1:1/r21] QURTUBI, d. 671 · أبو سعيد الخدري | reports | Abū Saʿīd reports that the Prophet began night prayer with praise and sought refuge before reciting.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r210] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الجمهور | reports | Most scholars derive al-Raḥmān from mercy as an intensive form, uniquely divine and not dualized or pluralized.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r211] QURTUBI, d. 671 · عبد الرحمن بن عوف | reports | A report graded ṣaḥīḥ by al-Tirmidhī quotes God saying “I am al-Raḥmān,” who created kinship and derived its name from His own.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r212] QURTUBI, d. 671 · المبرد | rejects | Al-Mubarrad claims al-Raḥmān is Hebrew paired with Arabic al-Raḥīm; Qurṭubī rejects the claim.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r213] QURTUBI, d. 671 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says the basmala is God praising Himself; al-Zajjāj approves it as adjectival praise.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r214] QURTUBI, d. 671 · قطرب | reports | Quṭrub says al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm are paired for emphasis; al-Zajjāj approves this rhetoric.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r215] QURTUBI, d. 671 · محمد بن يزيد | reports | Muḥammad ibn Yazīd explains the paired names as favor after favor, renewed blessing, and a promise sustaining hope.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r216] QURTUBI, d. 671 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda treats al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm as synonyms, like nadmān and nadīm.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r217] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الجمهور | prefers | The majority distinguish them: faʿlān marks overwhelming action, while faʿīl can be active or passive; al-Raḥmān is specific in name but broad in action.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r218] QURTUBI, d. 671 · أبو علي الفارسي | reports | Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī says al-Raḥmān covers all mercy but is exclusive to God, while al-Raḥīm especially concerns believers.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r219] QURTUBI, d. 671 · العرزمي | reports | Al-ʿArzamī says al-Raḥmān’s mercy reaches all creation through rain and senses, while al-Raḥīm guides believers.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r22] QURTUBI, d. 671 · أبو القاسم | reports | Sulaymān ibn Sālim gives an expanded formula including refuge in God the Mighty and the basmala; Ibn ʿAṭiyya dislikes embellishments without declaring them forbidden.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r220] QURTUBI, d. 671 · ابن المبارك | reports | Ibn al-Mubārak says al-Raḥmān gives when asked while al-Raḥīm is angered when not asked; hadith supports this.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r221] QURTUBI, d. 671 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās calls the names soft, one softer than the other; al-Khaṭṭābī objects and al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl corrects it to “gentle.”

[QURTUBI:1:1/r223] QURTUBI, d. 671 · أكثر العلماء | reports | Most scholars reserve al-Raḥmān for God, citing 17:110 and 43:45; Musaylima’s self-title became attached to him as “the liar.” | mentions 17:110, 43:45
[QURTUBI:1:1/r224] QURTUBI, d. 671 · ابن العربي | reports | Ibn al-ʿArabī reports al-Raḥmān may be the greatest name of God.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r225] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Al-Raḥīm can describe creatures; al-Raḥmān precedes it because it is more comprehensive, matching Qurʾānic order.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r226] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | reports | Another interpretation makes al-Raḥīm a description of Muḥammad, through whom people reach God’s favor by following his message.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r227] QURTUBI, d. 671 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | A saying attributed to ʿAlī calls the basmala a cure and aid; al-Raḥmān aids believers and al-Raḥīm belongs to the repentant righteous.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r228] QURTUBI, d. 671 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | An esoteric report interprets basmala letters and says al-Raḥmān shows compassion to all creation, while al-Raḥīm is gentle toward believers.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r229] QURTUBI, d. 671 · كعب الأحبار | reports | Kaʿb al-Aḥbār assigns basmala letters to divine glory, majesty, and sovereignty; another reading maps each letter to a divine name.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r23] QURTUBI, d. 671 · سليمان بن صرد | reports | When two men quarreled and one became enraged, the Prophet said seeking refuge from Satan would dispel his anger; Muslim and al-Bukhārī transmit it.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r230] QURTUBI, d. 671 · أم سلمة | reports | A report from Umm Salama pauses after al-Raḥīm with a cut hamza at al-Ḥamd; some Kūfans read this way.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r231] QURTUBI, d. 671 · جمهور الناس | reports | Most readers connect al-Raḥīm to al-Ḥamd, using the genitive and connecting hamza.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r232] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisāʾī reports an Arab reading al-Raḥīma al-ḥamdu; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says no reader transmitted it.

[QURTUBI:1:1/r31] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Any rebellious being among jinn, humans, or animals may be called a shayṭān, marking distance from truth and insolence.

[QURTUBI:1:1/r33] QURTUBI, d. 671 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | ʿAlī reports seeing the Prophet curse an elephant-shaped figure at al-Ṣafā; it identifies itself as Satan and says it joins the conception of anyone who hates ʿAlī.

[QURTUBI:1:1/r35] QURTUBI, d. 671 · أبو سعيد بن المعلى | reports | In al-Bukhārī’s report, the Prophet calls al-Fātiḥa the greatest sūra, the seven oft-repeated verses, and the magnificent Qurʾān.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r36] QURTUBI, d. 671 · ابن عبد البر | reports | Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr notes uncertainty over the narrator’s name; Qurṭubī lists variants but identifies him as a leading Anṣārī.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r37] QURTUBI, d. 671 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid reports that Satan rang four times, including when al-Fātiḥa was revealed, and says it was revealed in Medina.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r38] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الأشعري والقاضي أبو بكر وابن حبان | reports | A group including al-Ashʿarī, al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr, and Ibn Ḥibbān denies superiority among sūras, verses, or divine names.

[QURTUBI:1:1/r4] QURTUBI, d. 671 · عطاء | reports | Al-Naqqāsh reports that ʿAṭāʾ regards seeking refuge in prayer as obligatory.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r40] QURTUBI, d. 671 · البستي | reports | Al-Bustī explains al-Fātiḥa’s superiority over Torah and Gospel as greater reward for this community, not intrinsic superiority in God’s speech.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r41] QURTUBI, d. 671 · البستي | reports | Al-Bustī interprets “greatest sūra” as greatest in reward.

[QURTUBI:1:1/r43] QURTUBI, d. 671 · أبي بن كعب | reports | The Prophet asks Ubayy which verse is greatest; Ubayy answers the Throne Verse, and the Prophet praises his knowledge.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r44] QURTUBI, d. 671 · ابن العربي | reports | Ibn al-ʿArabī argues that Torah, Gospel, and Qurʾān are the best scriptures, so superiority over the best entails superiority over all.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r45] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Al-Fātiḥa’s twenty-five words contain Qurʾānic sciences: praise, attributes, worship, dependence, guidance, and lessons about rejecters.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r46] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Its honor includes being divided between God and servant; worship is not valid without it, like al-Ikhlāṣ equaling a third through comprehensive tawḥīd.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r47] QURTUBI, d. 671 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | A report attributed to ʿAlī says al-Fātiḥa, the Throne Verse, 3:18, and 3:26 hang at the Throne without a veil. | mentions 2:255, 3:18, 3:26

[QURTUBI:1:1/r50] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | It is called Sūrat al-Ḥamd because it contains praise.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r51] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | It is called the Opening of the Book because it begins Qurʾānic recitation, muṣḥaf writing, and prayer.

[QURTUBI:1:1/r57] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | It is called the magnificent Qurʾān because it contains praise, worship, dependence, supplication for guidance, and lessons about rejecters.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r58] QURTUBI, d. 671 · أبو سعيد الخدري | reports | A report from Abū Saʿīd calls al-Fātiḥa a cure for every poison; al-Dārimī transmits it.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r59] QURTUBI, d. 671 · أبو سعيد الخدري | reports | The ruqya name is established by Abū Saʿīd’s report of the man who recited al-Fātiḥa over a sick chief.

[QURTUBI:1:1/r60] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الشعبي وابن عباس | reports | Al-Shaʿbī recommends al-Fātiḥa for flank pain and transmits Ibn ʿAbbās’s account naming it the basis of the Qurʾān.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r61] QURTUBI, d. 671 · سفيان بن عيينة | reports | Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna calls it al-Wāfiya because it cannot be halved across two prayer units.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r62] QURTUBI, d. 671 · يحيى بن أبي كثير | reports | Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr calls it al-Kāfiya because it suffices in place of other sūras, while none replaces it.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r63] QURTUBI, d. 671 · محمد بن خلاد الإسكندراني | reports | A report attributed to the Prophet says Umm al-Qurʾān replaces other passages, but nothing else replaces it.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r64] QURTUBI, d. 671 · المهلب | reports | Al-Muhallab locates al-Fātiḥa’s ruqya specifically in “You alone we worship and ask for help.”
[QURTUBI:1:1/r65] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | prefers | Qurṭubī says the whole sūra is ruqya: the Prophet asked how it was a ruqya, not how it contained one.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r66] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Calling al-Fātiḥa Umm al-Kitāb or al-Mathānī does not exclude other uses; the Qurʾān itself is called a repeated book. | mentions 39:23

[QURTUBI:1:1/r69] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الأمة | holds | The community agrees al-Fātiḥa has seven verses; reports of six or eight are anomalous.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r7] QURTUBI, d. 671 · مالك | reports | Mālik does not prescribe refuge in obligatory prayer but does prescribe it in Ramadan night prayer.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r70] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | Al-Fātiḥa is Qurʾān by consensus; Ibn Masʿūd explained its omission from his muṣḥaf as shorthand.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r71] QURTUBI, d. 671 · عبد الله بن مسعود | reports | Asked why he omitted al-Fātiḥa from his muṣḥaf, Ibn Masʿūd said he would have written it before every sūra.

[QURTUBI:1:1/r89] QURTUBI, d. 671 · أبو حنيفة والثوري والأوزاعي | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Thawrī, and al-Awzāʿī allow another passage to suffice if al-Fātiḥa is deliberately omitted.

[QURTUBI:1:1/r90] QURTUBI, d. 671 · أبو يوسف ومحمد بن الحسن | reports | Abū Yūsuf requires three verses or one long verse; Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan also permits one verse or a meaningful phrase.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r91] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الطبري | reports | Al-Ṭabarī requires al-Fātiḥa each unit but allows an equivalent passage; Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr rejects substitution.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r92] QURTUBI, d. 671 · العلماء | holds | By consensus, an imam’s recitation covers a latecomer who catches him bowing; one who catches him standing recites.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r93] QURTUBI, d. 671 · مالك وأصحابه | reports | In quiet prayer, Mālik’s school says one should not omit recitation behind the imam; omission is improper but does not invalidate prayer.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r94] QURTUBI, d. 671 · مالك | reports | Mālik’s well-known view bars the follower from reciting al-Fātiḥa or another passage when the imam recites aloud.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r95] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الشافعي وأحمد بن حنبل | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī’s Egyptian view and Aḥmad require every follower to recite al-Fātiḥa each unit, whether the imam recites aloud or quietly.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r96] QURTUBI, d. 671 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī first held that a follower reads when the imam is quiet but not loud; in Egypt he gave two views for loud recitation.
[QURTUBI:1:1/r97] QURTUBI, d. 671 · ابن وهب وأشهب وابن عبد الحكم وابن حبيب | reports | Ibn Wahb, Ashhab, Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam, Ibn Ḥabīb, and Kūfans say the follower recites nothing, relying on the imam’s recitation counting for him.

[QURTUBI:1:1/r99] QURTUBI, d. 671 · عمر وابن عباس وأبو هريرة وأبي بن كعب | reports | Qurṭubī cites Companions who require al-Fātiḥa in every unit.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r1] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Al-Fatiha is Umm al-Qur'an because it opens the Qur'an and is like its root and origin, hence al-Asās.

[BAYDAWI:1:1/r11] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · قراء المدينة والبصرة والشام وفقهاؤها ومالك والأوزاعي | reports | The reciters and jurists of Medina, Basra, and Syria, Mālik, and al-Awzāʿī reject its being part of every sūra.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r12] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abū Ḥanīfa gave no explicit ruling here; Bayḍāwī infers that he considered the basmala outside the sūra.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r13] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · محمد بن الحسن | reports | Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said that everything between the two covers is God's speech.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r14] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · النبي | reports | Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet saying al-Fatiha has seven verses and its first is the basmala.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r15] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · النبي | reports | Umm Salama reports the Prophet counted the basmala and “Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds” as one verse.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r16] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | The reports explain the disagreement whether the basmala is a separate verse or part of the following verse.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r17] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | There is consensus that the muṣḥaf text is God's speech and agreement to include the basmala in muṣḥafs despite rigorous exclusion of non-Qur'anic matter.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r18] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | prefers | The bāʾ attaches to omitted “I read,” since what follows is recited; this is better than “I begin,” unsupported by context, or “my beginning,” requiring extra ellipsis.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r19] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Fronting the phrase emphasizes exclusivity and reverence, accords with God's name preceding recitation, and makes it the instrument of an act not ritually complete without it. | mentions 11:41, 1:5
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r2] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | It is also Umm al-Qur'an because it gathers praise, worship of commands and prohibitions, promise and threat, theoretical wisdom, practical guidance, and knowledge of the blessed and wretched.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r20] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · النبي | reports | The Prophet is quoted saying every important matter not begun with the basmala is deficient.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r21] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | Alternatively, bāʾ denotes accompaniment: “I read while blessed by God's name.”
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r22] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | The basmala and rest of the sūra are put on servants' tongues to teach invocation for blessing, praise of God's favors, and asking His bounty.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r23] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | The bāʾ is kasra as a bound genitive preposition; command and possessive lām are likewise kasra before nouns to distinguish them from lām of inception.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r24] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · أصحابنا البصريون | reports | Basran grammarians derive ism from a form whose ending was dropped for frequent use; hamzat al-waṣl allows its consonant-initial form to begin a word.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r25] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Forms asmāʾ, asāmī, samā, and samīt support this derivation; poetry attests the form samy.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r26] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | prefers | Bayḍāwī rejects metathesis as irregular and derives ism from sumūw, elevation, since a name raises and marks its referent.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r27] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · الكوفيون | reports | The Kufans derive ism from sima, “mark”: its original was wasm, with initial wāw deleted and hamzat al-waṣl added to reduce irregularity.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r28] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | rejects | Bayḍāwī objects that Arabic has no precedent for hamza entering a word after its first letter has been deleted.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r29] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Sam and sim are also forms; a poem attests sam in the phrase “in the name of the one in every sūra.”
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r3] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Its other names include al-Kanz, al-Wāfiya, al-Kāfiya, al-Ḥamd, al-Shukr, al-Duʿāʾ, Taʿlīm al-Masʾala, and al-Ṣalāt; the latter names reflect its supplication and prayer recitation.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r30] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | If ism means the spoken word, it differs from its referent: transient sounds vary across peoples and eras and may be multiple or singular, unlike the named entity.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r31] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | If ism means the entity itself, it is the named thing, though this sense is not established in common usage.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r32] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | In Qur'anic commands to glorify God's name, “name” means the word: as God's essence and attributes must be kept from defects, so must their names from obscenity and discourtesy. | mentions 55:78, 87:1
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r33] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | Alternatively, “name” is an insertion without independent meaning, as in the poet's line “then the name of peace be upon you both.”

[BAYDAWI:1:1/r39] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | Other proposals compare worshippers' clinging in hardship to a calf clinging to its mother, or derive the word from fleeing in fear and receiving refuge.

[BAYDAWI:1:1/r40] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | A further proposal derives it from walaha, bewilderment, with wāw changed to hamza under kasra; Bayḍāwī objects that its plural is āliha, not awliha.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r41] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | Another derivation takes it from lāh, hidden and elevated: God is beyond sight and above all things; a cited poem uses lāh.

[BAYDAWI:1:1/r44] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | prefers | Bayḍāwī prefers that Allāh was originally descriptive but became name-like through exclusive use, allowing predicates while excluding descriptive use and partners.

[BAYDAWI:1:1/r46] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | Another proposal derives the word from Syriac lāhā, arabized by dropping the final alif and adding lām.

[BAYDAWI:1:1/r49] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm are intensive forms from raḥima, like ghaḍbān from ghaḍiba and ʿalīm from ʿalima.

[BAYDAWI:1:1/r50] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Mercy linguistically is tenderness of heart and an inclination entailing benefaction; a womb is named raḥim because it inclines over what it contains.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r51] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | Divine names are understood by resultant acts and ends, not by the passive beginnings of human mercy.

[BAYDAWI:1:1/r57] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | Alternatively, al-Raḥmān denotes great blessings and al-Raḥīm completes it by including blessings outside that category.
[BAYDAWI:1:1/r58] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | The order may also preserve the sūra's verse-end rhyme.

[BAYDAWI:1:1/r6] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | reports | One group counts the basmala but not “those upon whom You bestowed favor” as a verse.

[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r5] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · أم سلمة | reports | Umm Salama reports that the Prophet counted the basmala as a verse when reciting al-Fātiḥa.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The disagreement concerns whether the basmala is an independent verse or counted with what follows; Muslims agree it is Qur'an and is written in the codices, which were carefully kept free of additions such as آمين.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r7] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | prefers | The prefixed ب is attached to an omitted verb meaning “I read,” since what follows is read; each actor supplies the verb suited to what the naming begins.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r8] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | rejects | “I begin” is less suitable because nothing in the wording matches or indicates it, while “my beginning” requires an extra ellipsis.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r9] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Putting the governed phrase first gives emphasis, exclusivity, and reverence; the name precedes recitation and makes an act religiously complete, as in the cited verses. | mentions 11:41, 1:5
[NASAFI:1:1/r1] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | prefers | The Fatiha is Makkan, Madinan, or both; Nasafi prefers both: it descended at Mecca when prayer became obligatory and again at Medina when the qibla turned to the Kaaba.
[NASAFI:1:1/r10] NASAFI, d. 710 · قراء مكة والكوفة والشافعي وأصحابه | reports | Meccan and Kufan reciters and al-Shafi‘i’s school count the basmala as a verse of the Fatiha and every sura, and recite it aloud; they argue the early Muslims wrote it in the Qur’an despite orders to exclude non-Qur’anic material.
[NASAFI:1:1/r11] NASAFI, d. 710 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says whoever omits the basmala has omitted 114 verses from God’s Book.
[NASAFI:1:1/r12] NASAFI, d. 710 · أبو هريرة عن النبي | reports | Abu Hurayra reports God’s dialogue dividing the Fatiha between Himself and the servant: praise, glorification, and exaltation belong to God; the worshipper’s request for guidance and the response to it belong to the servant, while worship and aid are shared.
[NASAFI:1:1/r13] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | Since the division report begins with al-hamdu lillah, Nasafi takes it as evidence that the basmala is not part of the Fatiha; he says it is not part of another sura either, by consensus. | mentions 1:2
[NASAFI:1:1/r14] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | Nasafi answers that the basmala is still Qur’an, revealed to separate the suras; its Qur’anic status does not require it to belong to a sura’s verse count.
[NASAFI:1:1/r15] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | The basmala’s bā’ attaches to an omitted verb supplied from context, such as ‘I read’ or ‘I recite’; a traveler, slaughterer, or other actor similarly supplies the action being begun.
[NASAFI:1:1/r16] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | The omitted action comes after the basmala so the invoked name is foregrounded and exclusive: monotheists distinguish their beginning from those who invoked al-Lat and al-‘Uzza.
[NASAFI:1:1/r17] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | In ‘Read in your Lord’s name’ the verb comes first because it opens the first-revealed sura and the command to read is more important; alternatively, read is intransitive, or the following ‘in your Lord’s name’ is the object of a later ‘read.’ | mentions 96:1
[NASAFI:1:1/r18] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | The name relates to recitation as oil relates to growth in ‘it grows with oil’: reciting with God’s name seeks blessing and teaches worshippers to honor it. | mentions 23:20
[NASAFI:1:1/r19] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | The bā’ takes kasra because it is always a particle governing genitive, matching its vowel to its grammatical function.
[NASAFI:1:1/r2] NASAFI, d. 710 · النبي عليه السلام | reports | The Fatiha is called Umm al-Qur’an on the basis of the Prophet’s statement that prayer is invalid without reciting Umm al-Qur’an.
[NASAFI:1:1/r20] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | Ism begins with a silent consonant, so an initial hamza is added when starting speech but omitted in connected speech; some instead move the first consonant and say sim. Its ending is deleted, its original form is sumuw, and its derivation denotes elevation because naming publicizes and honors the named.
[NASAFI:1:1/r21] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | The alif of ism is omitted in this written basmala because it is frequent and unpronounced; the bā’ is lengthened to compensate, and ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz instructed his scribe to lengthen the bā’, distinguish the sīns, and round the mīm. | mentions 96:1
[NASAFI:1:1/r22] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | Allah derives from al-ilah, like al-nas from al-unas: the hamza drops and the definite article substitutes for it. Ilah once named any true or false object of worship, then chiefly the true one; Allah without hamza is exclusive to the true God.
[NASAFI:1:1/r23] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | Allah is a name rather than an attribute: one predicates unity and self-sufficiency of God but does not call another thing ‘a god’; divine attributes require a named subject to qualify.
[NASAFI:1:1/r24] NASAFI, d. 710 · الخليل والزجاج ومحمد بن الحسن والحسين بن الفضل | reports | Al-Khalil, al-Zajjaj, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl deny that the name Allah has a derivation.
[NASAFI:1:1/r25] NASAFI, d. 710 · قيل | reports | One derivation connects Allah with alih, ‘to be bewildered’: minds are dazed by trying to know God, which explains the spread of error and rarity of sound reflection.
[NASAFI:1:1/r26] NASAFI, d. 710 · قيل | reports | Another derivation makes Allah a verbal noun from alaha, ‘to worship,’ meaning ma’luha, ‘the worshipped’; Nasafi compares this noun-for-participle pattern to ‘God’s creation’ meaning what He created. | mentions 31:11
[NASAFI:1:1/r27] NASAFI, d. 710 · الجمهور | prefers | Most reciters emphasize the lām of Allah after fatḥa or ḍamma and lighten it after kasra; some lighten it in every context and others emphasize it throughout.
[NASAFI:1:1/r28] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | Rahman is fa‘lan from mercy and denotes mercy encompassing everything, like ghadban denotes being filled with anger; rahim is fa‘il. Rahman is more intensive because its form has two augmentations rather than one, and greater length signals greater meaning.
[NASAFI:1:1/r29] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | A supplication calls God Rahman of this world because mercy there reaches believer and unbeliever, and Rahim of the afterlife because there it is specific to believers.
[NASAFI:1:1/r3] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | Because the Fatiha contains the meanings found throughout the Q

ur’an, it is also called al-Wafiya and al-Kafiya.
[NASAFI:1:1/r30] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | Rahman is uniquely used as a name but broad in meaning; rahim can describe others but is specific to believers. Rahman therefore precedes the more intense form despite the usual progression from lesser to greater.
[NASAFI:1:1/r31] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | God’s mercy is His beneficence toward servants, while its root sense is affection. The poet’s use of rahman for Musaylima is treated as a taunting excess in unbelief.
[NASAFI:1:1/r32] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | prefers | Whether rahman declines depends on the proposed condition for non-declension: those requiring absence of fa‘lanah leave it indeclinable, while those requiring an existing fa‘la decline it; Nasafi prefers the first analysis.
[NASAFI:1:1/r4] NASAFI, d. 710 · الله تعالى | reports | A divine report calls the Fatiha a treasure from the treasures of God’s Throne, explaining its name Sura of the Treasure.
[NASAFI:1:1/r5] NASAFI, d. 710 · النبي عليه السلام | reports | A Prophetic report calls the Fatiha a healing for every illness except al-sam; this grounds its names al-Shifa and al-Shafiya.
[NASAFI:1:1/r6] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | It is called al-Mathani because it is repeated in every prayer; it is also called the Prayer based on reports and its obligatory status, and al-Hamd and al-Asas because it grounds the Qur’an.
[NASAFI:1:1/r7] NASAFI, d. 710 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas advises a person who falls ill or complains of pain to turn to the Fatiha, calling it al-Asas.
[NASAFI:1:1/r8] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | The Fatiha has seven verses by consensus.
[NASAFI:1:1/r9] NASAFI, d. 710 · قراء المدينة والبصرة والشام وفقهاؤها | reports | Medinan, Basran, and Syrian reciters and jurists, including Abu Hanifa and his followers, hold that the basmala is no verse of any sura, but is written to separate suras and for blessing; they therefore do not recite it aloud in prayer.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | Medina, Basra, and Syria's readers and jurists, with Abu Hanifa, hold that the basmala is not a verse of al-Fatiha or other surahs; it separates surahs and is blessed at the opening, so they do not recite it aloud.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r10] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The ba is kasra-marked because it is invariably a preposition governing genitive; the noun's initial hamza is added only when it begins speech, while medial pronunciation drops it.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r11] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The noun ism has a prosthetic hamza for initial pronunciation, can be shortened to sim, and derives from deleted-final form samw, “elevation”: naming raises and publicizes the named one's mention.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r12] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · عمر بن عبد العزيز | reports | Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz instructed his scribe to lengthen the ba, make the sin strokes clear, and round the mim; the written alif is omitted here through frequent use.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r13] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Allah is uniquely the name of the true God, not an attribute; the source derives it from al-ilah with hamza loss, while Khalil, al-Zajjaj, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl deny derivation and other accounts link it to bewilderment or worship.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | Meccan and Kufan readers, with al-Shafi'i and his companions, count it as a verse of al-Fatiha and every surah and recite it aloud; they cite its inclusion in the early codices despite the instruction to exclude non-Qur'anic material.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says that whoever omits the basmala has omitted 114 verses from God's Book.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · أبو هريرة | reports | A Prophetic report presents al-Fatiha as divided between God and His servant: God answers the praise, glorification, and magnification, shares the response to worship and aid, and grants the servant's request in the closing supplication.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | prefers | The report begins God's response when the servant says “Praise belongs to God,” which indicates the basmala is not part of al-Fatiha; if it is outside al-Fatiha, consensus excludes it from other surahs too.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r6] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | In the Hanafi account the basmala remains a Qur'anic verse revealed to separate surahs; this does not contradict its exclusion from the surahs themselves.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r7] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The initial ba attaches to an omitted verb such as “I read” or “I recite”; the act named is understood from the basmala that precedes it, as in a traveler saying it on departure or arrival.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r8] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The omitted verb follows the basmala because the act and its object matter most; placing the divine name first gives it exclusive priority over the polytheists' invocations of al-Lat and al-Uzza.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r9] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | In “Read in the name of your Lord,” the verb is brought forward because reading was the central command of the first-revealed surah; “read” may also mean perform reading absolutely, or take the following phrase as its object. | mentions 96:1
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The lām of Allah is generally emphatic after fatḥa or ḍamma and light after kasra; some readers lighten it in every position, others always emphasize it, while the first pattern is the majority practice.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Rahman and Rahim are both derived from mercy, but Rahman is more emphatic because it has two augmentative patterns versus one in Rahim; added form signals added meaning.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Rahman describes mercy encompassing all creation, believer and unbeliever, especially in this world; Rahim describes mercy particular to believers in the hereafter, explaining the supplicatory usage and the order of the names.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Rahman is restricted as a name to God but universal in meaning, while Rahim can describe others and is particular in its referent; Rahman is nevertheless placed first despite its greater force.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | A hostile poet applied “Rahman” to Musaylima as a taunt in unbelief, not as a genuine divine description.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r6] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | prefers | Grammarians differ on whether Rahman declines: those requiring the absence of a faʿlān feminine form leave it indeclinable, while those requiring a faʿlā feminine form decline it; the first analysis is preferable.
[QASHANI:1:1#2/r1] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The nineteenth letter signifies the human world as a distinct realm because humanity’s nobility and comprehensiveness gather the whole cosmos, as Gabriel is distinguished among angels. | mentions 2:98
[QASHANI:1:1#2/r2] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Three hidden alifs complete the twenty-two letters and signify the divine world in respect of essence, attributes, and acts: three in detailed consideration, one in realization.
[QASHANI:1:1#2/r3] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The three written alifs signify those worlds appearing in the supreme human manifestation while the divine world remains veiled.
[QASHANI:1:1#2/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Asked where the alif of the basmala went, the Messenger replies that Satan stole it; he orders the bāʾ lengthened in its place.
[QASHANI:1:1#2/r5] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Lengthening bāʾ compensates for the hidden alif: divinity is concealed in diffusive mercy and appears in human form, knowable only to its people, hence the indefinite form.
[QASHANI:1:1#2/r6] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | reports | A hadith says God created Adam in His image; the author explains a hierarchy of veils from essence by attributes, from attributes by acts, and from acts by beings and effects.
[QASHANI:1:1#2/r7] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Disclosure of acts beyond the veil of created effects yields trust; disclosure of attributes beyond acts yields contentment and surrender; disclosure of essence beyond attributes yields annihilation in unity and absolute unification.
[QASHANI:1:1#2/r8] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Unification of acts precedes unification of attributes, which precedes unification of essence; the three are reflected in the Prophet’s prostration supplication seeking refuge in pardon, pleasure, and God Himself.
[QASHANI:1:1/r1] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Names are the determinate forms by which divine attributes and essence are known: their identities signify attributes and essence, existence signifies His face, and their individuation His unity.
[QASHANI:1:1/r2] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Allah names the divine essence absolutely, without reference either to its being qualified by attributes or to its lack of attributes.
[QASHANI:1:1/r3] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The All-Merciful grants existence and perfection universally according to wisdom and each recipient’s capacity at the beginning.
[QASHANI:1:1/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The Especially Merciful grants the human kind its particular spiritual perfection at the end; the perfected human form gathers universal and special mercy and manifests the divine essence and all attributes.
[QASHANI:1:1/r5] QASHANI, d. 736 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet says he was given comprehensive speech and sent to complete noble character; existent things are realities, while noble character’s states and sources of action are gathered in the universal human being.
[QASHANI:1:1/r6] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | P

rophets placed alphabet letters opposite levels of beings; existence emerged from bāʾ because it follows the alif symbolizing God’s essence, and bāʾ signifies the first intellect, God’s first creation.
[QASHANI:1:1/r7] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | reports | The first intellect is addressed in a report that God created no creature dearer or more honored, and acts of giving, taking, reward, and punishment occur through it.
[QASHANI:1:1/r8] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The basmala has eighteen pronounced letters and nineteen written letters; when words are separated, the count becomes twenty-two.
[QASHANI:1:1/r9] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Eighteen signifies eighteen thousand worlds, whose principal realms are the dominion, kingdom, Throne, Footstool, heavens, elements, and three genera of offspring.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r1] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · علي وابن عباس وعلي بن الحسين وقتادة وأبو العالية وعطاء وابن جبير ومحمد بن يحيى بن حبان وجعفر الصادق | reports | These authorities hold that al-Fātiḥa is Meccan; Abū Ḥayyān says the claim is supported by the seven oft-repeated verses being mentioned in a Meccan sūra. | mentions 15:87
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r10] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الكوفي | reports | The Kufan derivation makes the root of ism w-s-m, whereas Abū Ḥayyān prefers the Basran s-m-w analysis.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r11] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | Grammarians assign al- uses including particular or generic reference, presence, evocation of a quality, predominance, relative meaning, and fixed or nonfixed augmentation.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r12] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الأكثرون | reports | Most authorities consider Allāh a proper name for the true deity only, originally un-derived.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r13] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · ابن إسحاق وأبو عمر والنضر والمبرد | reports | Competing derivations connect Allāh to rising, concealment, fear, bewilderment, worship, or rest; Abū Ḥayyān reports these without choosing among them.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r14] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الخليل والقناد | reports | Al-Khalīl and al-Qannād derive Allāh from w-l-h, “to be transported with delight,” with hamza substituted for wāw; Abū Ḥayyān calls the proposal weak.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r15] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | The plural āliha can be parsed as faʿāl with a passive meaning, like kitāb meaning “written.”
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r16] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | If Allāh derives from al-ilāh, al- marks predominance: ilāh can name true or false deities, while Allāh names only the true deity; the comparison to al-Najm is challenged.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r17] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | On the other proposed derivations, al- is an inseparable extra article; omitting it in lāh abūka is anomalous.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r18] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · أبو بكر بن العربي والسهيلي | rejects | They say al- is part of Allāh and the hamza became connective through frequent use; Abū Ḥayyān rejects this because the resulting form would be fʿāl and would not explain the lack of tanwīn.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r19] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · أبو يزيد البلخي | reports | Abū Yazīd al-Balkhī calls Allāh a foreign word, citing Jewish and Christian lāhā and saying Arabs adopted and changed it.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r2] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · أبو هريرة وعطاء بن يسار ومجاهد وسواد بن زياد والزهري وعبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير | reports | These authorities hold that al-Fātiḥa is Medinan, contrary to the Meccan attribution.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r20] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · قيل | reports | A reported view treats Allāh as an attribute rather than a personal name because God is not sensed or immediately apprehended and is known through His attributes; Abū Ḥayyān calls this unusual.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r21] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | reports | The final alif in Allāh is variously said to be omitted to distinguish its spelling from lāhū, to lighten it, or because of a spelling convention.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r22] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Raḥmān is an intensive faʿlān form from mercy, with al- marking predominance; it is used only of God, like His proper name.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r23] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · ثعلب | reports | Thaʿlab reports the unusual claim that raḥmān is foreign, with its khāʾ adapted to Arabic ḥāʾ.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r24] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Raḥīm is an intensive faʿīl form; faʿīl is one of the five standard intensive patterns, with some grammarians adding another faʿīl pattern.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r25] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · العملس بن عقيل | reports | The poet al-ʿAmalas ibn ʿUqayl uses raḥīm to mean marḥūm, “one shown mercy.”
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r26] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الكوفيون | reports | The Kufans parse the bāʾ as instrumental and the phrase as accusative with an implied “I begin”; they posit that implied verb for acts begun with the formula.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r27] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī supplies a delayed verb such as “I read” or “I recite,” and claims fronting yields exclusivity; Abū Ḥayyān disputes the latter claim.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r28] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh says fronting an object is good Arabic just as ordinary order is; Abū Ḥayyān cites this against the claim that fronting necessarily entails exclusivity.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r29] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · البصريون | reports | The Basrans parse ism as nominative in an implied nominal sentence, approximately “my beginning is fixed/stable in the name of God”; Abū Ḥayyān weighs this against the verbal parse.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r3] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · قيل | reports | A further view calls al-Fātiḥa both Meccan and Medinan.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r30] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Ism is a conventional word denoting an existent, perceptible or intelligible, without marking time; its referent is the named thing, while naming makes the word a sign for that meaning.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r31] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | holds | Abū Ḥayyān distinguishes the word, its referent, and the act of naming; a judgment attributed literally to a name can instead use “name” metaphorically for its referent.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r32] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · السهيلي | reports | Al-Suhaylī reads “glorify the name of your Lord” as an insertion directing people to glorify the Lord and ensuring remembrance includes spoken utterance as well as inward recollection. | mentions 87:1
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r33] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · السهيلي | reports | Al-Suhaylī explains “you worship only names” as a metaphor for idols with false, unreal names, so their worship is effectively worship of invented names. | mentions 12:40
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r34] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الكسائي والأخفش | reports | Al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash allow dropping the alif in bi-sm with other divine names; al-Farrāʾ restricts deletion to the full basmala.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r35] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الأعلم | reports | Al-Aʿlam treats raḥmān as a proper name and therefore appositional rather than adjectival, citing its independent use in other verses. | mentions 20:5, 55:1
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r36] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · السهيلي | rejects | Al-Suhaylī rejects apposition and explanatory apposition because Allāh needs no clarification; raḥmān is an epithet of praise, though it can function like a proper name.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r37] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · قيل | reports | One view says the two names are synonymous; another distinguishes them, making raḥmān more emphatic and encompassing major blessings while raḥīm completes it with subtle blessings.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r38] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī favors raḥmān for foundational blessings and raḥīm as a complement for finer, subtler blessings.
[ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r39] ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 · author | prefers | Abū Ḥayyān holds that the names intensify mercy in different ways, so their combination is not mere repetition: faʿlān suggests fullness or dominance, while faʿīl suggests repeated occurrence at objects of mercy.

[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Al-Rahim describes God as especially gentle toward believers.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Some treat Rahman and Rahim as synonyms like nadman and nadim, with one view saying the pair is emphatic; another says Rahman is paired with Rahim because Musaylima claimed the former title.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The Musaylima explanation is very weak because his claim is irrelevant and the basmala predates his rise.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Others assign each name a distinct object: mercy is universal to believers and unbelievers in this world but reserved for believers in the next; a reversed report also circulates, and the author doubts this distinction alone.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | prefers | Al-Zamakhshari and the author hold Rahman to be more intensive and exclusive to God; despite normal progression from weaker to stronger, Rahim follows to cover subtler blessings after Rahman covers great ones.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rej
<<part 43 ends; continues in part 44>>

<<1:1 notes, part 44 of 0..74>>
ects | Some make Rahim more intensive and cite a report of worldly Rahim and afterlife Rahman, but the author says it instead confirms Rahman is stronger because afterlife mercy is greater.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The author invokes the report that God has stored ninety-nine mercies for the Day of Resurrection to support Rahman's stronger intensity.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The patterns intensify differently: fa'lan conveys fullness and dominance, while fa'il conveys repeated occurrence at sites of mercy.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abu Ubayda says fa'lan marks an intensified act, while fa'il can mean either agent or patient; his poem calls someone in war compassionate.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Rahman is restricted in name but broad in action, whereas Rahim is broad in name but restricted in action; hence fa'lan is not transitive while fa'il is.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The article in al-Rahman marks dominance; most scholars restrict it to God, unlike Rahim, which also describes the Prophet toward believers. | mentions 17:110, 9:128
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The poet's use of Rahman for Musaylima is dismissed as obstinate excess; the name normally occurs with the article or in annexation.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ثعلب والمبرد | reports | Tha'lab and al-Mubarrad transmit an unusual claim that the word is non-Arabic and pronounced with khā', citing a poem with rakhman.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#13/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Most connect al-Rahim to al-hamd with kasra on mīm, normally as an inflectional ending; a second explanation treats it as a pause form restored with kasra before a consonant.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#13/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أم سلمة | reports | Umm Salama transmits stopping after al-Rahim and beginning al-hamd with a cut hamza.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#13/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisa'i reports a dialectal reading fathing mīm and connecting al-hamd by transferring the hamza's vowel; Ibn Atiyya says it is not established as a reading, and the author prefers parsing the fathah as an accusative cut-off construction. | mentions 3:1
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Most grammarians allow ba only for attachment or transitivity, reducing the other examples to those two senses.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | A poet uses ba in the predicate of inna, meaning you are the experienced one.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r11] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ba is also discussed as extra in the construction beginning a-wa-lam yaraw anna Allah and similar expressions. | mentions 46:33
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r12] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | A noun, technically, signifies a meaning in itself without time or meaningful parts; linguistically it identifies its referent, and naming makes a word signify that meaning.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ba may mark superposition, as in entrusting someone with a qintar. | mentions 3:75
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ba is regularly added to the subject of kafa, as in God sufficing his servant; a poem shows the preposition omitted with the same construction. | mentions 4:6
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ba is regularly added to predicates of laysa and its negative sister ma, and in the expression bisabika Zayd. | mentions 39:36, 6:132
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ba is irregularly added to the object of kafa; the quoted poem means the Prophet's love suffices us.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | One analysis treats ba in the subject phrase of Qalam 6 as extra; another takes al-maftun as a verbal noun, making ba non-extra. | mentions 68:6
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ba may be irregularly added to the predicate of la, the negative counterpart of laysa; the verse means no intercessor can avail anything.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ba can be added to a predicate after negated kana; the poet means I was not the quickest to the food.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ba may also be added in a negated circumstantial phrase or second object of ظن; the cited poems mean the caravan returned unsuccessful and he was not a coward.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Scholars dispute whether a name is identical with its named referent; this creates an apparent problem of a thing being annexed to itself.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Basrans derive ism from sumu, elevation, because the name raises and reveals its referent; Kufans derive it from wasm, a mark, semantically plausible but morphologically unsound.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | prefers | Abu al-Baqa's best answer is that name here means naming, which differs from the name itself and its referent.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The author reports Abu al-Baqa's second answer: supply an omitted annex, yielding in the name of the named God.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The author reports Abu al-Baqa's third solution, treating ism as superfluous, like the poetic phrase meaning peace be upon you.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو عبيدة والأخفش وقطرب | reports | Abu Ubayda, al-Akhfash, and Qutrub also adopt the analysis that ism is superfluous; poems by the cited poets illustrate it.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash says the alleged extra word shifts the phrase from an oath to an invocation of blessing.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · قطرب | reports | Qutrub says the added word serves honor and exaltation.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The author calls both addition and deletion explanations weak because neither is adopted without necessity.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Apparent self-annexation also occurs in name-plus-title and noun-plus-description phrases; grammarians explain these by meaning-name shifts or omitted annexes.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Basrans cite the plural asma, diminutive sumayy, and related Arabic forms as evidence for derivation from sumu; a wasm derivation would predict awsam and wasim, which are not used.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The Basran analysis also fits common deletion of a word-final weak radical and treats initial hamzat al-wasl as its replacement; deleting an initial radical is less common.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | A proposed reordered form underlying asma and sumayy is an irregular metathesis and is rejected absent necessity.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The etymology has theological consequences: Basrans say God always had names and attributes, the Sunni position; Kufans say creatures assigned them after creation, the Mu'tazilite position, which the author condemns as worse than created-Qur'an doctrine.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أحمد بن يحيى | reports | Ahmad ibn Yahya traces sam with damma to samawtu and with kasra to sammaytu; the two cited lines illustrate the forms, though the second line is specifically on kasra.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ism has five reported forms, including ism, sim in either vowel, and suma like huda; the cited poetry illustrates these variants.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The poem with samāka suman does not prove a nominative form, since it may reflect the shortened form with damma in the accusative; nominative or genitive would be decisive.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Some Kufans place an implicit verb before the phrase; others, including al-Zamakhshari, place it after to mark exclusive dedication against pagan formulas naming al-Lat or al-Uzza.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The initial hamza is hamzat al-wasl, usually omitted in connected speech but retained by poetic necessity; ism is one of ten words beginning with it.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The spelling alif was normally retained, but was omitted specifically before Allah because the phrase is frequent; another explanation says spelling follows pronunciation.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · النحاس | reports | Al-Nahhas explains there is no true deletion: the original short form loses a vowel after ba for ease, producing the written form; the author calls this a good account.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الكسائي والأخفش | reports | Al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash reportedly allow dropping the hamza when ism is annexed to another divine name, as in bism rabbika or bism al-khaliq.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Every genitive prepositional phrase needs a governor, except with an extra preposition and certain analyses of lalla and lawla; Ibn Asfur adds the simile kaf, which the author says is governed.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Basrans take the omitted governor of bismillah to be a noun, while Kufans take it to be a verb.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Some Basrans omit a nominal subject and predicate, such as my beginning or recitation is established by God's name; Makkī objects that this deletes a verbal noun while retaining its complement.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Other Basrans omit a predicate and its subject, leaving the prepositional phrase as

 predicate, either nominative or accusative according to its role.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The overt iqra bism rabbik is explained either by the priority of reading in the first-revealed sura or by attaching the phrase to a later iqra; the latter creates a long interruption and makes the second iqra redundant. | mentions 68:1
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra' takes the omitted governing verb as an imperative: you read in God's name.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj instead takes it as a declarative, I read or begin in God's name.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The genitive Allah may be governed by the annexed noun, the implicit preposition, or the annexation relation; the author prefers the preposition.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Allah is a proper name exclusively for the true deity; ilah before contraction also has this exclusive sense, while bare ilah can name false gods too. | mentions 21:22, 23:117, 25:43
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari says Allah became a proper name through common usage prevailing over other uses.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The author prefers that Allah is primitive rather than derived and says it is the most definite of nouns; a dream story has Sibawayh praise God for making its name the most definite.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | One derivation links the name to lāha, to rise, and the sun-name ilāha; an elaborate explanation of lahanaka from lillahi innaka is condemned as contrived.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The author calls the derivation of lahanaka in the cited verse by deleting the preposition, article, alif, and shifting a vowel an ugly analysis.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Another derivation is from lāha yalūhu, to be hidden; on both analyses the original form is lāh and later article assimilation yields Allah.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A third derivation is alaha, with senses worship, find repose, be bewildered, and fear; the name describes creatures worshipping, seeking refuge, wondering, and fearing God. | mentions 7:127
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · رؤبة | reports | Ru'ba's word ta'alluh witnesses the worship sense; the verse phrase wa-yadharuka wa-ālihataka is also read as your worship. | mentions 7:127
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A report urging thought about God's blessings, not God Himself, and Ali's saying that reflection on divine attributes ends in bewilderment support the bewilderment sense.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | On the al-ilah derivation, hamza is dropped through frequent use, like anās becoming nās; an alternative account transfers its vowel before deletion.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil derives Allah from walah, because all creatures long for God; philosophers say all things love God, supported by the verse that everything glorifies Him. | mentions 17:44
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | This derivation changes initial waw to hamza, like ishaah and i'aah from wishah and wi'aah; the name then has the pattern fa'al meaning worshipped or wondered at.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The author rebuts al-Khalil: if hamza replaced waw, the original forms should remain pronounceable, and the word should pluralize as awliha; neither occurs.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil can answer that the replacement became obligatory because this name has unique grammatical properties and its plural preserves that replacement.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Whether the article in Allah is original depends on whether the name is derived; if derived it is original, otherwise added.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The alif was omitted in writing to distinguish Allah from the idol al-Lat; another explanation invokes the word al-lāh, while a third calls the spelling a rare form fixed by frequent use.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The lām of Allah is emphatic except after kasra; al-Zamakhshari's unqualified statement should be understood this way, while Abu al-Baqa's report of always-light pronunciation is rejected.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Readers disagree about the lām after an imāla-like open vowel; al-Susi has one reading with a light lām in hatta nara Allah jahratan.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · السهيلي وابن العربي | reports | Al-Suhayli and Ibn al-Arabi unusually say the article is original; the author objects that this would make the pattern fa'al regularly take tanwin, which Allah does not.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو زيد البلخي | reports | Abu Zayd al-Balkhi reports that Allah is a Syriac loan from laha; a poem preserves the supposed original form lahi.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | A strange proposal derives the name from the pronoun hu plus a possessive lām and article; the author says it resembles mysticism, not linguistic scholarship.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | rejects | Al-Zamakhshari rejects treating Allah as an adjective: it is used as a noun, while adjectives require a noun they describe and cannot all remain without one.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The verb basmala means to say bismillah, like hawqala, haylala, and hamdala for saying their respective formulas.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ba can mean exchange or substitution, as in the prophetic saying about red camels and in a poem wishing for replacement companions.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r11] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ba also marks an oath and location, as in swearing by God and saying Zayd is in Mecca.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r12] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ba can make a verb transitive, as in God taking away their light. | mentions 2:17
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r13] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | A poet's ba in drinking from seawater means from it, showing the partitive use.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r14] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ba can mark price or equivalence in buying something for a thousand.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r15] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ba can mean away from, as in the sky splitting away from clouds; some restrict this sense to contexts of asking, as in ask an expert about it. | mentions 25:25, 25:59
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r16] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Alqama's line uses ba with asking women to mean asking about them, illustrating the restricted sense of departure.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | These clipped verbs resemble nisba coinages that combine names, as in hadrami, abqasi, and abshami from tribal names; a poem uses abshamiyya.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Because basmala and haylala are non-analogical, some classify them as later colloquial coinages.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الماوردي | reports | Al-Mawardi calls the person who says bismillah mubasmil and labels that usage a later coinage.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · عمر بن أبي ربيعة | reports | Ibn Abi Rabi'a's verse attests basmala as established poetic usage, while Tha'lab and al-Mutarriz transmit it without calling it a late coinage.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The preposition ba here expresses seeking aid: the implied sense is that I recite while relying on God.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ba can mark real or figurative attachment, illustrated by wiping the head and passing by Zayd.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ba can mean cause, as in God forbidding things because of the wrongdoing of the Jews. | mentions 4:160
[SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ba can mark accompaniment, as in Zayd going out with his clothes.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r1] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The surah is called al-Fatiha because it opens the written Book and begins recitation in prayer.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r10] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas calls the surah the foundation of the Qur'an and says its foundation is the basmala.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r104] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The Companions opened God's Book with the basmala; scholars agree it is part of the verse in Surat al-Naml, while disputing its status at surah openings. | mentions 27:30
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r105] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A sound Abu Dawud report from Ibn ʿAbbas says the Prophet recognized a surah's division when the basmala was revealed; it is also reported mursal from Saʿid ibn Jubayr.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r106] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أم سلمة | reports | A report from Umm Salama says the Prophet recited and counted the basmala as a verse at the start of the Fatiha; Ibn Kathir notes the chain is weak because of ʿUmar ibn Harun.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r107] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس وابن عمر وابن الزبير وأبو هريرة وعلي | reports | These Companions are cited as holding that the basmala is a verse at the start of every surah except al-Tawba; several Successors and a group of later authorities agree. | mentions 9:1
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r108] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · مالك وأبو حنيفة وأصحابهما | reports | Malik, Abu Hanifa, and their followers say the basmala is not a verse of the Fatiha or any other surah.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r109] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الشافعي | reports | One Shafiʿi position makes the basmala a verse of the Fatiha alone; another makes it part of the first ver

se of every surah, and Ibn Kathir calls both views unusual.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r11] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · سفيان بن عيينة | reports | Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna calls the surah al-Waqiya, the protecting one.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r110] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · داود وأحمد | reports | Dawud and one narration from Ahmad treat the basmala as an independent opening verse of each surah, not part of the surahs.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r111] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafiʿi recites the basmala aloud with both Fatiha and the following surah when opening prayer; many early and later authorities also did so.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r112] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبو هريرة | reports | Abu Hurayra recited the basmala aloud and said his prayer most resembled the Prophet's; Ibn Kathir cites several scholars who authenticated the report.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r113] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas reports that the Prophet opened prayer with the basmala; al-Tirmidhi says its chain is not strong.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r114] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أنس بن مالك | reports | Anas describes the Prophet's recitation as prolonged, with lengthening on each word of the basmala.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r115] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أم سلمة | reports | Umm Salama says the Prophet paused phrase by phrase in recitation, and al-Daraqutni calls the report's chain sound.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r116] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أنس بن مالك | reports | When Muʿawiya omitted the basmala in Medina, the Muhajirun present objected; on his next prayer he recited it.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r117] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبو حنيفة والثوري وأحمد | reports | Another group does not recite the basmala aloud; Ibn Kathir says this is established from the four caliphs, Ibn Mughaffal, and other early authorities.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r118] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · مالك | reports | Malik does not recite the basmala in prayer either aloud or quietly, relying on reports that the Prophet and first caliphs began with al-Hamd and did not mention it.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r119] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The legal disagreement is narrow: scholars agree a prayer is valid whether the basmala is recited aloud or quietly.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r12] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · يحيى بن أبي كثير | reports | Yahya ibn Abi Kathir calls it al-Kafiya: it suffices in place of other surahs, while none can replace it; this is also stated in a mursal report.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r120] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | A report says the basmala is one of God's names, extremely close to the Greatest Name, like the closeness between the black and white of the eye.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r121] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · عيسى ابن مريم | reports | A report explains the letters as bāʾ for God's splendor, sīn for His glory, and mīm for His dominion; Rahman is merciful in both worlds and Rahim in the next. Ibn Kathir calls the report very strange and possibly Israelite rather than Prophetic.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r122] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Dahhak is said to have transmitted a similar explanation of the basmala.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r123] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from Burayda says the basmala was revealed to Muhammad and Solomon alone.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r124] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · جابر بن عبد الله | reports | Jabir's report describes clouds fleeing, winds and sea becoming still, animals listening, devils pelted, and God's promise of blessing when His name is said over something.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r125] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masʿud reportedly says reciting the basmala shields a person from each of the nineteen keepers of Hell; Ibn ʿAtiyya supports this with a report of more than thirty angels hastening to record praise.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r126] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report says not to curse Satan after a fall because that makes him swell with pride; saying “in God's name” makes him shrink like a fly (another version says like a house).
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r127] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Because the basmala humbles Satan, it is recommended at the beginning of actions and speech.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r128] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | A report recommends beginning a sermon with the basmala and calls an affair begun without it defective.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r129] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | The basmala is recommended on entering the toilet, based on reports transmitted on that practice.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r13] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari also records the names Surat al-Salah and al-Kanz.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r130] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A hadith judged hasan says there is no ablution for one who does not mention God's name; scholars differ over whether it is obligatory when remembered or absolutely.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r131] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | The basmala is recommended before slaughter according to al-Shafiʿi and a group; others require it if remembered, and some require it absolutely.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r132] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet instructed his stepson ʿUmar ibn Abi Salama to say God's name, eat with his right hand, and eat from what is nearest; some scholars make the basmala obligatory at meals.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r133] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet taught spouses to say God's name and ask protection from Satan before intercourse; if a child is conceived, Satan will not harm it.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r134] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The preposition bi in the basmala may attach to an implied noun, “my beginning,” or verb, “I begin”; Qur'anic usage supports both. | mentions 11:41, 96:1
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r135] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The implied action varies with the activity begun—standing, sitting, eating, drinking, reciting, ablution, or prayer—and the basmala seeks blessing, aid to completion, and acceptance.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r136] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | In a report on the first revelation, Gabriel tells Muhammad to say the basmala and explains it as beginning, standing, and sitting in remembrance of God; Ibn Kathir elsewhere calls the report weak and disconnected. | mentions 96:1
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r137] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبو عبيدة وسيبويه | reports | One position identifies a name with the named object; Abu ʿUbayda and Sibawayh hold this view, as do al-Baqillani and Ibn Furak.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r138] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · فخر الدين الرازي | reports | Al-Razi reports that the Hashwiyya, Karramiyya, and Ashʿariyya identify name and named but distinguish both from naming, while the Muʿtazila distinguish name from named and equate it with naming; he chooses a third view.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r139] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · فخر الدين الرازي | prefers | Al-Razi's preferred view is that the name differs from both the named thing and the act of naming.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r14] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس وقتادة وأبو العالية | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada, and Abu al-ʿAliya hold that the surah was revealed in Mecca.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r140] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · فخر الدين الرازي | reports | Al-Razi argues that names can exist without their referents, one thing can have many names, one name can refer to many things, and a word is an accident while its referent may be an entity.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r141] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · فخر الدين الرازي | reports | Al-Razi says God's many names refer to one God and that calling God by those names indicates their distinction from Him. | mentions 7:180, 56:74, 56:96
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r142] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · فخر الدين الرازي | reports | Those who equate name and named cite “blessed is the name of your Lord”; al-Razi answers that honoring the name honors the sacred essence, and a divorce utterance refers to the person bearing that name. | mentions 55:78
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r143] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Allah is the proper name of the Lord and is called the Greatest Name because all the other attributes are predicated of Him. | mentions 59:22, 59:23, 59:24, 7:180, 17:110
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r144] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A sound hadith says God has ninety-nine names; whoever comprehends them enters Paradise, though the enumerated lists in al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah differ.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r145] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Allah is a name not used for anyone else, and Arabic does not clearly derive it from an ordinary verb.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r146] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الشافعي والخطابي وإمام الحرمين والغزالي والخليل وسيبويه | reports | These scholars regard Allah as an underived, fixed proper name; al-Khattabi argues that the vocative “ya Allah” works, whereas “ya al-Rahman” does not.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r147] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · رؤبة بن العجاج | reports | Ruʾba's line uses taʾalluh, worship, as evidence that Allah is derived from the root for worship.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r148] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس ومجاهد | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas's reading “wa-yadharuka wa-ilahatak” is explained as “your worship”; Mujahid gives the same gloss.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r149] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | Those who derive Allah from divinity cite that God is worshipped in heaven and earth and is a god in both realms. | mentions 6:3, 43:84
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r15] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبو هريرة ومجاهد وعطاء بن يسار والزهري | reports | Abu Hurayra, Mujahid, ʿAta ibn Yasar, and al-Zuhri hold that the surah was revealed in Medina.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r150] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الخليل وسيبويه | reports | Al-Khalil and Sibawayh derive the word from ilah, with the article replacing an initial hamza, by analogy with al-nas from unas; another proposal takes it from lah for exalted.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r151] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الكسائي والفراء | reports | Al-Kisaʾi and al-Farraʾ derive it from al-ilah, with the hamza dropped and the two lams assimilated, like lakinna from lakin ana. | mentions 18:38
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r152] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · فخر الدين الرازي | reports | Al-Razi lists proposed derivations from bewilder
