ment, repose in God, concealment, a calf's attachment to its mother, and seeking refuge in God. | mentions 13:28, 23:88, 16:53, 6:14, 4:78
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r153] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · فخر الدين الرازي | reports | Al-Razi says God alone is the refuge and provider, citing that He protects and cannot be protected against, gives every blessing, feeds without being fed, and all things come from Him. | mentions 23:88, 16:53, 6:14, 4:78
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r154] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · فخر الدين الرازي | prefers | Al-Razi chooses Allah as an underived proper name; he argues that if it were derived, others could share its meaning, while the other names function as attributes.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r155] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | Al-Razi also cites 19:65, “Do you know anyone like Him?” as evidence for an un-derived name, but Ibn Kathir finds that argument debatable. | mentions 19:65
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r156] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · فخر الدين الرازي | rejects | Al-Razi rejects the claim that the name Allah is Hebrew rather than Arabic.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r157] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الخليل بن أحمد | reports | Al-Khalil explains that all creation is captivated by God, using a form of the root “to worship.”
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r158] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | A further proposal derives Allah from elevation: Arabs called something high lahan and said lahat when the sun rose.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r159] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The proposed form begins as al-ilah; deleting the hamza brings two lams together, which assimilate and are pronounced as one emphatic doubled lam.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r16] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | prefers | A third report says it was revealed twice, but Ibn Kathir prefers the Meccan account, connecting it with the seven oft-repeated in 15:87. | mentions 15:87
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r160] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Al-Rahman and al-Rahim are intensive forms derived from mercy, with al-Rahman more emphatic; Ibn Jarir's discussion suggests agreement.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r161] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · عيسى ابن مريم | reports | A report attributed to Jesus distinguishes Rahman as merciful in this life and the next, and Rahim as merciful in the next life.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r162] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · المبرد وأحمد بن يحيى | reports | Some grammarians claim Rahman is not derived or is Hebrew while Rahim is Arabic; al-Zajjaj rejects this as an objectionable view.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r163] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · القرطبي | reports | Al-Qurtubi cites the hadith, graded sound by al-Tirmidhi, in which God says He is Rahman and derived the womb's name from His own; he treats it as explicit evidence of derivation.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r164] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · القرطبي | reports | Al-Qurtubi says Arabs denied the name Rahman through ignorance of God and what is due to Him.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r165] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبو عبيد | reports | Abu ʿUbayd treats Rahman and Rahim as synonymous, like two parallel forms; others distinguish the intensive faʿlan form from faʿil.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r166] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبو علي الفارسي | reports | Abu ʿAli al-Farisi says Rahman encompasses every kind of mercy and is exclusive to God, while Rahim describes His mercy toward believers. | mentions 33:43
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r167] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas calls the two names tender and says one is more tender—that is, more merciful—than the other.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r168] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن المبارك | reports | Ibn al-Mubarak says Rahman gives when asked, while Rahim becomes angry if not asked, linking the distinction to the hadith that God is angered by one who does not supplicate.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r169] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · العرزمي | reports | Al-ʿArzami says Rahman covers all creation, while Rahim specifically describes mercy to believers. | mentions 25:59, 20:5, 33:43
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r17] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبو الليث السمرقندي | reports | Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi says half the surah was revealed in Mecca and half in Medina; Ibn Kathir calls this very strange, as transmitted by al-Qurtubi.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r170] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | This distinction is supported by verses that name Rahman at God's establishing the Throne and Rahim for believers, although a traditional supplication calls Him Rahman and Rahim of both worlds. | mentions 25:59, 20:5, 33:43
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r171] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Rahman is a name specific to God; Musaylima's self-title Rahman of Yamama became a byword for lying. | mentions 17:110, 21:26
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r172] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | rejects | The claim that Rahim must intensify Rahman because it follows it is mistaken: the second word is another adjective, not emphatic repetition.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r173] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The naming sequence moves from the unique name Allah, to the exclusive Rahman, to Rahim, which also describes the Prophet and human beings; naming starts with the most honored and specific names. | mentions 17:110, 9:128, 76:2
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r174] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · عطاء الخراساني | reports | ʿAta al-Khurasani explains that Rahim follows Rahman to prevent anyone claiming the exclusive title Rahman, since only God is described as both.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r175] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Quraysh's denial of Rahman at Hudaybiyya and in 25:60 was stubbornness: pre-Islamic poems already used Rahman for God. | mentions 25:60
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r176] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · سلامة بن جندب | reports | Salama ibn Jundub's pre-Islamic verse calls God Rahman, showing the name was already known among Arabs.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r177] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas calls Rahman an intensive Arabic form of mercy and glosses the two names as gentle to whom God wills mercy and severe toward whom He wills to chastise.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r178] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الحسن | reports | Hasan says Rahman is a protected name that people cannot assume for themselves.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r179] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | Umm Salama's report says the Prophet paused between the basmala, al-Hamd, Rahman al-Rahim, and Malik yawm al-din; some Kufans pause at the basmala while most connect it to al-Hamd. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r18] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | There is no disagreement that the surah has seven verses; reports of eight from ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd and six from Husayn al-Juʿfi are aberrant.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r180] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisaʾi says some Arabs connect the basmala to al-Hamd by transferring the vowel of the connecting hamza to the mīm; Ibn ʿAtiyya says he knew of no transmitted canonical reading for it. | mentions 2:1, 2:2
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r19] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | Scholars differ over whether the basmala is an independent opening verse, part of a verse, or not counted as part of the Fatiha.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r2] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الجمهور | reports | The majority call it Umm al-Kitab; Anas is cited for this name.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r20] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The surah has twenty-five words and one hundred thirteen letters.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r21] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · البخاري | reports | Al-Bukhari explains Umm al-Kutub by its being written first in Qur'anic codices and recited first in prayer.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r22] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | Another explanation of Umm al-Kitab is that the meanings of the whole Qur'an return to what the Fatiha contains.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r23] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن جرير | reports | Ibn Jarir says Arabs call a comprehensive or leading thing with dependent parts an umm, such as the head's covering or an army's banner.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r24] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ذو الرمة | reports | Ibn Jarir cites Dhu al-Rumma's verse calling a spear an umm, a focal point followed in affairs.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r25] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | Mecca is called Umm al-Qura because it precedes and gathers the other settlements, or because the earth was spread from it.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r26] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The Fatiha opens recitation and was placed first when the Companions wrote the master codex.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r27] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | The title al-Sabʿ al-Mathani is explained by its repetition in every prayer unit, though Ibn Kathir notes another meaning will follow.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r28] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Reports from Abu Hurayra identify Umm al-Qur'an as the Fatiha and the seven oft-repeated; al-Daraqutni says its transmitters are trustworthy. | mentions 15:87
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r29] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · علي وابن عباس وأبو هريرة | reports | Al-Bayhaqi reports that ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu Hurayra interpret the seven oft-repeated in 15:87 as the Fatiha, with the basmala its seventh verse. | mentions 15:87
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r3] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الحسن وابن سيرين | reports | Hasan and Ibn Sirin dislike the name Umm al-Kitab, taking it to refer to the Preserved Tablet; Hasan also calls the clear verses Umm al-Kitab.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r30] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masʿud explains that he omitted the Fatiha from his codex because he would have written it at the start of every surah where it is recited in prayer; Muslims' memorization sufficed.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r31] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | One view makes the Fatiha the first revelation, based on a report in al-Bayhaqi and listed by al-Baqillani among three views.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r32] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | A second view makes “O you wrapped up” the first revelation, based on Jabir's sound hadith. | mentions 74:1
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r33] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | prefers | Ibn Kathir says the correct view is that “Read in the name of your Lord” was first revealed. | mentions 96:1
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r34] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Abu Saʿid ibn al-Muʿalla reports that the Prophet promised to teach him the Qur'an's greatest surah and identified it as al-Hamd, the seven oft-repeate

d and the great Qur'an.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r35] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir distinguishes the Muwatta's Abu Saʿid, a Successor and client of Khuzāʿa, from the Companion Abu Saʿid ibn al-Muʿalla; the former report appears disconnected unless he heard it from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r36] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report through Abu Hurayra from Ubayy repeats that the Fatiha has no equal in the Torah, Gospel, Psalms, or Qur'an; al-Tirmidhi calls it hasan sahih.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r37] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Another report from Ubayy calls Umm al-Qur'an the seven oft-repeated, divided between God and His servant; al-Tirmidhi grades it hasan gharib.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r38] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · عبد الله بن جابر | reports | The report that the Prophet called the Fatiha the best surah has a good chain according to Ibn Kathir; the Companion's identity is uncertain between al-ʿAbdi and al-Ansari al-Bayyadi.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r39] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · إسحاق بن راهويه وأبو بكر بن العربي وابن الحصار | reports | These scholars infer that some verses and surahs are superior to others from the superiority reports.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r4] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الحسن | reports | Hasan also objects to calling the surah Umm al-Qur'an.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r40] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الأشعري وأبو بكر الباقلاني وابن حبان ويحيى بن يحيى | reports | Another group denies ranking Qur'anic passages, since all are God's speech and ranking could imply deficiency in what is less preferred; a report from Malik agrees.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r41] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبو سعيد الخدري | reports | In a report judged by the Prophet, a companion recited the Fatiha as ruqya over a stung man who recovered; the Prophet approved the reward of thirty sheep and asked how he knew it was ruqya.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r42] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas reports that Gabriel announced two lights given to Muhammad alone: the Fatiha and the closing verses of al-Baqara; each letter brings a response. | mentions 2:285, 2:286
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r43] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet says prayer without Umm al-Qur'an is deficient, and the divine hadith answers the servant's praise verse by verse as the Fatiha is divided between God and servant. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r46] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبو حنيفة وأصحابه | reports | Abu Hanifa and his followers hold that Fatiha is not specifically required in prayer; any Qur'an passage suffices, citing 73:20 and “recite what is easy.” | mentions 73:20
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r47] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · مالك والشافعي وأحمد والجمهور | reports | The other major view requires the Fatiha in prayer, using the deficient-prayer hadith and reports that prayer does not count without it.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r48] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الشافعي وجماعة من أهل العلم | reports | Al-Shafiʿi and a group require the Fatiha in every prayer unit; others require it in most units, while Hasan and most Basrans require it in one unit.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r49] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الحسن وأكثر البصريين | reports | Hasan and most Basrans require the Fatiha in only one unit, relying on the unrestricted wording, “There is no prayer without Fatiha.”
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r5] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In a hadith graded sound by al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet calls it Umm al-Qur'an, Umm al-Kitab, the seven oft-repeated, and the great Qur'an.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r50] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · أبو حنيفة والثوري والأوزاعي | reports | Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, and al-Awzaʿi again hold that another Qur'anic passage can replace the Fatiha, citing 73:20. | mentions 73:20
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r51] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | A report that each prayer unit needs al-Hamd and another surah is questionable in authenticity.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r52] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | reports | Scholars have three views on whether a follower must recite: that the follower must recite the Fatiha just like the imam.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r53] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · مالك | reports | A second view says a follower recites nothing, whether prayer is audible or silent, based on “one with an imam has the imam's recitation”; the marfuʿ routes are weak, and Malik transmits it as Jabir's own statement.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r54] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · الشافعي في قوله القديم وأحمد في رواية | reports | A third view requires the follower's recitation in silent prayer but not audible prayer, combining the general requirement with the command to listen when the imam recites.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r55] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Al-Bazzar reports that reciting the Fatiha and Surat al-Ikhlas before sleep protects from everything except death. | mentions 112:1
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r6] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Al-Hamd is another name for the surah.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r7] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | It is also called al-Salah because the divine hadith names recitation of al-Hamd as the servant's praise, and the surah is a condition of prayer.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r8] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from Abu Saʿid calls the Fatiha a healing from every poison.
[IBNKATHIR:1:1/r9] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The surah is called a ruqya because the Prophet affirmed its use in healing a stung man and asked how the companion knew it was a ruqya.
[BURHAN:v1p100/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The basmala is counted differently because it came as part of a verse in some readings; readers of those modes count it, while others omit it and count a replacement after اهدنا to keep al-Fatiha seven verses. | mentions 27:30, 1:6
[BURHAN:v1p194#2/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن عباس والضحاك ومقاتل وعطاء | reports | Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, Muqatil, and Ata classify al-Fatiha as Meccan, while Mujahid classifies it as Medinan.
[BURHAN:v1p198/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | Other reports say al-Fatiha descended with eighty thousand angels, the Throne Verse and Yunus with thirty thousand each, and “Ask those We sent before you” with twenty thousand. | mentions 1:1, 2:255, 10:1, 43:45
[BURHAN:v1p207/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · أبو ميسرة | reports | An account through Abū Isḥāq from Abū Maysara says al-Fātiḥa was the first revelation; it describes the Prophet hearing a voice, fleeing, and then the angel's descent and the opening of the sūra. | mentions 96:1
[BURHAN:v1p207/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · القاضي أبو بكر | rejects | Al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr calls the report that al-Fātiḥa came first disconnected.
[BURHAN:v1p207/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · القاضي أبو بكر | holds | The views can be reconciled: اقرأ was the first verses, المدثر the first preaching commands, and al-Fātiḥa the first complete sūra revealed. | mentions 74:1, 1:1
[BURHAN:v1p251/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The basmala is counted in readings where it descended with the sūra and omitted in readings where it did not.
[BURHAN:v1p267/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن العربي | reports | Ibn al-Arabi cites reports that al-Fatiha has seven verses and al-Mulk thirty, and that the Prophet recited Aal Imran's final ten; verse counts should follow early Muslims' practice.
[BURHAN:v1p29/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | An ayah may descend twice to magnify its importance and recall it when a new cause arises; the Fatiha is said to have descended once in Mecca and once in Medina, and this resolves the report about the Makkan Hūd verse.
[BURHAN:v1p348/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · أم سلمة | reports | A report from Umm Salama says the Prophet divided his recitation verse by verse; some later scholars therefore objected to stopping mid-verse for meaning.
[BURHAN:v1p390/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The omitted alif in bism signals the name’s elevated, unique rank and its connection to God, whose name gathers all names; the spelling also evokes manifestation and hiddenness.
[BURHAN:v1p390/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The omitted alif in al-Rahman reflects that people know mercy’s effects but entrust knowledge of its full reality to God.
[BURHAN:v1p390/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · علماء الظاهر | reports | The outward scholars explain the omission as abbreviation from frequent use: the alif of ism is dropped only when appended to Allah and preceded by ba according to the majority.
[BURHAN:v1p390/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisaʾi does not require the preceding ba and permits deletion in forms such as bism al-malik; the majority requires ba.
[BURHAN:v1p390/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Alif is also omitted from some active-participle forms such as qadara and ʿalima because it lies inside the word.
[BURHAN:v1p390/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | In sound and broken plurals, a surplus alif is deleted when the detailed meaning is latent and retained when it is manifest.
[BURHAN:v1p438/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن حبان | reports | Ibn Hibban reads the report comparing al-Fatiha with the Torah and Gospel as a difference in reward granted by God’s favor, not as intrinsic superiority within the Quran.
[BURHAN:v1p438/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن حبان | reports | Ibn Hibban says calling al-Fatiha the greatest surah means greatest in reward, not that one part of the Quran is intrinsically superior.
[BURHAN:v1p439/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Abu Said reports the Prophet calling al-Fatiha the greatest surah in a Bukhari narration; al-Zarkashi says this does not conflict with Ayat al-Kursi’s rank among verses, since the comparisons concern surahs and verses respectively.
[BURHAN:v1p73/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | prefers | Al-Shafiʿi counts the basmala and makes the rest of 1:7 one verse; Abu Hanifa omits the basmala and divides its two phrases. Both count seven verses, but al-Shafiʿi's division better preserves the endings because anʿamta ʿalayhim does not match prior endings.
[BURHAN:v3p110/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The preposition in بسم الله requires a comp

[BURHAN:v3p199/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · البصريون | reports | The Basrans analyze بسم الله as part of a nominal sentence, meaning my beginning is in God's name.
[BURHAN:v3p199/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · الكوفيون | reports | The Kufans analyze بسم الله as part of a verbal sentence.
[BURHAN:v3p199/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | prefers | Al-Zamakhshari follows the Kufans but puts the implied verb after God's name and varies it by context; the author prefers this for contextual fit and foregrounding God's name.
[NASHR:v1p229/r1] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | A pause on an incomplete fragment such as “bi-smi,” “al-ḥamdu,” or “rabbi” leaves the utterance unfinished and without an intelligible meaning.
[BIQAI:1:1/r1] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | In the opening invocation, Allah is the ever-living witness who knows everything and permits all events; His mercy encompasses creation, while His special grace perfects the worship of His devotees.
[BIQAI:1:1/r10] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The Fātiḥa establishes God's right to all praise and perfection, His exclusive sovereignty over this world and the next, and His sole right to worship and assistance, while asking guidance to the successful and rescue from the doomed.
[BIQAI:1:1/r11] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Its central purpose is servants' vigilant awareness of their Lord so they worship Him alone; all other themes serve that end.
[BIQAI:1:1/r12] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | This purpose requires proving God's encompassing knowledge and His unique status as Creator, King, and Owner; prophets and revealed laws gather people to truth and teach them their Sovereign and what pleases Him, a purpose the Fātiḥa gathers in knowledge and action.
[BIQAI:1:1/r13] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Since people are gathered to know God for worship, invoking His name at every movement and stillness leads to watchfulness, reverent fear, and belief that affairs originate from and return to Him; hence the Fātiḥa begins with the basmala.
[BIQAI:1:1/r14] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Seeking refuge precedes the basmala as a way of warding off harm and honoring the Qur'an: its reciter should purify the heart, gather scattered concerns, turn from the envious enemy to the loving protector, and seek its stores of felicity.
[BIQAI:1:1/r15] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The two refuge sūras are therefore appropriately connected to the Fātiḥa.
[BIQAI:1:1/r16] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Biqāʿī reads the refuge formula's initial hamza and final mīm as signs of creation's beginning and return; the basmala's labial opening and repeated final mīm point to return in worldly governance, death in the intermediate realm, and resurrection.
[BIQAI:1:1/r17] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Here, “name” means God's supreme attributes.
[BIQAI:1:1/r18] BIQAI, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | Al-Ḥarālī says the initial bāʾ manifests God's wisdom in causation, while ism makes what is hidden or obscure apparent to hearts through hearing and articulated individual forms.
[BIQAI:1:1/r19] BIQAI, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | Al-Ḥarālī mystically explains Allah as the name toward which hearts turn when intellect reaches its limit: they are bewildered by Him and find in Him sufficiency from everything.
[BIQAI:1:1/r2] BIQAI, d. 885 · أبو الفضل محمد المشدالي | reports | Al-Mashdali's general rule for Qur'anic coherence is to identify a sūra's purpose, its necessary premises and their distance from that goal, then satisfy the listener's anticipation of resulting rulings and consequences.
[BIQAI:1:1/r20] BIQAI, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | For al-Ḥarālī, al-Raḥmān denotes mercy encompassing all that divine lordship covers.
[BIQAI:1:1/r21] BIQAI, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | For al-Ḥarālī, al-Raḥīm denotes the particular mercy associated with what divinity approves.
[BIQAI:1:1/r22] BIQAI, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | Al-Ḥarālī says people stop at apparent causes or trace causes back only as far as reason allows; the basmala folds away those intermediaries and declares everything to be through God's name, with no other ultimate cause.
[BIQAI:1:1/r23] BIQAI, d. 885 · أبو الحسن الحرالي | reports | Al-Ḥarālī says the basmala begins the Mother of the Qur'an because it folds up the causal order as the Mother of the Qur'an gathers earlier scriptures; it also holds the secret of acts appearing through divine care in 1:5, and should open people's words and deeds, outwardly and inwardly. | mentions 1:5
[BIQAI:1:1/r24] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The basmala stands to the Fātiḥa as the Fātiḥa stands to the Qur'an: by referring all things to God alone, it indicates that He alone is God and summarizes the Fātiḥa and the Qur'an's roots, branches, knowledge, and subtleties.
[BIQAI:1:1/r25] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Because Allah is the proper name encompassing the beautiful names, al-Raḥmān precedes al-Raḥīm: it is exclusive to Him and more intensive, so the stronger description comes first.
[BIQAI:1:1/r26] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Their order follows existence: creation, then universal blessings, then the particular blessing of worship. The two attributes encourage, while the second's implication folds in punishment as a restrained warning.
[BIQAI:1:1/r27] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | God deserves both attributes essentially; their repetition stresses their fitness for lordship and sovereignty and that mercy outweighs anger. All beautiful attributes follow, since encompassing mercy excludes deficiency; Biqāʿī promises further explanation at 3:8. | mentions 3:8
[BIQAI:1:1/r28] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The basmala has nineteen written letters but eighteen pronounced, signaling protection from Hell's nineteen keepers and the drawing of mercy through the five prayers and witr, among the greatest devotions.
[BIQAI:1:1/r3] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | After reaching Saba in his tenth year of writing, Biqāʿī concluded that each sūra's name gives a general indication of its purpose; that purpose guides the sūra's coherence.
[BIQAI:1:1/r4] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Biqāʿī states each sūra's purpose, aligns it with its name, and explains its basmala in a way suited to that purpose without leaving the words' meanings.
[BIQAI:1:1/r5] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Al-Fātiḥa is also called the Mother of the Book, Foundation, Oft-Repeated, Treasure, Healer, Sufficient, Fulfilling, Protector, Incantation, Praise, Gratitude, Supplication, and Prayer.
[BIQAI:1:1/r6] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | These names converge on vigilant awareness of God, the hidden reality sufficient for every aim and the Fātiḥa's central purpose; opening actions without it makes them unworthy of regard.
[BIQAI:1:1/r7] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The Fātiḥa is mother and foundation of every good, repeated continually, a treasure, cure, sufficiency for worries, fulfillment of aims, protection from evil, and remedy for every affliction.
[BIQAI:1:1/r8] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The sūra establishes praise as encompassing all perfections and gratitude as magnifying the Benefactor.
[BIQAI:1:1/r9] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Supplication is the very act of turning to the One invoked, and prayer is the greatest encompassing expression of that turn.
[BIQAI:1:7/r26] BIQAI, d. 885 · العلامة سعد الدين مسعود ابن عمرو التفتازاني الشافعي | reports | The first creation is named in praise of God, since bringing creatures from nonexistence into existence is the greatest nurturing.
[BIQAI:1:7/r32] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The opening praise moves from a particular expression toward the universal, explaining why consequential matters begin with praise; the relation of praise to gratitude is revisited in Sūrat al-Naḥl and Sabaʾ.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | God is the ever-living witness whose knowledge misses nothing and whose permission governs all things; His universal mercy reaches creation and His special mercy favors His devoted servants.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو الفضل محمد المشدالي المغربي | reports | Al-Mashdali's method for Qur'anic coherence is to identify a surah's purpose, its prerequisites and their distance from the goal, then answer expectations raised as the discourse unfolds.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | A surah's name summarizes its purpose, as a title signals the details within; Adam demonstrated this naming principle when he named things before the angels.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The Fatiha's many titles converge on مراقبة: it is the Mother of the Book, foundation, oft-repeated, treasure, healing, sufficing, complete, protecting, incantation, praise, thanks, supplication and prayer.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The Fatiha is a treasure, cure, sufficiency, fulfillment, protection and incantation; it gathers praise, gratitude and supplication, with prayer as their greatest assembly.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The Fatiha's purpose is to establish God's exclusive right to all praise and perfection, sovereignty over both worlds, worship and aid, and to ask for the path of the successful rather than the doomed; its center is مراقبة.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Prophets, scriptures and laws ultimately gather people to truth so they may know their sovereign and what pleases Him; knowledge and practice together serve the Qur'an's purpose.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | God's name should accompany every movement and stillness because it leads to مراقبة, fear and recognition that affairs begin and end with Him, so the Fatiha opens with the basmala.

:v1p12/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The prior refuge seeks to clear the reciter's inner life and focus scattered concerns; the basmala's opening and closing letters symbolize return in worldly governance, death in the intermediate realm and resurrection.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali glosses the basmala: باء manifests causal wisdom; ism reveals what is hidden to hearts through hearing; Allah names the one hearts seek beyond reason; Rahman is universally merciful and Rahim grants mercy approved by divinity.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali says the basmala shows that all things proceed through God's name alone, folding apparent causes back to Him; it should therefore begin people's words and deeds.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | The basmala relates to the Fatiha as the Fatiha relates to the Qur'an: each is a compact synthesis of what the larger whole details.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Allah is a proper name encompassing all beautiful names; Rahman precedes Rahim because it is exclusive and more emphatic, following the order of existence, general mercy, then worship-specific mercy.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The basmala has nineteen written and eighteen spoken letters, alluding to the nineteen guardians of Hell and to mercy drawn by the five prayers and witr.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Since the basmala is a kind of praise, it naturally leads to comprehensive al-hamd: begin affairs by praising God as the one deserving every praise, with hope and awe guiding the way.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali says all Qur'an is God's speech, but some verses voice what creatures at different levels ought to say yet cannot express; God teaches them words that fulfill their duty.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali explains the sound report that God divided prayer between Himself and His servant: the first three verses are God's praise, which He accepts from the reciting servant as praise and glorification.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The Qur'an's arrangement is miraculous, so the Fatiha must retain its required order in prayer; rearrangement or insertion of foreign material invalidates it. Al-Isfahani locates its clearest inimitability in order.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali says the seven repeated verses are the Qur'an's gathered essence and its contents will be disclosed at creation's completion; earlier scriptures progress from changeable scrolls and lasting books to the Qur'an, which completes religion. | mentions 5:3
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali contrasts the Qur'an's detailed, dispersed sequence with the Fatiha's seven complete universals, and makes the Fatiha a mirror of the servant's move from misguidance to guidance. | mentions 93:7
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A Prophetic report says he was sent to complete noble character; the author links this completion with the Fatiha's comprehensive opening and the Qur'an's culmination. | mentions 5:3
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali describes the Qur'an's majesty through rulings spanning immediate and deferred realities, witnessed experience, and reports of the past and patterns that recur in time.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali distinguishes gradual descent that moves understanding between states and rulings from descent from high to low, which may occur with or without intermediaries.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The passage names al-Baqara 2:281 as the last revealed verse and says its recitation position between the debt verse and the verse before it shows revelation and recitation order can differ. | mentions 2:281, 75:17
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali says the Qur'an's sevenfold gathering in Muhammad's heart relates to the Mother of Qur'an's universals as the Qur'an's gathering in his heart relates to the Mother.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali says the Qur'an reached the Prophet on his tongue over the span of the prophetic mission, after its descent to the lowest heaven.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · عائشة | reports | Aisha reports that Muhammad's character was the Qur'an, making his conduct the visible form of its inner reality.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali says the Fatiha is the Qur'an's mother: its first three verses encompass the divine names and attributes, while its last three cover the creature's way to God, mercy or failure. | mentions 2:281, 75:17, 33:50, 33:52
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Recitation order can differ from revelation chronology; the verse allowing the Prophet to marry certain women was placed before a later restriction. | mentions 33:50, 33:52
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو هريرة | reports | In the authentic report in Muslim and the four Sunan, God says the Fatiha is divided between Himself and His servant: He answers praise, glorification and worship, and grants the servant's final requests.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Al-Baqara aims to prove the Book is guidance to follow; belief in the unseen, especially resurrection and the afterlife, is its greatest guidance and organizing theme.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The cow story makes the surah's title apt because resurrection occurs through an apparently slight human cause; it is a clearer sign of divine power than Abraham's story or earlier Israelite resurrections.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The following comparison of hearts and stones shows the guided and astray: hearts become hard and wretched, while stones display fear and yield benefit that reaches God's servants.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The Book functions like a caliph from the resolute messengers, guiding every matter to the right exit: rejecting it fails, hesitation nearly perishes, and accepting it brings piety and excellence.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Al-Baqara is also called the Radiant and the Hump: it illuminates guidance and sufficiency, brightens believers' faces at judgment, and exalts belief in the afterlife above every other good after monotheism.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali transmits a report attributed to the Prophet from Ibn Masud: earlier books came through one gate and letter, whereas the Qur'an came through seven gates and seven letters encompassing commands, prohibitions, rulings, ambiguities and parables.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو عمر بن عبد البر | reports | Ibn Abd al-Barr says the seven-letter report is unestablished: Abu Salama did not meet Ibn Masud, his son Salama is not authoritative, and its chain is agreed to be weak; Ahmad ibn Abi Imran also rejected it.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · البيهقي | reports | Al-Bayhaqi transmits an alternative mursal route through al-Layth, Uqayl, Ibn Shihab, Umm Salama and Abu Salama; he calls the mursal report good because Abu Salama did not meet Ibn Masud.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو شامة | reports | Abu Shama says that if sound, seven letters means seven forms or categories of Qur'anic content, not the dialects in which recitation was permitted.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · ابن الجزري | reports | Ibn al-Jazari cites the Prophet's report to Ibn Masud from al-Tabarani: the Qur'an's seven categories include lawful, forbidden, clear, ambiguous, parables, commands and warnings, each with its proper response.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو هريرة | reports | Al-Bayhaqi also reports from Abu Huraira a version that describes five Qur'anic forms: lawful, forbidden, clear, ambiguous and parables.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali reads the seven letters as a completion of creation and religious, worldly and afterlife well-being: Muhammad is the comprehensive final prophet and his book seals the scriptures; he cites the report I was sent to complete noble character.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The quoted supplication asks God to set right religion as the safeguard of one's affairs, worldly livelihood and the afterlife to which one returns.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | Al-Harali divides the three domains of well-being into action and restraint, yielding six letters; God then grants Muhammad a seventh, inclusive letter, so the Qur'an descends in seven letters.
[BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي | reports | The worldly pair is halal and haram: lawful things cultivate body and soul, forbidden things must be purified away; the pair originates in the Torah and is completed in the Qur'an.

[ITQAN:v1p104/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · قوم | reports | Some authorities include al-Fātiḥa among verses revealed repeatedly.
[ITQAN:v1p114/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Among the material granted to Muhammad but not to any earlier prophet are al-Fatiha, Ayat al-Kursi, and the conclusion of al-Baqara.
[ITQAN:v1p183/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · الجمهور | reports | The majority count al-Fatiha as seven verses, with Kufan and Meccan counters counting the basmala but not “anʿamta ʿalayhim,” and others doing the reverse.
[ITQAN:v1p183/r4] ITQAN, d. 911 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan counts al-Fatiha as eight verses by including both the basmala and “anʿamta ʿalayhim.”
[ITQAN:v1p183/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · بعضهم | reports | Some count al-Fatiha as six verses by counting neither the basmala nor “anʿamta ʿalayhim.”
[ITQAN:v1p183/r6] ITQAN, d. 911 · آخر | reports | Another view counts al-Fatiha as nine verses, including both the basmala and “iyyāka naʿbud.”
[ITQAN:v1p183/r7] ITQAN, d. 911 · أم سلمة | reports | Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited al-Fatiha verse by verse, counted the basmala as a verse, and did not count “ʿalayhim”; al-Suyuti says this supports the majority's seven-verse count.
[ITQAN:v1p209#2/r6] ITQAN, d. 911 · المالكية | reports | Malikis and others who deny the basmala’s Quranic status argue that it was not mutawatir at surah openings and therefore is not Quran.
[ITQAN:v1p209#2/r7] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | rejects | The author denies that the basmala lacked tawatur: its unmarked inclusion in Companion and later codices proves its Quranic status, since they prohibited writing non-Quranic material there and would not mislead Muslims.
[ITQAN:v1p210/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Treating the basmala merely as a separator between sūras is an unsafe claim; if that were its sole function, it would not appear between al-Anfal and Bara'a.
[ITQAN:v1p210/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Umm Salama reports that the Prophet counted the basmala as a verse in his recitation of the opening sūra, but did not count عليهم as one.
[ITQAN:v1p210/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says Satan concealed from people the Quran’s greatest verse, the basmala.
[ITQAN:v1p210/r4] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن عباس | reports | In a report through Mujahid, Ibn Abbas says people neglected a verse revealed only to Muhammad, perhaps also Solomon: the basmala.
[ITQAN:v1p210/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A weak report through Burayda has the Prophet identify the basmala as the verse given to him after Solomon and recited at the opening of prayer.
[ITQAN:v1p210/r6] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas reports that the Prophet learned a sūra’s boundary when the basmala was revealed; al-Bazzar adds that it marked a completed sūra and the next one.
[ITQAN:v1p210/r7] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says Muslims knew a sūra had ended when the basmala descended; al-Hakim’s chain meets the standards of the two Sahih collections.
[ITQAN:v1p210/r8] ITQAN, d. 911 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Ibn Abbas reports that when Gabriel recited the basmala, the Prophet knew it was a sūra; al-Hakim grades the chain sound.
[ITQAN:v1p41/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | prefers | Most authorities consider al-Fātiḥa Meccan. Its identification with the seven oft-repeated verses in a Meccan sūra implies it was already revealed, and prayer was obligatory in Mecca with no known prayer omitting it.
[ITQAN:v1p41/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | A report transmitted by al-Wāḥidī and al-Thaʿlabī says al-Fātiḥa descended in Mecca from a treasure beneath the Throne.
[ITQAN:v1p41/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid is reliably reported by al-Firyābī and Abū ʿUbayd to consider al-Fātiḥa Medinan; al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl calls this a slip, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya also names several who held it.
[ITQAN:v1p41/r4] ITQAN, d. 911 · أبو هريرة | reports | A good-chain report from Abū Hurayra says Satan groaned when al-Fātiḥa was revealed in Medina, but al-Suyūṭī allows that the Medina clause may be Mujāhid's insertion.
[ITQAN:v1p41/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · بعضهم | reports | Some say al-Fātiḥa was revealed twice, once in Mecca and once in Medina, to magnify its honor; a fourth view divides it between the two cities.
[ITQAN:v3p283/r9] ITQAN, d. 911 · البيهقي | reports | The most specialized form of a fine opening is barāʿat al-istihlāl, which signals the subject to come; al-Bayhaqi cites al-Hasan that knowledge of the earlier scriptures and Qur’an was concentrated into the Fatiha.
[ITQAN:v3p284/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | By signaling all Qur’anic aims, the Fatiha achieves an exemplary opening and combines beautiful words, pleasing cadence, and rhetorical forms.
[ITQAN:v4p337/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن العربي | reports | Ibn al-Arabi estimates Qur'anic sciences by multiplying its words by four—outer meaning, inner meaning, limit, and point of access—yielding vast totals, and says combinations and relations are beyond counting or human knowledge.
[ITQAN:v4p337/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن العربي | reports | Ibn al-Arabi divides Qur'anic knowledge into monotheism (creatures and God's names, attributes, and acts), reminder (promise, threat, afterlife, and purification), and rulings (duties, benefits, harms, commands, prohibitions, and recommendations).
[ITQAN:v4p337/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن العربي | reports | For Ibn al-Arabi, al-Fatiha is the Qur'an's mother because it contains all three domains, while al-Ikhlas is a third because it contains monotheism alone.
[ITQAN:v4p337/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · علي بن عيسى | reports | Ali ibn Isa enumerates thirty Qur'anic subjects, including signs, analogy, commands and prohibitions, promise and threat, paradise and hell, divine names and acts, gratitude, argument, ethics, wisdom, praise, blame, and moral instruction.
[ITQAN:v4p420/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari says the Fatiha encompasses praise, worship through commands and prohibitions, and promise and warning; every Qur’anic verse falls under one of these topics.
[ITQAN:v4p420/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · البيضاوي | reports | Al-Baydawi says the Fatiha contains theoretical wisdom, practical rulings in walking the straight path, and knowledge of the ranks of the blessed and abodes of the wretched.
[ITQAN:v4p421/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · الزركشي وناصر الدين بن الميلق | reports | They reconcile the hadith calling the Fatiha two-thirds of the Qur’an by saying it indicates all Qur’anic aims through inclusion and implication, but not direct correspondence; those are two of three modes of indication.
[ITQAN:v4p421/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · ناصر الدين بن الميلق | reports | A second explanation counts three kinds of rights—God’s claim on servants, servants’ claim on God, and people’s claims on one another—and says the Fatiha explicitly covers the first two, hence two-thirds.
[ITQAN:v4p421/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | There is no conflict between hadiths calling the Fatiha the greatest surah and al-Baqara the greatest: al-Baqara is greatest among surahs other than the Fatiha because o

[ALUSI:1:1/r1] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī says most authorities classify al-Fātiḥa as Meccan, even counting it among the earliest revealed passages.
[ALUSI:1:1/r10] ALUSI, d. 1270 · النابغة | reports | Al-Nābigha’s verse uses sūra for an elevated rank or station, supporting the sense of height.
[ALUSI:1:1/r100] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The bāʾ is kasra-marked despite the preference for light vowels on isolated particles: its prepositional function and genitive effect distinguish it.
[ALUSI:1:1/r101] ALUSI, d. 1270 · ابن الفارض | reports | Ibn al-Fāriḍ’s verse makes the bāʾ’s kasra a sign of servile humility that is raised by divine generosity, not by human contrivance.
[ALUSI:1:1/r102] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الشبلي وابن عربي | reports | Al-Shiblī identifies himself with the dot under bāʾ, and Ibn ʿArabī makes that dot a reminder of the heart and the secret of servanthood.
[ALUSI:1:1/r103] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī’s allusion makes alif signify the divine essence and bāʾ its manifested attributes; its genitive kasra signifies lowered humility and mercy’s priority.
[ALUSI:1:1/r104] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | He links the basmala’s bāʾ to Muḥammad’s merciful reality and cites 21:107 and 9:128; the basmala’s opening then signals the Prophet’s mercy and mission. | mentions 21:107, 9:128
[ALUSI:1:1/r105] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | He associates the missing basmala in al-Tawba with that sūra’s manifest severity, while claiming a concealed allusion to the Prophetic reality remains.
[ALUSI:1:1/r106] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The Basrans derive ism from sumūw, “height,” with a deleted wāw; its function is to raise what is named from obscurity into recognition.
[ALUSI:1:1/r107] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الكوفيون | reports | The Kufans derive ism from wasm, “mark,” and posit a compensatory hamza; al-Ālūsī rejects this as unsupported and prefers the Basran derivation.
[ALUSI:1:1/r108] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī records eighteen dialect forms for ism, including sim, sumā, and samāʾ, using inflected forms such as asāmī and summiyy to support the Basran root.
[ALUSI:1:1/r109] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الأشاعرة والمعتزلة | reports | Ashʿarīs say the name is the named, whereas Muʿtazilīs say it is other than the named; al-Ālūsī argues the dispute confuses essence with verbal designation.
[ALUSI:1:1/r11] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | He defines a sūra as Qurʾān containing an opening and a conclusion; another definition, an independent portion, distinguishes named units such as Āyat al-Kursī.
[ALUSI:1:1/r110] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | He argues that “glorify the name of your Lord” and “names you invented” can use name for the divine essence or idols, not merely their words. | mentions 87:1, 12:40
[ALUSI:1:1/r111] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | He distinguishes God’s eternal names in eternal speech from later names used of Him; the former follow the dispute about divine speech, while created designations are other than God.
[ALUSI:1:1/r112] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Al-Ālūsī says objections that identity would multiply or change the named apply only to names as created expressions, not names used for the essence.
[ALUSI:1:1/r113] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | Some take ism here as God’s essence because help cannot be sought through a bare word and none of the ninety-nine names is literally “name”; al-Ālūsī distinguishes constructions with bi-

[ALUSI:1:1/r115] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The written basmala omits the alif of ism; explanations include frequent usage, the bāʾ replacing the initial hamza, and whether the governing word is stated. | mentions 96:1
[ALUSI:1:1/r116] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | Al-Ālūsī treats the Uthmānic spelling’s hidden alif as an allusion to the fullness of the bāʾ-sīn-mīm connection and universal mercy. | mentions 4:80, 35:45, 7:156, 25:1
[ALUSI:1:1/r117] ALUSI, d. 1270 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report says the Prophet instructed Muʿāwiya in calligraphy, including elongating the bāʾ, separating the sīns, and shaping the mīm; ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz gave similar advice.
[ALUSI:1:1/r118] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | Authorities derive Allāh either from al-ilāh or ilāh with hamza loss and compensatory alif-lām; Ibn Mālik instead argues for a distinct root and original proper name.
[ALUSI:1:1/r119] ALUSI, d. 1270 · السيد السند والسعد والرضي | reports | Al-Sayyid, al-Saʿd, and al-Raḍī differ on whether al-ilāh is generic or already exclusive, and whether Allāh became a proper name through deletion or assimilation.
[ALUSI:1:1/r12] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Fātiḥa was originally an adjective for the first part because it opens the whole; alternatively it is a verbal noun used for the object, as with al-Khātima.
[ALUSI:1:1/r120] ALUSI, d. 1270 · ابن مالك | reports | Ibn Mālik denies that Allāh derives from al-ilāh, arguing their forms and meanings differ and that deletion or hamza transfer lacks a sound morphological parallel.
[ALUSI:1:1/r121] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | Proposed roots for Allāh include worship, bewilderment, finding refuge, seeking, and a calf’s attachment to its mother; al-Ālūsī weighs these as conjectural alternatives. | mentions 13:28
[ALUSI:1:1/r122] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الأعشى | reports | Al-Aʿshā’s verse uses lāh as a divine designation, supporting the proposal that Allāh comes from a root meaning to be exalted or veiled.
[ALUSI:1:1/r123] ALUSI, d. 1270 · البلخي | rejects | Al-Balkhī says Allāh is an Arabized Hebrew or Syriac word meaning powerful; al-Ālūsī rejects this without evidence and notes that Arabic morphology weighs against it.
[ALUSI:1:1/r124] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | prefers | Al-Ālūsī favors Allāh as an Arabic proper name for the essence encompassing every attribute, following major theologians and the Naqshbandī tradition.
[ALUSI:1:1/r125] ALUSI, d. 1270 · البيضاوي | reports | Al-Bayḍāwī says Allāh began as an adjective but became proper through exclusive use; al-Ālūsī rejects his arguments from description, the heavenly predicate, and derivation. | mentions 6:3
[ALUSI:1:1/r126] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The exclusive declaration “no god but God” supports a proper name: an adjective or generic noun would not itself prevent sharing, even if conventionally reserved. | mentions 2:163
[ALUSI:1:1/r127] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The lām is emphatic after fatḥa or ḍamma according to common recitation practice; deletion of the alif is reported in pause, but retention is more eloquent.
[ALUSI:1:1/r128] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ reports dropping Allāh’s alif; al-Taysīr confines it to pause, and some jurists call it erroneous enough to invalidate prayer or an explicit oath.
[ALUSI:1:1/r129] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | Al-Ālūsī points readers to Ibn ʿArabī’s extensive mystical treatment of the word’s letters, hidden and audible alif, and opening and ending structure.
[ALUSI:1:1/r13] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | rejects | He finds an instrumental reading of fātiḥa unsuitable: the instrument need not share the action, and it could wrongly imply that the opening part is incidental.
[ALUSI:1:1/r130] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | The conventional analysis makes al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm intensive adjectives from rahima, sometimes positing transfer to intransitive rahuma; al-Ālūsī disputes this derivation.
[ALUSI:1:1/r131] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | Interpreters explain divine mercy as its effect, the will to do good, a king’s compassion by analogy, or a metaphorical attribute; some call it a revealed technical sense.
[ALUSI:1:1/r132] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī rejects metaphorical reduction: mercy is truly God’s attribute in a manner befitting Him, without likening it to created emotion or specifying its modality.
[ALUSI:1:1/r133] ALUSI, d. 1270 · السكوني والأشعري | reports | Al-Sakūnī condemns interpreting mercy metaphorically as an Muʿtazilī tendency; al-Ālūsī says al-Ashʿarī’s final position follows affirmation without asking how.
[ALUSI:1:1/r134] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الأشعري | reports | Al-Ālūsī says reports that al-Ashʿarī interpreted mercy are either unestablished or superseded by the creed in his later al-Ibāna.
[ALUSI:1:1/r135] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الراغب وابن المبارك | reports | Al-Rāghib says raḥīm marks frequent action and raḥmān frequent, repeated action; Ibn al-Mubārak says the Merciful gives when asked, while the Compassionate is angered if not asked.
[ALUSI:1:1/r136] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الجويني | reports | Al-Juwaynī treats the two names as equal in force, distinguishing repeated abundance in raḥmān from enduring action in raḥīm.
[ALUSI:1:1/r137] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | Some distinguish raḥmān as the attribute of mercy and raḥīm as its relation to recipients, citing human use of raḥīm in 9:117 and 33:43 but not raḥmān. | mentions 9:117, 33:43
[ALUSI:1:1/r138] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Al-Ālūsī challenges the rule that greater form means greater intensity and disputes whether raḥmān is more abundant, more enduring, or simply equal to raḥīm.
[ALUSI:1:1/r139] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | One distinction makes raḥmān’s worldly mercy encompass believers and unbelievers and raḥīm’s afterlife mercy favor believers; al-Ālūsī questions the allocation and its assumptions.

[ALUSI:1:1/r145] ALUSI, d. 1270 · ابن الحاجب والزمخشري والرضي وابن مالك والبيضاوي والسعد | reports | Grammarians dispute whether raḥmān declines: most prefer diptote treatment by analogy with the predominant faʿlā feminine pattern, while al-Saʿd allows both.
[ALUSI:1:1/r146] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | Banū Ḥanīfa called Musaylima “the Merciful of Yamāma”; al-Ālūsī treats this as blasphemous excess, not evidence that the sacred name is ordinarily shared.
[ALUSI:1:1/r147] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The basmala opens God’s discourse because it summarizes what follows and is a profound blessing; analyzing even its brief wording draws on many disciplines.

[ALUSI:1:1/r149] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | Al-Ālūsī finds layered triads in its articulation, omitted letters, written and spoken forms, word classes, genitives, divine names, grammatical roles, and connections.
[ALUSI:1:1/r15] ALUSI, d. 1270 · ابن كيسان والسيرافي وجمع | reports | Ibn Kaysān, al-Sīrāfī, and others treat the part-to-whole addition as partitive, with some grammarians extending that analysis to all such constructions.
[ALUSI:1:1/r150] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | A second reason for opening with the basmala is to teach people how to begin: invoking God declares dependence on His power in every undertaking.
[ALUSI:1:1/r151] ALUSI, d. 1270 · أبو هريرة | reports | Abū Hurayra transmits the Prophet’s maxim that an important matter begun without God’s name is incomplete; al-Ālūsī interprets it broadly to include trivial matters.
[ALUSI:1:1/r152] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī takes dhū bāl as comprehensive—anything that enters the mind—rather than restricting it to dignified matters, since God’s aid matters in small acts too. | mentions 6:38
[ALUSI:1:1/r153] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | Reports urge asking God even for a sandal strap, and God tells Moses to ask for salt and a shoe strap; these support invocation in minor needs.
[ALUSI:1:1/r154] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Reciting the basmala over forbidden acts is itself forbidden without being disbelief according to the sound view; over disliked acts it is disliked, unless contempt makes it disbelief.
[ALUSI:1:1/r155] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | The maxim’s variants include beginning with praise, “praise of God,” or another remembrance, and incomplete versus severed; al-Ālūsī calls it unstable in wording and chain but strengthened in meaning.
[ALUSI:1:1/r156] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī reconciles variants by taking the intended opening as remembrance that manifests divine perfection; matters may be outwardly complete yet deficient in meaning without it.
[ALUSI:1:1/r157] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Since the basmala is a kind of praise, it fittingly precedes the comprehensive praise that follows. | mentions 1:2

[ALUSI:1:1/r18] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Umm al-Kitāb and Umm al-Qurʾān reflect its priority, like a mother preceding what follows, a banner leading an army, or its encompassing the Qurʾān’s aims.
[ALUSI:1:1/r19] ALUSI, d. 1270 · الحسن البصري | reports | The alleged prophetic prohibition on calling it Umm al-Kitāb has no basis; sound reports establish that title, and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī also used it.
[ALUSI:1:1/r2] ALUSI, d. 1270 · علي وابن عباس وقتادة وأكثر الصحابة | reports | Reports from ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and most Companions support its Meccan origin.
[ALUSI:1:1/r20] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī says al-Fātiḥa gathers praise, worship, and promise or warning; these summarize the guidance sent through messengers and revealed books for worldly and final welfare. | mentions 1:2, 1:4, 1:7
[ALUSI:1:1/r21] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Praise appears in al-ḥamdu lillāh; worship is taught by its implied command, guidance-seeking, or the declaration of worship, while command entails prohibition. | mentions 1:2, 1:5, 1:6

[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Rahim is the grace through which ethical people compete in compassion and good works.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Rahman's first mercy brings everyone into existence and sustains them regardless of effort.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Rahim's further mercy grants the goals achieved by those who work.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Rahman gives absolute hope and prevents universal despair; without it humans would lack existence and essential natural gifts.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Rahim answers particular despair, sustains specific aims and effort, and rewards responsibility.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Under Rahman's universal grace believers and unbelievers, and this world and the next, are equal; Rahim's grace sharply distinguishes them, as the two groups in 42:7 show. | mentions 42:7
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r16] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Thus the inherited formulations call God Rahman of this world and the next but Rahim of the next, or Rahman of believer and unbeliever but Rahim of the believer.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r17] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Şeyh Abduh | rejects | Abduh neglects the inherited distinction because he assumes the lexicon does not support it; Elmalılı says this is mistaken.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r18] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Lexically Rahman is a predominant attribute specific to God, without an active relation and suggestive of eternity and the beginning; Rahim has an active relation and continues without end.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r19] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Rahman's mercy is an essential attribute of willing good at the outset, while Rahim's is an active attribute of doing good at the end.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Every creature's original gifts and existence arise from Rahman's grace, received without anyone's earned choice.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r20] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Rahman and Rahim are not repeated merely for emphasis: each has its own foundational meaning and distinct mode of intensification.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r21] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Rahman is more emphatic in encompassing every creature, while Rahim is more emphatic in actual beneficence, which also operates through servants.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r22] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Bazı tefsirler | reports | Some commentaries associate Rahman's mercy with great blessings and Rahim's with the subtleties of blessings.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r23] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The grammatical pattern distinguishes them: Rahman's subject is restricted while its object is general; Rahim's subject is general while its object is restricted.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r24] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Together these attributes replace pessimism with boundless optimism, the spirit of faith; the first benefit received from the basmala is this hope, affirmed by 28:83. | mentions 28:83
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Primordial creation is compelled and bestowed: stones, trees, and humans have their kinds through this unchosen mercy.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | All realms and beings, from obedient and believing to rebellious and idolatrous, are immersed in Rahman's mercy and freed from fear in that respect.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | If this universal grace were all, distinctions between knowledge and ignorance, life and death, effort and idleness, obedience and disobedience, and faith and unbelief would disappear.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Without a further mercy enabling agency, people would be determinists and compelled beings, unable to act on what they know or desire.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | God's wisdom requires that He display His own will and create creatures who possess will, rather than make all action compulsory.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | God advances creatures according to good choices and grants enjoyment of mercy, while bad choices bring deprivation, pain, and punishment; this harmonizes their wills with His.
[ELMALILI:1:1#7/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Rahman is the instinctive grace seen in mother birds beating their wings over their young.
[ELMALILI:1:1#8/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The basmala has an apparent structure of one genitive relation, two adjectival relations, and an initial attachment; its hidden relation makes it a complete, concise statement.
[ELMALILI:1:1#8/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | This fronting makes the beginning exclusive to Allah's name, rejecting the pagan practice of starting with Lat or Uzza and expressing tawhid.
[ELMALILI:1:1#8/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Turkish word order

[ELMALILI:1:1#8/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | He proposes eight possible Turkish renderings, using both lamiyya and bayaniyya forms such as Allah's name with the two attributes or Allah, Rahman, Rahim as one name.
[ELMALILI:1:1#8/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Ism Allah may be read as a genitive meaning either Allah's name or the name Allah.
[ELMALILI:1:1#8/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | On the lamiyya reading the adjectives can be construed before or after the genitive; on the bayaniyya reading the whole epitheted name is cited as one name and then explains ism.
[ELMALILI:1:1#8/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The bayaniyya analysis treats the genitive inflection as distributed over three words to stress the divine proper name, a necessary inflection rather than ordinary narration grammar.
[ELMALILI:1:1#8/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Müfessirînin çoğu | prefers | Most commentators prefer the lamiyya construction because its parsing is explicit and the meanings of the names and attributes are directly intended.
[ELMALILI:1:1#8/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Bazıları | prefers | Some prefer the bayaniyya construction, citing Labid's line using ism al-salam; the Mevlid author also reflects it with Allah adı.
[ELMALILI:1:1#8/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The omitted verb is the action the speaker is about to undertake, such as reading, writing, eating, or beginning, and the opening ba attaches the name to it.
[ELMALILI:1:1#8/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The verb and subject are omitted to let anyone connect the basmala to any intended act; ba and the speaker's situation identify the ellipsis, as in Turkish formulas like devletle selâmetle.
[ELMALILI:1:1#8/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Although Arabic normally delays a complement, placing the ba phrase first gives emphasis and exclusivity; compared with 96:1, basmala foregrounds Allah's name rather than the act of reading. | mentions 96:1
[ELMALILI:1:1#9/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Combining Allah with Rahman and Rahim as one name foregrounds Allah but still fails to connect the act directly with mercy.
[ELMALILI:1:1#9/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | rejects | Elmalılı says Abduh's deputyship reading amounts to acting as God's representative and self-effacement, appropriate only to special stations such as prophethood, sainthood, rule, and authority.
[ELMALILI:1:1#9/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | rejects | That meaning cannot apply generally: saying one eats in God's name is improper, though saying one eats food God bestowed would be sound; worship is for God but not done as His deputy.
[ELMALILI:1:1#9/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Reports that the basmala is the key to every book and every important act imply a general meaning for lawful acts; one of the commentators' attachment or seeking-aid senses supplies it.
[ELMALILI:1:1#9/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Abduh's explanation is sound for the Quran's revelation, recitation, and writing because of the basmala's position at their beginnings, and it matters in special settings too.
[ELMALILI:1:1#9/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Removing the participle still leaves Allah's proper name insufficiently foregrounded and separates it from the mercy attributes; listing three names may imply three divine essences, though singular ismiyle helps avert that implication.
[ELMALILI:1:1#9/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The basmala's words, composition, rhetoric, sound, and even its sweet pattern of letters cannot be fully carried into Turkish, so it should be recited in Arabic and understood through explanation.
[ELMALILI:1:1#9/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | rejects | He rejects corrupting the tawhid key with a rendering like esirgeciyi bağışlayıcı tanrı adıyla.
[ELMALILI:1:1#9/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The basmala's interpretive pivot is ba, which connects Allah's name, the first source and ultimate object of existence and progress, to the intended act.
[ELMALILI:1:1#9/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Human acts are not their own complete cause: will is a moment in the stream of existence, and success depends on the outpouring between the First Cause and human will, first Rahmani and finally Rahimi.
[ELMALILI:1:1#9/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The basmala's ba makes this universal relation conscious; its secret is said to lie in the ba's dot, and Hâkânî's poem links the basmala's continuity to the existence of things.
[ELMALILI:1:1#9/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · E‘âzım-ı müfessirîn | reports | The great commentators say ba here means either attachment and accompaniment or seeking aid; the former makes the basmala circumstantial, the latter an indirect object.
[ELMALILI:1:1#9/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Şeyh Abduh | reports | Abduh says customary in the name of means acting for an authority, by its command and on its behalf; the Muslim's basmala can express beginning an act for Allah and by His command.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The basmala in 27:30 is plainly part of that verse and certainly Qurʾān by explicit, unanimously established transmission; surah-opening basmalas raise a separate question. | mentions 27:30
[ELMALILI:1:1/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | The Shāfiʿī argument concludes that even if the basmala is not a whole verse of al-Fātiḥa, it is part of a verse, making its recitation obligatory and audible in prayer.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Ahmed b. Hanbel | reports | Like al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal has two transmitted positions, reflecting uncertainty between the two hadith reports.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · İmam Mâlik | reports | Mālik holds that opening basmalas are neither part of al-Fātiḥa or other surahs nor a separate Qurʾānic portion; they are written for separation and blessing and are not recited in prayer.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · İmam Mâlik | reports | Mālik bases his view on the need for Qurʾānic status to be explicit and mutawātir at every locus and on the practice of Medina’s people.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | prefers | The sound Ḥanafī position reconciles the other arguments: each opening basmala is an independent Qurʾānic verse, revealed to separate surahs and for blessing, and belongs to none of them.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Because the basmala is independent rather than part of al-Fātiḥa, reciting it in every prayer is not obligatory like al-Fātiḥa, though beginning each recitation and important undertaking with it is sunnah.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r16] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Ḥanafīs say it at the start of each prayer unit’s recitation, not in the middle, and recite it silently even in audible prayers so it will not appear part of the surah.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r17] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Outwardly the basmala has four words, but in reality and legal reckoning it has seven because bāʾ and the two definite articles count as words, while bāʾ also implies a verb and its agent.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r18] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | In the basmala’s special orthography the alif of ism is omitted and the opening bāʾ is lengthened; frequent use explains this abbreviation, while the writing also hints at the force of connection.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r19] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Certain hadith allusions read the letters bāʾ, sīn, and mīm as signs of God’s splendor, radiance, and sovereignty.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Whether the basmala written before surahs is a verse within them, a verse-part, or an independent Qurʾānic unit is a scholarly issue tied to faith, prayer, and recitation.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r20] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The Qurʾānic wisdom concerns the relation of God to the world, especially people and their acts; the basmala’s bāʾ expresses this relation of divinity and servitude.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r21] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The basic meaning of bāʾ is attachment, with senses such as accompaniment, assistance, connection, and oath; commentators read it here as accompaniment or assistance, with an omitted verb meaning begin, read, or the like.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Saîd b. Cübeyr, Zührî, Atâ, İbn Mübârek | reports | These early authorities hold that every surah-opening basmala is one verse of that surah, yielding 113 such verses in the Qurʾān.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · İmam Şâfiî ve ashâbı | reports | In his later position al-Shāfiʿī and his followers adopt the view that each surah-opening basmala is a verse.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | On this view the basmala is al-Fātiḥa’s first verse, while anʿamta ʿalayhim is not a verse ending, so they recite the basmala aloud in prayer.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Their argument is that the early community wrote the basmalas in the muṣḥafs while preserving the Qurʾān’s purity and excluding even Āmīn.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · İbn Abbas | reports | A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says that omitting the basmala omits 114 verses from God’s Book.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Ebû Hüreyre | reports | A report from Abū Hurayra says the Prophet counted al-Fātiḥa as seven verses and named the basmala as its first.
[ELMALILI:1:1/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Ümmü Seleme | reports | A report from Umm Salama says the Prophet counted the basmala together with al-ḥamdu lillāh as one verse.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r1] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Al-Fatiha is Meccan and has seven verses; Muslims recite it at least seventeen times daily, more with voluntary prayers, and may repeat it without limit.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r10] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · auth
