or | holds | Beginning in God's name expresses the first major Islamic worldview principle, God's oneness and proper reverence; comprehensive mercy expresses the second and defines the bond between God and servants.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r2] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · رسول الله [ ص ] | reports | The Prophet says prayer is invalid without reciting the Opening of the Book; the report is in both Sahih collections.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r3] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | The short surah gathers core Islamic creed, worldview, feelings, and guidance, explaining its repetition in every rakʿa and why prayer without it is invalid.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r4] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | prefers | Against disagreement over the basmala's status, Quṭb prefers counting it as a verse of al-Fatiha, making the surah seven verses.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r5] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | reports | An unnamed view takes the seven oft-repeated verses in 15:87 to be al-Fatiha, seven verses repeated in prayer. | mentions 15:87
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r6] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Beginning in God's name is the etiquette revealed to the Prophet at the first revelation and accords with God as First, Last, Manifest, and Hidden. | mentions 96:1, 57:3
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r7] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Because God is the true existent from whom every existence and beginning derives, every beginning, movement, and direction should start in His name.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r8] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Rahman and Rahim together encompass every meaning and condition of mercy; God alone bears both, and alone may be called Rahman, though a servant may be called Rahim.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r9] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Quṭb leaves aside which mercy-name has broader scope and stresses that together they cover mercy in all its meanings, conditions, and domains.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:7/r2] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · رسول الله | reports | Abu Hurayra reports in Sahih Muslim that God calls al-Fatiha a prayer divided between Himself and His servant: praise, mercy, and glorification are the Lord's; worship and aid are shared; guidance and the servant's request belong to the servant, who receives what he asks.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r1] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Al-Fatiha has many circulating names, but reliable Sunnah establishes only Fātihat al-Kitāb, al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī, and Umm al-Qurʾān/Umm al-Kitāb; Ibn ʿĀshūr limits discussion to these.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r10] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | In Sūrat Fātiḥat al-Kitāb, general-to-specific annexation is acceptable when both terms are generic nouns and the broader term is shortened by adding the narrower one; convention makes it idiomatic.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r100] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Omitting the action makes the formula concise and reusable before any deed without altering Qur’anic wording; omitted elements differ from stable adverbs whose governors are never expressed.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r101] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The bāʾ means association or accompaniment, also including attachment; this is its commonest sense and offers a fuller blessing than construing it as an instrument. | mentions 23:20
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r102] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The noun ism denotes a word assigned to a particular concrete or abstract entity, whether an individual or a kind.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r103] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · أئمة البصرة | reports | Basran grammarians derive ism from sumūw, elevation, since names often denote things esteemed; its original form had a final weak wāw deleted for ease or frequent use.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r104] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The forms asmāʾ, asāmī, sumayy, and sammaytu support a weak final wāw; Ibn ʿĀshūr says these inflections make the Basran morphology stronger.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r105] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · أبو خالد القناني | reports | A rajaz line by Abū Khālid al-Qanānī uses suman for name; Ibn Yaʿīsh doubts it proves the form, while ʿAbd al-Ḥakīm appeals to its written ya.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r106] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | prefers | Ibn ʿĀshūr favors the Basran derivation on morphological evidence; spelling does not establish pronunciation, while the Kufan account has stronger semantic motivation.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r107] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · الكوفيون | reports | Kufan grammarians derive ism from wasm, mark, because a name is a sign; they say initial wāw was dropped and hamzat al-waṣl preserves the form.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r108] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | rejects | The Kufan counterargument that Basran forms arose through metathesis is unlikely: it violates the default and would not persist across inflections; morphology reveals original and altered letters.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r109] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · ابن حزم | rejects | Ibn Ḥazm calls both derivations false inventions and ism a non-derived word; Ibn ʿĀshūr condemns this as reckless and cites the instruction to ask learned people. | mentions 16:43
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r11] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | He also allows Sūrat Fātiḥat al-Kitāb as an annexation of a described noun to its adjective: a sura characterized as the opener of the Book.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r110] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Bismillah says in the name of God, not by God, because it marks the deed as monotheistic practice and associates it with God’s name rather than invoking His essence.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r111] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | In sacrifices and actions seeking blessing or aid, scripture uses the name of God and in the name of your Lord; the name accompanies the deed, while by God would imply appeal to divine power. | mentions 6:118, 6:119, 96:1
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r112] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Commands to glorify God’s name mean to say Glory be to God, whereas commands to glorify Him mean declaring His essence and attributes free of imperfection. | mentions 56:74, 76:26, 87:1
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r113] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | God’s name functions like a tribe’s identifying brand or an army’s recognized slogan, signaling affiliation with the one Lord.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r114] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The full basmala means: I read in a way accompanied by the blessing of this blessed name.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r115] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Arabic may use ism for the named thing itself, insert it redundantly to mean peace, or use it as a metonym for proving a referent exists. None explains the basmala. | mentions 13:33, 48:26
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r116] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ibn ʿĀshūr conjectures that the elongated bāʾ was first written in Solomon’s letter to mark its opening, then copied as a sign of a new discourse at sura beginnings. | mentions 27:30
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r117] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · البيضاوي | reports | Al-Bayḍāwī says the supplicant names God’s essence to show aid is sought from Him, then invokes al-Raḥmān for His favors and al-Raḥīm for further reasons discussed later.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r118] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · محمد عبده | reports | Muḥammad ʿAbduh proposes that the Islamic opening counters Christian formulas invoking Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: one God’s multiple names are attributes, not multiple beings; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it subtle if the premise is true.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r119] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ibn ʿĀshūr suspects the formula continues Abrahamic monotheist practice: Abraham invokes the Merciful and the compassionate, and Solomon opens his letter with the basmala, likely inheriting that prophetic tradition. | mentions 19:45, 19:47, 2:128, 27:30, 27:31, 22:78
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r12] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Annexing Fātiha to the Book is a true relation: here the Book means the rest of the Qur’an apart from this sura, like a preface belonging to a work.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r13] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · أبو سعيد الخدري | reports | Al-Bukhari’s Book of Medicine reports that Abu Saʿid al-Khudri used Umm al-Qurʾān in a cure for a stung person; the account includes a fuller story.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r14] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A sound hadith calls a prayer deficient when Umm al-Qurʾān is not recited.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r15] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Umm means the origin or source of a thing, which explains the title Umm al-Qurʾān.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r16] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | One explanation of Umm al-Qurʾān is that Fātiha begins the Qur’an and is therefore like a mother as origin and source of what follows.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r17] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | A second explanation is that Fātiha gathers the Qur’an’s three central aims: praise, commands and prohibitions, and promise and warning; the rest elaborates them. | mentions 1:2, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r18] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Commands and prohibitions guide people toward well-being in both abodes; knowing the divine Commander and hoping for reward while fearing punishment complete the rationale for the Qur’an’s central aims.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r19] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | A third explanation is that Fātiha compresses all Qur’anic theoretical knowledge and practical rulings, including creed, prophecy, admonition, stories, worship, transactions, ethics, and legal manners.
[IBNASHUR:1:1/r2] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The name Fātihat al-Kitāb is established in several hadith, including the Prophet’s rule that prayer is invalid without reciting it.
